articles.title: Fixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilation | Simon Tisdall
articles.body:
Humankind has fearfully and sometimes joyfully anticipated the end of the world ever since it began. The Bible’s Book of Revelation speaks of “end times”, a period of tribulation, war, famine, plague, floods and environmental catastrophe that may seem a less absurd prospect today than perhaps it once did. Islam, too, posits a fateful day of judgment or day of reckoning. Christian evangelicals believe that, in the final rapture, a chosen few – the righteous or the “elect” – will be saved while sinners burn. It’s a minority view. Matthew’s gospel predicts most people will defy, ignore or ridicule warnings of imminent Armageddon. Peter, another of Jesus’s disciples, agreed: “In the last days, scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires.” Yet such worldly scepticism does not mean a universal cataclysm is less likely. It may make it more probable.
Donald Trump’s blanket denials of the dangers ostensibly posed by artificial intelligence, whose uncontrolled development is seen by some as the latest harbinger of apocalypse, could be interpreted as fulfilling Peter’s prophecy. This US president, the nearest thing the world has to a one-man doomsday machine, is a great one for scoffing and evil desires. In Robert Harris’s 2019 novel, The Second Sleep, a worried scientist lists half a dozen ways the world might end. They include devastating climate change, pandemic disease, a giant asteroid collision with Earth, or some other overwhelming calamity. Few heed the fictional scientist’s fears. In the event, what destroys him and almost everybody else is a disturbingly plausible cyber crash – a global digital and internet meltdown.
While arguments rage over whether large language models will acquire consciousness and moral agency – and the power to delete humanity – existential AI threats remain, as of now, open to mitigation. In sharp contrast, extraordinary complacency surrounds the most pressing, avoidable and proven human-made threat to life on Earth. It is as if the world has been seized by collective deafness and by a blind refusal to see what’s staring it in the face. This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating, global proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing real-time “end times” closer to home by the day. The question increasingly is not “if” but “when” limited or full-scale nuclear warfare will erupt. Eighty-one years after Hiroshima, how much longer can our luck hold?
Alarm bells are ringing, if only people would listen. Desperate Vladimir Putin recently threatened to deploy Russia’s entire nuclear arsenal, comprising about 4,400 warheads, against Nato countries if they activated a supposed plan to invade the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad. He offered no evidence for his claim, and it’s true that the frequent Kremlin nuclear sabre-rattling since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine went pear-shaped has diminished Moscow’s credibility. Yet that in itself is destabilising. To work, nuclear deterrence relies on an adversary believing the threat is real. Disbelief invites miscalculation. At the same time, Putin’s inability to halt Ukraine’s conventional drone and missile attacks deep inside Russia may be edging him closer to pressing the nuclear button, possibly in the form of low-yield tactical or “battlefield” nukes.
Trump’s bottom-line justification for the illegal US-Israel war on Iran is his wilfully mendacious claim that Tehran was weeks away from obtaining the bomb. He claims to be protecting the world from nuclear war. Yet his reckless threat, issued at the UN, to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” implies a possible US nuclear attack. Trump’s hypocrisy is stunning. The US is upgrading its nuclear arsenal of 3,700 warheads and may resume nuclear tests. It unreservedly supports Israel’s hidden nuclear weapons programme. And Trump is pursuing a lucrative deal with Saudi Arabia, another bitter foe of Iran, to provide civilian nuclear technology that he knows could be repurposed to make weapons. That has prompted regional countries such as Turkey and Egypt to consider going nuclear.
Similarly perilous trends are evident across Asia. North Korea’s great panjandrum, Kim Jong-un, has succeeded in gaining de facto international acceptance of his country’s status as a nuclear weapons state. South Korea said in August that Pyongyang now possesses up to 120 warheads – which Kim brandishes to intimidate neighbours. All but discarded are the twin principles that underpinned the west’s postwar Korea policy: reunification and denuclearisation. Heedless of first-term humiliations, Trump is again seeking a summit with Kim, whom he bizarrely terms a friend. “As long as I’m around, he [Kim] is going to be fine,” he boasted. Japan and South Korea don’t share his confidence. Both debate acquiring nuclear weapons in self-defence. Meanwhile, China’s president, Xi Jinping, having again bamboozled a fawning Trump at their Washington summit, is reportedly building nukes like there’s no tomorrow – which, at this rate, there may not be.
Addressing the UN general assembly, secretary-general António Guterres warned the world has reached “the most dangerous nuclear moment” since 1989. Global military spending reached nearly $3tn last year, while AI is increasing uncertainty over nuclear command-and-control, the UN was told. Annual spending on nukes is up by 20%. In a new paper published by the non-partisan Arms Control Association (ACA), Daryl Kimball, the head of the ACA in Washington, bemoaned the absence of high-level disarmament talks between the main nuclear powers and the lapsing of strategic arms limitation treaties. “The nuclear sword of Damocles still hangs over all of us. The threat has become more complex, and in the absence of new arms-control breakthroughs, we are headed for an unprecedented three-way buildup of Chinese, Russian, and US nuclear forces,” Kimball warned.
The fragmentation of the rules-based international order provides aggravating context. Trump-era blasphemies – that might makes right, that international law and the non-proliferation treaty’s binding obligation to disarm can be ignored, and that the UN charter and human rights norms don’t apply to authoritarian “strongman” leaders – all grease the slide into nuclear anarchy. Unresolved forever wars in Palestine, Iran, Ukraine, Myanmar, Yemen and Sudan are base components of a third world war. Potentially earth-shattering, too, is the fast-developing contest for control of space, notably the race to build nuclear-powered lunar bases. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, under which more than 130 countries agreed the moon is no one’s property, is now routinely flouted by both governments and billionaires such as Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos. The weaponising of space by the US and others advances rapidly. Russia, for example, is reportedly developing an orbiting nuclear-armed anti-satellite weapon.
If the human race really is determined to bring the heavens crashing down in a mad dash for eschatological self-destruction, this is the surest, quickest way to go about it. More surprising than the irresponsible behaviour of politicians is the deafening public silence, the absence of large-scale protest in much of the world, the complacency, bordering on indifference, that accompanies this global march to oblivion. If and when a final reckoning comes, individuals who stayed silent will be complicit in their own undoing. Hiroshima is not a shrine. It’s the future.
- Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

articles.title: European Leaders Back Zelenskyy After Trump's Diesel Deal; Russia, Ukraine Continue To Trade Strikes
articles.body:
European leaders have reaffirmed their support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy following US President Donald Trump's decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports and his subsequent call for a leadership change in Kyiv, as Russia and Ukraine continued to exchange strikes.
"This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas wrote on X on October 10, condemning the diesel agreement and warning it would increase Moscow's war revenues.
She added that EU foreign ministers planned to approve new sanctions listings on October 12. Meanwhile, some of the bloc's biggest member states, including Germany, confirmed they would maintain their strict sanctions regime despite Washington's shift.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo described Trump's agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin as a "terrible disappointment," while Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson noted that the upcoming EU package would target 1,600 entities within Russia's military-industrial complex.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Trump announced a deal to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports following their phone call on October 9, with the US Treasury authorizing certain transactions through April 7, 2027.
Zelenskyy characterized Washington's policy reversal as a sign of US "weakness" and a "gift" to Putin, arguing that renewed Russian energy revenues would encourage Moscow to prolong its long-running invasion, now in its 56th month.
Trump later said that Ukraine should "get a new leader," blaming Zelenskyy for the lack of a deal to end Russia's war against his country and demanding Kyiv "damn well stop" hitting Russian oil refineries amid a global energy shortage largely caused by the US war with Iran.
The US president made ending Russia's war on Ukraine war a priority when he began his current term in January 2025, but Kyiv and Moscow remain far apart in their negotiating positions, with the Kremlin offering no concessions and repeatedly rejecting calls for a full cease-fire.
In addition, Russia has been pounding Ukraine's energy and civilian infrastructure, leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid freezing temperatures in winter. Since this year, however, Kyiv has increasingly responded with its own campaign.
Ukrainian long-range strikes have been targeting Russian military and energy facilities in an effort to curb revenues for the invasion and bring the war home to Russian civilians by causing fuel shortages.
Zelenskyy said on October 11, Ukraine was prepared to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow reciprocated.
"Ukraine will be ready to stop attacks on Russian refineries if Russia stops attacking our energy infrastructure. Any de-escalation steps must be mutual and with real guarantees," he wrote on Telegram.
Moscow Continues Daily Strikes, Kyiv Targets Yandex
Zelenskyy also said Russia had launched around 1,450 aerial bombs, 75 missiles, and more than 1,640 attack drones against Ukraine over the preceding week.
Hours after Russian strikes on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhya killed at least 20 people, including three children, and disrupted electricity and water supplies in Kyiv, Moscow continued to launch attacks overnight into October 11.
In Slovyansk, in the eastern Donetsk region, a Russian air strike damaged two apartment buildings, destroying an entire entrance section of a five-story block. At least four people were reported injured, while rescuers worked to free residents trapped in apartments amid fears that others remain trapped under the rubble, according to RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service.
In the southeastern city of Dnipro, Russian drones damaged an apartment building and set fire to warehouses and vehicles, injuring four people, including two eight-year-old girls, according to regional authorities.
In the southern port city of Odesa, an attack late on October 10 damaged a two-story residential building, destroying three apartments and setting the roof ablaze.
Ukraine has meanwhile continued its retaliatory strikes on Russian technology infrastructure, targeting facilities operated by Yandex, the country's leading Internet search and technology company.
A drone strike on October 11 forced the complete shutdown of a Yandex data center in Russia's Vladimir region.
Yandex said the facility had ceased operations and that some of its services were unavailable as a result. It reported no casualties. According to Russian reports, Yandex's taxi and food delivery services were disrupted in Moscow following the drone attacks.
Often described as the Russian Google, Yandex operates widely used search, mapping, and other digital services, and is a major developer of artificial intelligence. Its data centers support both consumer services and computing infrastructure used to develop AI models, making their disruption potentially significant for Russia's technology sector.
The latest attack followed a strike on Yandex's Sasovo facility in the Ryazan region overnight on October 7-8, which reportedly disabled two of the company's three main AI-development supercomputers, and another on October 9 that knocked out part of its data center in Kaluga.
'Difficult For Ukraine,' UK Says
Amid the US pressure and almost daily Russian strikes, Zelenskyy sought to shore up European support in a series of calls on October 10 with French President Emmanuel Macron, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, discussing air defense and continued pressure on Moscow.
“The Russians must feel that they will have no capacity left to prolong the war,” Zelenskyy said after speaking with Macron.
He also confirmed that Finland would deliver specialized ammunition for Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets in the coming days to assist in intercepting Russian Shahed drones.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on October 10 that “the past 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine,” according to Downing Street, adding that the UK would continue strengthening sanctions on Russia independently.
Meanwhile, the US-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) warned in an assessment on October 9 that the unilateral easing of restrictions would benefit Russia's war effort without securing a comparable concession from Moscow.
In a follow-up assessment on October 10, the think tank noted that Putin utilized the call to blame Ukraine for stalled peace talks, citing alleged Ukrainian strikes on Russian election infrastructure during September's State Duma elections.
ISW said that this allegation was unsupported by evidence and that Putin's "unchanged war aims demonstrates the Kremlin’s continued unwillingness to accept any compromised peace proposals on any terms that fall short of fulfilling Russia’s maximalist demands of Ukraine’s complete capitulation."

articles.title: 'He better damn well stop' — Trump slams Zelensky for attacking Russian refineries, says Ukraine should get 'new president'
articles.body:
'He better damn well stop' — Trump slams Zelensky for attacking Russian refineries, says Ukraine should get 'new president'
Editor's Note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
U.S. President Donald Trump lashed out at President Volodymyr Zelensky on Oct. 10, demanding he halt attacks on Russian refineries and suggesting the Ukrainian people replace him if they want an end to the war.
The comments came in response to questions from reporters about his recent deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease sanctions on Moscow by opening up global markets to Russian diesel supplies.
When asked if such a deal would prolong Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine, Trump told reporters he sees the situation "differently."
"Zelensky could have settled this war many times, many many times, and he chooses not to," Trump claimed.
Trump then lambasted Zelensky for exacerbating the global diesel supply crisis, despite evidence that shows the U.S. war against Iran is the major culprit behind the current shortage.
"We said you could do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries, because that's a world problem that's caused," Trump said.
"And he wants to make problems for the world, he wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel. ... We have a world problem, and the problem is caused by the lack of refinereis for diesel fuel. So what does he do? He goes and hits the refineries."
read also
Trump made no mention of his war against Iran, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, or Russia's relentless attacks against Ukrainian energy infrastructure and civilian neighborhoods. Instead, he framed the failure of the U.S. peace push as a result of Zelensky's stubbornness.
"And he's not going to affect our farmers, he's not going to affect our ranchers, and he's not going to affect the rest of the world," Trump said. "So he better damn well stop."
When asked about the daily suffering of Ukrainians under Russia's intensifying attacks, Trump had nothing to say about accountability for Moscow — and one main suggestion for the people of Ukraine.
"You know what I suggest? I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal. Because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Trump said.
"I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."
Trump has previously called for elections in Ukraine, amplifying Kremlin propaganda narratives about Zelensky's lack of legitimacy — often shortly after meetings with Russian delegates.
The tactic of blaming Zelensky has also allowed Trump to sidestep questions about Washington's warming relations with Russia amid mass attacks on Ukrainian cities.
read also
Trump's diesel deal with Putin came as a shock to Ukrainian officials, who felt they had been invited to diplomatic talks with U.S. officials in Miami on Oct. 9-10 as part of "a trap."
Officials involved in the negotiations told the Kyiv Independent that they believed they would be discussing the terms of an energy ceasefire with Russia — one that would place equal demands on both sides.
Instead, the U.S. struck an economic deal with Moscow while pressuring Kyiv to halt refinery attacks, without any reciprocal demand for Russia to suspend strikes.
The deal seemed to be a way for Trump to dodge consequences — including skyrocketing gas prices and a steep drop in approval ratings — from his decision to wage war in Iran.
But Russian diesel may not provide relief at the pump or the polls, according to Seton Hall University Professor Margarita Balmaceda, an expert in the political economy of energy and associate at the Harvard Ukrainian Research Institute (HURI).
"As I see it, this deal has the potential to do much to help Russia — and to help Russia pursue its war against Ukraine — but not so much to help ease the diesel and gasoline crunch, the causes of which lie largely in the continued tensions around the Strait of Hormuz," Balmaceda said.
Zelensky has said repeatedly that Ukraine is ready to pause attacks against Russian energy infrastructure — as long as Russia agrees to the same terms. Thus far, Russia has shown no interest in de-escalating attacks.
Ukraine has long considered Russian oil refineries valid military targets, as Russian oil exports fund the Kremlin's war chest and refineries produce fuel for the armed forces. According to the Defense Ministry, Ukrainian attacks have disabled over 51% of Russia's total refining capacity.
When Trump announced the deal on Oct. 9, Zelensky said it was "a weak decision by our strong partners" that would allow Putin to prolong the war against Ukraine.
The next day, Kyiv was greeted by Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered strike drones in yet another daytime attack against the city's power grid. Residents were left without power and water.
"The consequences of allowing Russia to sell oil products were most clearly felt in Kyiv today, when, following numerous attacks with jet-powered Shahed drones against energy facilities, a ballistic missile attack began as well," Zelensky said in a message published on Telegram following the attack.
The money Russia earns from diesel exports will fund further destruction in Ukraine, the president warned.
"Every additional billion dollars Russia manages to earn from exports will be spent precisely on this: finding and importing critical components, equipment for weapons production, upgrading Shahed drones, manufacturing missiles, and recruiting additional mercenaries for the front," he said.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia targeted a residential building, killing 20 civilians, including three children.

articles.title: Russian air strike on Kharkiv kills at least 1, injures 8
articles.body:
Rescuers going through rubble to search for victims of a Russian air attack on Kharkiv, Oct. 11, 2026 (Head of Kharkiv military administration Oleh Syniebuhov / Telegram)
Russia attacked Ukraine's second-largest city of Kharkiv on Oct. 11, killing one and injuring at least eight others, the head of the region's military administration said.
Two guided air bombs struck the Nemyshlyanskyi district of Kharkiv, Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Oblast military administration, posted on Telegram.
Rescuers are still going through the damage, but Syniebuhov said that a 36-year-old woman was killed in the attack.
An additional eight people have been reported as injured, among which a seven-year-old boy.
"All those injured are receiving highly specialised medical care," Syniebuhov said.
A man wearing badges after a Russian air attack on Kharkiv, Oct. 11, 2026 (Head of Kharkiv military administration Oleh Syniebuhov / Telegram)
After an attack earlier the same day on the city of Sloviansk, President Volodymyr Zelensky said "this week alone, the Russians have launched around 1,450 aerial bombs, 75 missiles of various types and over 1,640 attack drones, around 60% of which are jet-powered."
"Today we will continue to coordinate with our partners — there will be discussions with European leaders," Zelensky added, with a view to securing air defense systems and ammunition for combat aircraft.
Chris Powers is the Brussels Correspondent with the Kyiv Independent. He reports on EU news and policy developments relevant to Ukraine, bridging the gap between Brussels and Kyiv. He was formerly the Defense and Tech Editor at the EU media outlet Euractiv. Chris holds a BA in History from the University of Cambridge and an MA in European Studies from the College of Europe.
A press release from the defense ministry notes that its procurement agency has contracted for 5.5 times as many drones as in the same period of 2025, and that the volume of deliveries has increased by almost 3.7 times.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said "this week alone, the Russians have launched around 1,450 aerial bombs, 75 missiles of various types and over 1,640 attack drones, around 60% of which are jet-powered."
"These things are important now to put clearly on the record and, I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia," media reports Burnham saying.
In this interview, the Kyiv Independent’s Kateryna Hodunova speaks with Pavlo Kazarin, a Ukrainian journalist, publicist and serviceman, about Ukraine’s mobilization crisis, draft evasion, soldiers going absent without leave (AWOL), and the growing divide between those serving and those remaining in civilian life.
"The real cause of the war in Europe is Russia, and Russia alone. It is already possible today to halt the attacks on our energy sector, but Putin does not want to do so," Zelensky said.
Three children were among those killed by a Russian airstrike in the early hours of Oct. 10. Some victims were trapped for hours beneath the rubble as rescuers searched for survivors.
On Oct. 10, Yandex updated its user agreement to include drone and missile attacks among circumstances of force majeure that could exempt the company from contractual obligations.
Ukraine continues to quietly coordinate evacuations from temporarily Russian-occupied territories, where residents’ quality of life is severely diminished, particularly those who are elderly, disabled or require medical treatment.
The latest attacks in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast follow several days of deadly Russian strikes across Ukraine, hitting residential buildings and critical civilian infrastructure, killing civilians, disrupting power and water supplies, and damaging bridges and other infrastructure.

articles.title: Trump says Ukraine needs a new president who will agree to end the war
articles.body:
Trump calls on Ukraine to replace Zelenskyy amid tensions over Russia deal
US president suggests Zelenskyy has not done enough to end war as tensions rise over a diesel supply deal with Russia.
United States President Donald Trump has called on Ukraine to replace Volodymyr Zelenskyy, lashing out at the Ukrainian leader for strikes on Russian oil refineries that have contributed to high global diesel prices.
The criticism on Saturday came as tensions between the US and Ukraine have risen after Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Russia.
The steep rise in global fuel prices, which followed the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran, has become a political liability for Trump’s Republican Party as it heads into next month’s midterm elections, in which opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress.
“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters at the White House, saying Zelenskyy had hurt global diesel supplies with strikes on Russian refineries.
“He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world,” Trump said.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, however, defended Zelenskyy in a post on X.
“He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide,” Sybiha wrote. “Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support.”
Trump, who has been urging Zelenskyy to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure for weeks, struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to reduce high fuel prices.
The deal marked a stunning reversal of years of Washington’s pressure on Russia over its full scale invasion of Ukraine.
Trump has sought to blame record-high US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran.
Mass casualty attacks
The US-Russia deal drew a furious reaction from Zelenskyy, who said it had emboldened Moscow. He linked the agreement with a Russian attack on Saturday that killed 20 people, including three children, in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia.
“Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said.
“Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities,” he said. “Different signals are needed.”
The Zaporizhzhia assault was the third mass-casualty attack on Ukraine in four days.
Nearly 80 civilians were killed in Russian strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, including at least 30 killed by a bomb in the eastern garrison city of Kramatorsk and 22 others by a missile in the town of Pryluky, about 130km (80 miles) east of Kyiv.
Trump’s announcement about the diesel deal was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month aimed at clamping down on Moscow’s oil and gas revenues that fuel the war against Ukraine.
He announced the deal amid talks between Ukrainian and European officials with US negotiators in Miami, Florida, on Friday, which were aimed at developing a common proposal for ending the war, according to the Reuters news agency.
In his remarks at the White House, Trump criticised Zelenskyy over the lack of a peace deal while demanding an end to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities.
“I said to him, ‘Do what you want. Don’t hit refineries. There’s plenty of targets. Don’t hit refineries.’ And he went out and he hit,” Trump said. “He better damn well stop.”
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason, he never does,” Trump added.
The diesel deal was criticised by US lawmakers, including one of Trump’s fellow Republicans, Representative Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions that Congress had recently passed, not roll them back.
Ukraine’s European allies have also expressed dismay at the Russian deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions.
United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke with Zelenskyy on Saturday and said London would strengthen its sanctions on Russia, according to a Downing Street spokesperson.
Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said every additional $1bn Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries and Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was coordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive and he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up Ukraine’s air defences.
He went on to warn of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days.
Zelenskyy also said he had discussed the developments with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Ukraine would receive ammunition in the coming days for the F-16 fighter jets used to intercept Russia’s Shahed drones.

articles.title: US military has lost 81 aircraft in Iran war according to Congressional report
articles.body:
Eighty-one aircraft in the US military have been destroyed or damaged during the war with Iran, a congressional Research Service report released this week said.
Among the aircraft lost are some of the most advanced weapons in the US arsenal, including the F-35A fighter jet and the E-3 Sentry, which has four jet engines and a radar dome on its fuselage used to track targets and manage airspace during engagements.
MQ-9 Reaper drones accounted for more than half of the losses found in the report. Reaper drones are used in the Iran war for gathering intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance.
The total cost of the aircraft lost since February is between $1.9 billion and $3.3 billion, according to the report, which cited figures from the congressional Budget Office.
US Central Command estimated that the ongoing war with Iran has cost the US roughly $44 billion total in September. However, that number does not include damage to infrastructure at US bases in the Middle East, according to reporting from the Washington Post.
CNN reported that some of the aircraft may have returned to service after being damaged, including eight F-15 Strike Eagle fighter jets after they were damaged during an Iranian strike on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on the night of September 8.
The report examined statements and figures from the Department of Defense; its inspector general; CENTCOM; and external media reports reviewed by the CRS.
Senators accuse Pentagon of withholding information
Bipartisan criticism of the Pentagon has mounted over defense officials' unwillingness to be transparent with Congress about the cost of the Iran war and the Trump administration’s National Defense Strategy.
Following a meeting with Defense Undersecretary Elbridge Colby and the Senate Armed Services Committee, Senator Jacky Rose of Nevada said Colby “was not forthcoming” and “did not really address our concerns or issues.”
In a separate instance this week, US Senator Chris Murphy said on Tuesday that the US Defense Department denied him access to a key military base in Qatar during a visit to the Middle East. He described it as part of a US government effort to conceal the impact of the Iran war.
"This trip confirmed for me that there is an active, unprecedented, unconstitutional effort underway to hide the costs of this war and the implications of this war from Congress and the American people," Murphy told a group of journalists in Riyadh, the second stop on his trip.
Analysts cited by CNN said actions in the Middle East, including the Iran war and conflicts with Iran’s proxies, have taken a toll on the MQ-9 Reaper drones. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach told Congress that the MQ-9 was the “most valuable player” in the war with Iran
The US military is believed to have roughly 135 MQ-9 drones in its arsenal, the Air Force Times reported in May, 2026.
The military lost 45 of the drones in the Middle East this year alone, in what the Atlantic Council describes as losses at an “alarming rate.”
The US military has not experienced loss of aircraft at such a rate since Operation Desert Storm in 1991.

articles.title: Exclusive: 'It felt like a trap,' how Ukraine was blindsided by Trump's Putin pivot
articles.body:
Exclusive: 'It felt like a trap.' How Ukraine was blindsided by Trump's Putin pivot
U.S. President Donald Trump and Russia's President Vladimir Putin arrive for a press conference at Joint Base Elmendorf- Richardson, Aug. 15, 2025, in Anchorage, Alaska. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)
When U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner told Ukraine's delegation on Oct. 9 that President Donald Trump was preparing to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, the Ukrainians struggled to believe what they were hearing.
The delegation had traveled to the United States to discuss a possible energy ceasefire with Russia. Instead, Kyiv's negotiators found themselves blindsided by a decision they feared would hand Moscow fresh revenue to finance its war against Ukraine while undermining Kyiv's leverage in negotiations.
"It was not just our delegation there, but a European one as well," one senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent. "It's just that everyone was sitting there like fools."
Washington was asking Ukraine to restrain its attacks on Russian energy while giving Moscow an economic reprieve — all as Trump faced consequences from the war against Iran.
"And yet he's the one who got everyone dragged into a war in Iran — a war with no way out — and is selling us out… Just to get a temporary, deceptive reprieve a few weeks before the election," the official said.
The Kyiv Independent spoke with several Ukrainian officials involved in or close to the negotiations. All of them were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
For Ukraine, the key question was why Kyiv should surrender a major means of pressuring Moscow if Russia faced no obligation to stop attacking Ukraine's energy system.
A deal Kyiv never saw coming
President Volodymyr Zelensky had sent a Ukrainian delegation to the United States for talks scheduled for Oct. 9-10. The agenda included a possible energy ceasefire with Moscow and a separate arrangement to halt attacks in the Black Sea.
Instead, the talks were derailed after Trump announced that Russia would supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Kyiv had not been informed of the decision in advance. Although Zelensky publicly acknowledged that Washington was considering a deal with Moscow, Ukrainian officials said they had not known the details before the announcement that evening.
For the delegation, the revelation raised questions about whether Washington had already negotiated terms with Moscow while Ukrainian and European officials were still trying to establish the parameters of an energy truce.
"It felt like a trap," the senior Ukrainian official said.
"To be honest, everyone was shocked as f*ck."
The timing of the U.S. decision only deepened the suspicion.
Following Trump's direction, the U.S. Treasury Department announced that its Office of Foreign Assets Control was "immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
One Ukrainian official pointed to April 7, the date on which the waiver was set to expire, as evidence that Washington had planned the measure around a specific timetable.
"They lifted the sanctions until April 7... So they were preparing this for Oct. 7. It's a birthday present for Putin. They're counting the six months," the official said.
Trump's demand to stop Ukraine's strikes
The dispute had been building for weeks.
Trump had previously pressed Zelensky to stop Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities, arguing that Kyiv should stop disrupting Russia's fuel production.
"Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump told Zelensky on Sept. 13.
Kyiv rejected the premise that Ukraine should halt its strikes unilaterally. Ukrainian officials said Zelensky had repeatedly made clear that any energy ceasefire would have to apply to both sides, with Russia also stopping its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
That distinction is central to Kyiv. Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, terminals, and other energy facilities aim to disrupt a major source of funding for Moscow's war effort. Russia, meanwhile, has systematically targeted Ukrainian power plants and substations, seeking to deprive civilians of electricity and heating.
A ceasefire that stopped only Ukrainian attacks would therefore leave Russia's campaign against Ukraine's energy system intact while protecting infrastructure that helps sustain the Russian war machine.
Yet, Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent that U.S. negotiators presented the issue differently during the talks, framing Zelensky as responsible for the impasse because he had refused to halt attacks on Russian refineries.
The Ukrainians were also told that Washington would cut off intelligence sharing that has helped Kyiv identify and strike targets inside Russia, one person present at the talks told the Kyiv Independent.
U.S. intelligence has played an important role in Ukrainian attacks, and restricting access to it would weaken Kyiv's ability to conduct strikes deep inside Russian territory.
One senior Ukrainian official involved in the talks responded with bitter humor.
"I hope the Americans don't give them Patriot (air defense systems) to protect their oil refineries," the official said.
The remark, however, captured a broader fear in Kyiv.
Washington already ended up helping Moscow shield the infrastructure that finances its war while pressuring Ukraine to surrender a means of striking back.
Another senior Ukrainian official said Ukraine had not agreed to stop attacking Russian refineries and would not commit to doing so without reciprocal Russian action.
For Kyiv, the principle remained unchanged. An energy truce could work only if both countries accepted the same restrictions.
"It was just f**king stupid to bury the idea of an energy truce with that move," one official said, suggesting that Washington was trying to strip Ukraine of its greatest source of leverage in the negotiations.
The war continues on both sides
Events on the ground showed how little the announcement had changed.
Just hours after Trump's announcement, Ukrainian drones struck an oil loading terminal in Russia's Rostov-on-Don. The terminal handles petroleum products for export and supplies fuel to Russia's military.
Russia, meanwhile, launched a drone attack followed by a missile strike on Kyiv on Oct. 10, also targeting Ukrainian energy facilities.
Neither side had agreed to stop striking energy infrastructure, and the U.S. announcement had done little to bridge the gap between their positions.
Zelensky addressed the decision in a voice message to reporters late on Oct. 9, warning that allowing Russia to export diesel would just give Moscow additional revenue to sustain its war.
"This only fuels Putin and enables him to wage more war," Zelensky said. "And at the moment when we are talking about peace, the U.S. is allowing Russia to export diesel."
He also questioned the purpose of sending a Ukrainian delegation to negotiations under those circumstances.
"I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. This is certainly not honest, and it is certainly not how partners should act," Zelensky said, calling the decision "a weak decision by our strong partners."
Ukraine was being asked to make concessions on the battlefield even as Moscow continued to attack its cities and energy infrastructure.
For one senior Ukrainian official, the explanation for Washington's move was straightforward: Trump was trying to deflect blame for the consequences of his own foreign policy.
"Clearly, Trump doesn't want to admit that it was his war against Iran that caused so many problems for Americans," the official said.

Russia’s Ballistic Attack on Kyiv Shows the Real Cost of Trump-Putin Diesel Deal, Zelenskyy Says
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the Trump-Putin diesel deal after Russia launched a daytime ballistic missile attack on Kyiv on October 10, warning that allowing Moscow to earn more from petroleum exports would fuel further Russian attacks on Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In a statement on October 10, Zelenskyy said Russian forces launched ballistic missiles at Kyiv following repeated attacks by jet-powered Shahed drones against Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Ukrainian air defenses managed to intercept some of the incoming missiles.
“What allowing Russia to sell petroleum products means was heard most clearly in Kyiv today,” Zelenskyy said, warning that Moscow intends to continue its war, terrorize civilians, and destroy infrastructure.
According to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko on October 10, a Russian missile struck a restaurant building in the capital’s Obolonskyi district, sparking a fire and injuring four people, one of whom was in serious condition.
At another location in the same district, missile debris fell into the courtyard of a residential building.
Ukraine’s Air Force had warned of multiple missiles heading toward Kyiv shortly before explosions rocked the capital. Local reports described three to four explosions during the attack, while Ukrainian air defenses engaged incoming threats.
Zelenskyy warned that additional Russian oil revenues would directly finance Moscow’s military operations.
“Every additional billion dollars they can earn from exports will be spent precisely on this,” he said, referring to the purchase of critical components, weapons-production equipment, upgraded Shahed drones, missiles, and additional troops.
“Russia’s choice is war,” Zelenskyy declared, adding that Moscow would only be prepared to stop fighting once its ability to prolong the invasion was reduced. He called for stronger action from Washington, Europe, and other international partners to support Ukraine and restrict Russia’s ability to wage war.
The remarks followed Trump’s October 9 announcement of a diesel supply agreement with Putin, under which Russia would deliver petroleum products to the United States and global markets.
Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, with additional shipments planned afterward. The US Treasury also issued a temporary license easing sanctions on Russian diesel exports.

articles.title: Ukraine Ready to Halt Refinery Strikes for Energy Truce, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Oct. 11, that Ukraine is prepared to halt long-range strikes against Russian oil refineries if Russia ceases attacks against Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
In a statement on Facebook reviewing weekly Russian aerial bombardments, Zelensky said halting attacks on power and utility networks is achievable immediately, but asserted that Moscow remains unwilling to de-escalate.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It is feasible to stop strikes on energy today, but [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not want to do this,” Zelensky stated.
“Ukraine will be ready to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries if Russia ceases strikes against our energy infrastructure. Any de-escalation steps must be mutual and with real guarantees.”
Zelensky emphasized that Russia bears sole responsibility for the war in Europe, noting that diplomatic engagements with European leaders are scheduled throughout Sunday to coordinate additional defense packages, primarily surface-to-air defense systems and ammunition for combat aviation.
Weekly strike toll and escalating civilian casualties
Zelensky highlighted the operational scale of Russian standoff strikes over the preceding seven days, reporting that Russian forces launched approximately 1,450 guided aerial bombs (KABs), 75 missiles of various types, and more than 1,640 strike drones against Ukrainian territory.
According to the president, roughly 60 percent of the unmanned aerial vehicles deployed during the weekly barrages were high-speed, turbojet-powered variants engineered to challenge low-altitude air defense interception networks.
Zaporizhzhia Bombing Death Toll Reaches 20 as Rescue Ends
The weekly barrage produced casualties and structural destruction across multiple provinces.
Zelensky confirmed that search and rescue operations in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia concluded on Sunday morning following a Russian guided bomb strike on a residential apartment building, with the final death toll rising to 23, including four children.
In the Kharkiv region, Russian munitions struck a healthcare facility on Saturday, while overnight attacks engaged municipal civilian infrastructure, residential housing, and regional utility grids.
“I am grateful to all our emergency services, who are always alongside our people and resolving consequences after Russian strikes,” Zelensky said.
Petrochemical targeting and the energy armistice framework
Zelensky’s proposal for a reciprocal cessation of energy attacks comes amid an intensified Ukrainian interdiction campaign directed against downstream petrochemical logistics across the Russian Federation.
Overnight into Saturday, Oct. 10, Ukrainian Defense Forces conducted a repeat strike against the Samara linear production and dispatching station (LVDS) near Prosvet in Russia’s Samara region.
The critical petrochemical junction blends petroleum streams to formulate standardized export-grade Urals crude while supplying refined petroleum products to the Russian armed forces.
The attack followed an earlier precision strike on Oct. 7 that destroyed four large-capacity RVS-50000 crude oil storage reservoirs at the facility.
The interdiction of refining and transshipment nodes forms part of a wider asymmetric campaign that has also engaged deep logistical facilities, including the Yug Rusi oil terminal in Rostov-on-Don and multiple corporate data centers in Vladimir, Kaluga, and Ryazan regions.
The issue of refinery strikes has emerged as a central point of friction between Kyiv and Washington.
US officials have urged Ukraine to unilaterally halt drone strikes on Russian refining capacity to mitigate pressure on international fuel benchmarks, a request that coincided with a controversial bilateral agreement between US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin to permit Russian diesel exports onto global markets.
Ukrainian officials have consistently rejected calls for unilateral restraint, arguing that degrading Russian refining infrastructure directly restricts fuel supplies to frontline Russian military units and diminishes state revenues supporting Moscow’s war effort.
Zelensky reiterated that a suspension of deep interdiction operations can occur only within the framework of an enforceable, bilateral agreement that shields Ukraine’s domestic power and heating grid ahead of the winter season.
