articles.title: Ukraine’s worst diplomatic nightmare just got closer
articles.body:
Ukraine’s worst diplomatic nightmare just got closer
On the evening of October 9, the presidents of the United States and Russia spoke by phone. The announcement that followed was straightforward: Russia would sell the US 1.8 million metric tons of diesel over the next three months, followed by a million tons a month, and the US would issue temporary licenses authorizing the shipments.
The news drew a furious, bordering on hysterical, response from Kiev and stunned silence from Europe.
Let’s look at why this deal matters, what it has to do with Ukraine, and what might come next.
The tug-of-war championship
Ever since US President Donald Trump returned to office, the central aim of Russian diplomacy has been to separate relations with the US from the Ukraine issue. The White House is open to the idea, too: The US needs Russia as a counterweight to China, and there are substantial economic opportunities. But as we explored in an earlier piece, until recently, neither side managed to pull it off.
Ukraine and its supporters in Europe and the US, meanwhile, have pursued the opposite goal: keeping US-Russia relations tied to the Ukraine conflict.
In February and March 2025, Trump relieved America of responsibility for Ukraine’s fate and handed the job of financing it squarely to Europe. The US retained just three commitments: the relatively modest military supply programs already approved under former President Joe Biden, intelligence sharing, and weapons sales for cash, with Ukraine waiting in line like any other customer.
This maneuver cemented a status quo that neither Europe and Ukraine on one side nor Russia on the other would allow to change, with their respective allies in the US also weighing in. Everyone tried to bring Trump over to their side on Ukraine. Nobody succeeded.
This is why the understandings reached in Anchorage went nowhere: Ukraine’s supporters torpedoed them. It is also why those supporters failed to use Trump to escalate the conflict. Russia prevented deliveries of Tomahawk missiles, the expansion of Starlink coverage over Russian territory, and so on.
Despite the apparent stalemate, Russian officials kept talking to Witkoff and Kushner. The aim was to maintain a channel to Trump and deny Ukraine’s supporters an opening to drag the US back into the war on their side or steer him back onto Biden’s course.
This is why Russian officials at every level distinguish between US and European actions, often explicitly contrasting the two.
A few numbers on oil
Russia is one of the world’s largest diesel exporters, supplying just under 40 million metric tons to the global market in 2025. On July 8, 2026, Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries prompted a temporary ban on diesel and gasoline exports.
Since then, Russia’s refining situation has improved considerably. Gasoline remains in short supply, but a domestic diesel surplus has emerged, and the export ban has begun to loosen in practice. According to Reuters, diesel deliveries to Central Asian countries were already up 19% in September.
Rising diesel production was only part of the story. The end of the harvest season also reduced demand. And as the seasons change, Russia switches to winter-grade fuel, traditionally selling off its remaining summer-grade stocks to countries with warmer climates.
One way or another, seaborne diesel exports were heading toward a restart. Trump had also raised that possibility, publicly linking it to Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries.
The Krivoy Rog school of diplomacy
Back to geopolitics. Until yesterday, Russia had been unable to separate its relationship with the US from the Ukraine issue. Even the war with Iran failed to do the trick, despite keeping oil and petroleum product shipments from the Persian Gulf blocked for more than six months.
Help came from an unexpected quarter. Hoping to bring US diesel prices down at least a little before the congressional elections, Trump asked Zelensky to stop attacking Russian refineries.
Zelensky responded by demanding a sweeping energy truce. We’ll stop hitting refineries, he effectively said, if Russia stops attacking our energy infrastructure and blockading our ports. And you, Trump, have to supply us with missiles for our Patriot systems, and so on.
Getting nowhere with Zelensky, Trump struck a deal directly with Russian President Vladimir Putin, who offered to supply diesel in exchange for a suspension of sanctions, without any preconditions.
The transaction itself is not particularly consequential. Yes, it could cool speculative trading ahead of the elections and push prices down somewhat. But the 1.8 million metric tons due to arrive over three months will cover just three or four days of American consumption.
For Russia, the US is an ordinary customer in purely commercial terms. Moscow will make some money selling to America, but it could just as easily have sold these volumes elsewhere. Petroleum products are in short supply worldwide, while Russia has a diesel surplus.
Yet the deal gave both sides what they had been seeking since February 2025: a bilateral relationship detached from Ukraine. So far, that applies to just one specific issue, but getting started is the hard part. Zelensky tried to twist Trump’s arm, pushing him to make Putin stop bombing Kiev, and overplayed his hand. Now Kiev can be bombed relentlessly, and Trump has no reason to care. He got what he wanted.
This does not mean sanctions are finished or that the two powers are entering an era of warm friendship. Oil sanctions are probably here to stay, and as soon as global market conditions change, Washington will turn them back up to full blast. But the sanctions wall can now be taken apart brick by brick, restoring ties wherever both sides stand to gain: launching new energy projects in the Arctic, for example, jointly taking over the surviving Nord Stream 2 pipeline, or resolving the sale of Lukoil’s overseas assets. Ukraine no longer has anything to do with that process or any influence over it.
The art of the backroom deal
Cynics insist that the Trump administration is a complete mess, with the right hand oblivious to what the left is doing. The way this agreement came together suggests otherwise.
After the campaign of long-range strikes against Russia went badly off script, Zelensky once again tried to secure a ceasefire through Trump. He has been trying since early 2025, with no success, but he still held out hope.
Trump could have publicly given Zelensky the boot again. But on Ukraine, he faces opposition not only from Congress but also from parts of his own administration. And an election is just around the corner.
Instead of staging a public showdown, Trump’s team spent more than two months visibly engaged in intensive talks with Ukraine about an energy truce. His envoys, Witkoff and Kushner, traveled to Kiev, and Trump himself showered Zelensky with compliments. In reality, all of it proved to be a screen for a quiet, swift, informal deal with Moscow.
It has since emerged that the first tanker carrying diesel to the US left St. Petersburg on September 22 and is expected to reach the US any day now. In other words, the deal was already well advanced three weeks ago, and both sides were confident it would go through.
That takes some skill. This episode shows that Trump keeps a firm grip on his team and can prevent leaks when he needs to. Even Rubio, prone to breaking ranks, played his part exactly as the boss wanted.
And once the deal was done, there was no longer any need to smile at Zelensky in public. The masks came off. For the first time, Trump publicly declared that Ukraine needs a new president and must hold elections.
The liberal media will inevitably say that Trump is repeating Russian propaganda narratives. In fact, he was saying what he thinks.
***
The diesel deal does not mean Moscow and Washington will now live in perfect harmony. The differences between them are deep and fundamental, and the recently enacted ‘Graham law’ makes lifting any sanctions impossible for at least the next five years.
But this Friday, Putin and Trump finally managed to get past Ukraine and leave it behind. US-Russia relations now depend on Russia and the US alone.

articles.title: Middle East crisis live: Houthis warn passengers against using Saudi airport after deadly attack on Riyadh
articles.body:
Houthi state media says capital's airport hit by Saudi strike
Houthi-run state TV is reporting that Saudia Arabia has carried out a strike on the main airport in Sana’a, the Yemeni capital currently controlled by the Houthis.
Al Masirah TV said the strike had hit Sana’a International Airport.
No comment yet from Saudi authorities or the Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen.
Earlier however, the coalition had issued a issued a statement saying they would “respond decisively” to the Houthis’ “terrorist attack” on Riyadh’s airport on Saturday which killed 12 people and injured 309.
The Saudis have launched hundreds of air strikes on Houthi positions in Yemen since fighting recommenced last month.
Houthi airport attack forces swift rethink of Trump’s new 'Blame Ukraine' strategy
Patrick Wintour
The reckless missile attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday did not just export the death and misery inside Yemen to Saudi Arabia, it also left Donald Trump forced to reconsider his diplomatic and political strategy designed to take him into the midterm elections next month.
The US president’s plan had only been unveiled on Saturday.
It was to blame what he described as “a world problem” – spiralling diesel prices – on the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, saying his attacks on Russian oil refineries were the cause. He was going to keep the political temperature down on his war of choice in Iran and its spillover in Yemen until after the midterms.
In pursuit of this strategy, he claimed the Iranian blockade in the strait of Hormuz was in effect broken, producing figures on daily oil barrel exports to assuage the markets. As a further insurance he also claimed it was impossible to negotiate with the Iranians since there was no single leadership in Tehran.
Saudi Arabia, in conjunction with Turkey, and Pakistan, were largely to be left to sort out the Houthis along the Red Sea. The fate of Yemen, the poorest country in the world according to the International Monetary Fund, was not going to shift votes in Kansas or Alaska.
Now, after the Riyadh airport attack, it is doubtful, for a basket of reasons, that this anyway threadbare strategy, largely born of desperation, can hold.
For all the talk of the Gulf becoming responsible for its own security, it is doubtful that Saudi Arabia can be left to fend for itself after the carnage in Riyadh. One of the the 12 dead is an American and there may be more among the severely injured. Something is clearly wrong with Saudi defences since the Houthis are firing rockets from 500 miles away, and they are reaching their target too often.
The US has had a unilateral ceasefire with the Houthis since 2025, and once the hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis recommenced in the summer, the pact was quietly renewed.
Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help. Can he spurn them three times? The pressure to act as allies are expected to may prove overwhelming.
Egyptian flight attendant and Syrian woman among 12 killed at Saudi airport
We have some more detail on the 12 people killed in the Houthi missile strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airporton Saturday.
The attack on a civilian space – the airport had no military facility- has drew widespread condemnation from Arab and Western leaders and the UN.
Saudi authorities said the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.
The Egyptian woman killed has been identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, a flight attendant who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to the Egyptian state-run TV.
The Syrian woman has been identified as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida by the Syrian embassy in Riyadh.
She was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for the past five years after fleeing the Syrian civil war, her niece told AP. She had been visiting her sister in Riyadh and was on her way home to Mecca, where she lived, when she was killed in the attack.
There is attention too on the still yet to be identified American citizen who was killed at the airport because that will add to Saudi pressure on Donald Trump for the U.S. to join in the fight.
As we await more detail on this reported blast in the Saudi capital, it’s worth noting that there’s been a distinct lack of information coming from Saudi authorities on the Houthi attacks and other dangers.
Officials have announced that schooling will move online until the end of the week, meaning schools and campuses are closed.
But they have otherwise been largely quiet on the major attack on the country’s largest airport yesterday which killed 12 people and injured 300 more.
They have not issued a wider emergency alert, nor given a national address or even officially announced the closure of King Khalid International Airport with the suspension of flights detected through air traffic sites instead.
This is in line with a pattern of communication from not just Saudi but other Gulf state authorities these past seven months since they’ve come under attack from Iranian missiles and drones.
Gulf state authorities have tended to suppress the flow of information out about attacks – ostensibly for national security purposes and to maintain public confidence in the country’s defences.
However, the lack of information is also leading to confusion and speculation online, particularly as the Houthis continue to threaten new strikes against the kingdom.
Houthi state media says capital's airport hit by Saudi strike
Houthi-run state TV is reporting that Saudia Arabia has carried out a strike on the main airport in Sana’a, the Yemeni capital currently controlled by the Houthis.
Al Masirah TV said the strike had hit Sana’a International Airport.
No comment yet from Saudi authorities or the Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen.
Earlier however, the coalition had issued a issued a statement saying they would “respond decisively” to the Houthis’ “terrorist attack” on Riyadh’s airport on Saturday which killed 12 people and injured 309.
The Saudis have launched hundreds of air strikes on Houthi positions in Yemen since fighting recommenced last month.
UK advises against travel to parts of Saudi Arabia
The UK Foreign Office has updated guidance for British nationals following the deadly Houthi attack on Saturday.
It has advised against:
All travel to within 10km of the border with Yemen
All but essential travel to Aseer province, Riyadh province, Najran province, Jizan province and Taif city and Taif International Airport
There are an estimated 20,000- 30,000 British nationals living in Saudi Arabia, although those numbers have presumably fluctuated since the war began and Iran and its allies fought back against US and Israeli strikes by targeting cities like Dubai and Doha, in Gulf states allied with the US.
In the first fortnight of the war earlier this year in March, more than 102,000 Britons across the Middle East registered with the Foreign Office for help.
Some more Gulf reaction to Houthi’s deadly airport attack and continued threats to target Saudi airspace.
In a significant message, the United Arab Emirates has issued a statement in solidarity with Saudi Arabia – expressing support for “all measures aimed at safeguarding the kingdom’s security and stability”.
The UAE message is improtant given the major rupture in relations this year between the two oil-rich kingdoms, first sparked by lingering divisions in Yemen, and made worse by the Iran War and arguments over oil prices which led to the UAE quitting OPEC (currently led by the Saudis) after six decades of membership.
In Yemen in particular, the two Gulf states have significant history.
Both the UAE and Saudi Arabia bankrolled anti-Houthi forces in Yemen during the civil war from 2015-2022, and the UAE-backed forces were seen as particularly successful.
But relations broke down in January this year when the UAE-backed force in Yemen, which was a seperatist group trying to create a breakaway southern state, was attacked and defeated by Saudia Arabia.
That led the UAE to pull out of Yemen altogether. But the UAE were viewed as the most knowledgeable and effective authorites on the ground in the fight against the Houthis; when the Houthis launched their lightning offensive in September to take areas along the Red Sea and secure the Bab al-Mandab chokepoint, they were able to quickly seize areas and defeat the authorities in them previously backed by the UAE.
It’s since been suggested that Saudi Arabia might need to reconcile with the UAE to form a military alliance again to drive the Houthis back.
So this latest message from the UAE’s foreign ministry will be closely read.
The UAE foreign ministry criticised the “flagrant violation” of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and “reaffirmed the UAE’s full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and its support for all measures aimed at safeguarding the kingdom’s security and stability.”
The Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour has offered some context on the latest between the Houthis and the Saudi kingdom.
Saturday’s incident comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis on the kingdom. The airport has already been attacked twice this week, leaving four people dead and others wounded, and badly damaging an aircraft.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.
The attack came as forces allied to the UN-recognised government in Yemen claim to have mounted a successful offensive to retake the Bab al-Mandab strait from Houthi rebels, but accounts vary as to whether the push has been repelled.
Houthi foreign ministry says 'worse yet to come' if Saudi strikes continue
The Houthi’s foreign ministry in Yemen has also put out a statement being carried by Houthi media.
They threatened again that continued Saudi military action in Yemen would lead to an even stronger response. Echoing what military spokesman Saree said earlier in his airport warning – they said their actions were “guided by reciprocity” – as in they say they’re responding to Saudi strikes on their area in Yemen.
“Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing,” the ministry said in statements carried by Houthi-run Al Masirah television.
As I reported earlier, the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces launched a major counter-offensive this week to drive back the Houthis from the Bab al-Mandab strait and hit other Houthi positions along the Red Sea. How successful that has been is still unclear.
But the Houthis are striking back with slightly different targets- choosing to escalate their attacks on civilian airspaces as well as Saudi oil facilities. They have repeatedly said their aim is to remove Saudi influence from Yemen.
Why else has the US been reluctant to intervene so far in Saudi Arabia’s fight?
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.
Saturday’s attack might change things but Donald Trump has been reluctant so far to help out Saudi Arabia for several reasons, as my colleague Patrick Wintour explains:
The US has its hands full and its munitions stocks are empty due to the war in Iran.
Ahead of the midterms, Donald Trump does not want to launch another forever war.
After bombing the Houthis for 50 days in spring 2025, he struck a bilateral ceasefire with the Houthis – a deal that excluded Israel.
He has twice rejected Saudi pleas that the fate of the strait is a matter for the world.
An American citizen was among the 12 killed in the airport attack yesterday. For weeks now there’s been speculation over whether the US will join Saudi Arabia in carrying out air strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
When fighting recommenced last month with the Houthis, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had reportedly called Donald Trump to request military assistance. The US president committed only military intelligence and targeting help rather than send war planes.
On Saturday, following the deadly airport attack, Trump was asked by reporters if the US would take a more active position and join in the Saudi strikes.
“We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he said.
He later said he also planned to speak with Saudi Arabia’s leader.
Asked again by reporters if the U.S. might get involved, Trump responded, “We’ll find out.”
The fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen this past month have marked a new front in the Iran war, further driving up global oil and fuel prices as Saudi Arabia is the world’s top oil exporter and had been delivering its output through the Red Sea which has seen shipping attacks by Iran’s ally in recent weeks.
The US is now in the seventh month of the war it began against Iran in February, and across American states gasoline prices have surged 47%.
Trump’s approval rating has also dropped from 41% in Feburary to 37%- his lowest level yet ahead of the midterm elections next month.
There’s been a strong condemnation of this morning of the Houthi’s deadly strike on Saudi Arabia’s largest airport. Global leaders say attacks on civilians must stop.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply shocked” by Saturday’s strike.
“Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately,” he said.
Meanwhile EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the European Union stands “in solidarity with Saudi Arabia”, noting the “murderous attack on civilians” as a “dangerous escalation” in the wider war.
These “attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shockwave sent through the world,” she said.
The EU as a bloc has not sent any direct military aid to Saudi Arabia since fighting recommenced with the Houthis last month. The Saudis have asked France and Germany directly for aid; France has sent military equipment.
The UK meanwhile has sent air defences and RAF Voyager refuelling aircraft to Saudi Arabia since late September, in part says the government to help keep Red Sea oil flows open.
This morning UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said Houthi attacks on civilian sites “is one of the reasons why the UK is providing support to Saudi Arabia in the form of air defences and air-to-air resupplying”. Meanwhile in the Middle East region, Iraq, which neighbours Saudi Arabia, warned this morning that the attack endangered “regional security and stability”.
As you can expect, passengers have been avoiding Saudia Arabia’s main international airport since the major attack yesterday.
King Khalid remains closed today. It remains to be seen if operations will continue at other Saudi airports.
The Houthis earlier in the week had warned commercial airlines “for the last time” about the consequences of flying into Saudi airspace, noting it was a theatre of fighting.
Several airlines have previously suspended flights during the past month as the Iran War has expanded to this new front. Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines had all temporarily paused their routes into Riyadh and other Saudi cities.
The Houthis this morning have just also issued a warning to travellers and airlines to stay away from Saudi airports following yesterday’s attack.
It’s the first public message from the group since Saturday’s deadly assault.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Mecca and Medina – the holiest cities in Islam - were excepted but the other Saudi airports and airspace “are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces”.
He warned the public to “take our warning seriously” and also claimed that “Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions”.
The Gulf state has been asking the US and other Western allies for more missile interceptors since the fighting escalated.
Saree ended his post by saying his group is pursuing: “airport for airport, siege for siege, and escalation for escalation” until they achieved their goals.
All week the Houthis have been striking the main airport in the Saudi capital as Saudi Arabia has increased strikes on Houthi territory in Yemen. The Houthi-run health ministry says 91 Yemenis have been killed and 168 injured in the past five weeks due to Saudi-led attacks. It said 60% of those killed were women and children.
This week, the Saudi-led coalition backing the Yemeni government forces launched a major counter-offensive to try and push back the rebel group who’ve rapidly seized and gained territory since September.
The Houthis have taken over islands in the Bab al- Mandab strait and also staked positions along the Red Sea, tightening their grip on the crucial passageway through which Saudi Arabia, a top oil exporter, had been diverting flows as the Strait of Hormuz remains shut off.
12 killed at Riyadh airport and hundreds wounded in Saturday strike
Saturday’s attack was the third launched on the Saudi capital’s main airport this week- with the missile making it past Saudi air defences to strike terminals 3 and 4 of King Khalid airport where hundreds of passengers were awaiting domestic flights.
The attack killed at least 12 people and injured 309 at last count, say Saudi officials.
The dead include four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.
A projectile also fell near the King Fahd international airport in Dammam, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis.
The Dammam airport has been an important alternative to Riyadh amid the recent spate of attacks.
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of rapidly unfolding events in the Middle East.
After attacking Saudi Arabia’s main international airport on Saturday in strikes which killed at least 12 people and injured 309, the Houthis have issued another message this morning about the kingdom’s airports.
In response to the Houthi’s assault – the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in over a decade – US President Donald Trump has said Washington may join the Saudis in carrying out air strikes against the Iran-backed group in Yemen.
Trump said: “We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

articles.title: Hackers use security cameras to track troops, military targets in Israel, Ukraine - report
articles.body:
Internet-connected security cameras and webcams around the world are increasingly being hacked and turned into military intelligence tools, allowing countries including Israel, Iran, Russia, and Ukraine to monitor troop movements, track targets, and assess attacks, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.
The growing threat has emerged across multiple conflicts, including those involving Israel and Iran and Russia and Ukraine, as governments and hackers exploit vulnerabilities in devices originally intended to protect homes, businesses, and public spaces.
According to the report, an estimated 1.2 billion internet-connected cameras operate worldwide, creating an enormous network of potential intelligence-gathering devices. Many are inadequately secured, making them attractive targets for cyber operations.
One incident highlighted in the investigation involved a poultry farmer in northern Israel who discovered that the language settings on a camera overlooking his chicken coop had unexpectedly changed to Arabic during the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran earlier this year.
The farmer contacted the Israel National Cyber Directorate, which determined that hackers had compromised the Chinese-made device. The camera's position provided a view of Israeli security activity near the Lebanese border, giving the intruders potential access to military intelligence rather than simply images of the farm.
The directorate subsequently helped the farmer improve the camera's security and change its viewing angle to prevent the surveillance of military operations, according to the WSJ.
Civilian surveillance becomes military intelligence
The incident illustrates a growing challenge for military and civilian cybersecurity authorities: Cameras installed for routine security purposes can become intelligence assets when hostile actors access them.
In Israel, the threat has already prompted warnings from the National Cyber Directorate about the vulnerability of residential and commercial surveillance equipment.
During the June 2025 Israel-Iran war, the directorate urged homeowners and businesses to secure their cameras, warning that hostile actors could exploit compromised devices to gather intelligence and identify security vulnerabilities.
The agency identified weak passwords, outdated software, and cameras directly exposed to the internet as common security weaknesses.
Israel National Cyber Directorate chief Yossi Karadi subsequently revealed that Iran had infiltrated parking and road cameras during the June conflict to monitor the movements of prominent Israelis.
Speaking at a cybersecurity conference in December 2025, Karadi said Iranian hackers had sought to track Israeli figures for potential attacks.
He also disclosed that Iranian operatives had accessed a street camera overlooking the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot shortly before an Iranian ballistic missile struck the institute during the conflict.
The incident demonstrated how compromised surveillance systems could potentially contribute to both intelligence collection and the assessment of military strikes.
In March 2026, Karadi again warned about Iranian efforts to compromise Israeli surveillance cameras, describing the devices as a valuable intelligence-gathering resource. He said the directorate had blocked 50 camera-hacking attempts that could have enabled broader network intrusions.
Israel also exploited Iranian surveillance networks
The intelligence value of compromised cameras works both ways.
Israel reportedly infiltrated Tehran's traffic camera network to monitor senior Iranian officials and collect information used in planning military operations against the Islamic Republic.
According to a Financial Times investigation published in March, Israeli intelligence agencies used hacked traffic cameras and artificial intelligence to establish patterns of movement among senior Iranian figures ahead of the operation that killed then-supreme leader Ali Khamenei.
The reported operation demonstrated the potential military value of combining widely available surveillance infrastructure with advanced data-processing capabilities.
Rather than relying exclusively on satellites, reconnaissance aircraft, or intelligence operatives, security services can potentially exploit networks that already monitor streets, intersections, and buildings.
Iranian officials have publicly acknowledged concerns about foreign access to the country's surveillance infrastructure.
In November 2025, Gholamreza Jalali, then head of Iran's Passive Defense Organization, alleged that Israel and the US were exploiting Tehran's surveillance systems for intelligence operations.
Jalali claimed that foreign code had been discovered in Iranian systems that redirected camera footage to external servers. The allegations were not independently verified.
Russia, Ukraine exploit the same vulnerabilities
The WSJ investigation also described how Russia and Ukraine have used compromised surveillance systems to obtain battlefield intelligence.
According to the report, both sides have exploited cameras to monitor military activity and improve their understanding of enemy positions and operations.
The same vulnerabilities extend beyond active battlefields. Russian-linked cyber actors have reportedly targeted surveillance cameras in European countries to monitor military movements.
The widespread availability of internet-connected cameras creates opportunities for intelligence collection far from conventional military installations.
Artificial intelligence can increase the usefulness of compromised video networks by helping operators process large amounts of footage, identify relevant activity, and recognize patterns that would otherwise require extensive manual monitoring.
Security warnings for camera owners
Cybersecurity specialists warn that many connected cameras are installed without adequate safeguards or ongoing technical maintenance.
Unlike computers and smartphones, which often receive regular security attention, cameras may operate for years with outdated firmware, weak login credentials, or insufficient protection against unauthorized access.
The growing number of cameras connected to private and commercial networks also creates potential entry points for attacks extending beyond the devices themselves.
Israeli cyber authorities have recommended replacing default passwords with strong, unique credentials, enabling two-factor authentication where available, installing security updates, and monitoring devices for unauthorized access.
The risks are especially high near military facilities, transportation routes, government installations, and other sensitive locations, where a seemingly ordinary camera may capture operationally valuable information.
As warfare increasingly combines conventional military operations with cyberattacks and digital intelligence collection, the WSJ investigation underscores how civilian surveillance infrastructure has become another contested element of modern conflict.

articles.title: ‘It’s a constant race’: the volunteers protecting Kyiv’s skies from new jet-powered drones
articles.body:
Several hours into Kyiv’s nightly curfew, much of the capital lay dark and quiet. High above, on the roof of a grey tower block on the city’s outskirts, a small group of men in uniform stood beside two heavy machine guns, scanning the horizon. Soon, a drone appeared.
Once, its unmistakable buzz would have sent the men scrambling towards their weapons. Now, the air defence unit will check speed and altitude on a monitor before taking a decision.
This one flew too high and too fast. It was one of Russia’s new jet-powered attack drones, a weapon that has transformed the battle for the skies over Kyiv in just a few months.
“They’re so fast, it’s extremely difficult to hit them. Our weapons simply can’t reach them. Often, we can hear them but can’t see them. It drives us crazy,” said the group’s commander, who goes by the call sign Sensei, looking over the city’s skyline.
Over three days and nights, the Guardian accompanied Mriya, Kyiv’s largest volunteer air-defence formation, across its network of outposts around the capital, from high-rise rooftops to truck-mounted machine gun positions in deserted fields on the city’s outskirts.
Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine has relied on unpaid volunteers, often armed with Soviet-era weapons, as one layer of the air-defence network protecting its cities, homes and families.
For years, they proved remarkably effective, emerging as a key part of the response to the Iranian-designed Shahed drones, which Russia calls Geran-2 and began launching en masse in late 2022.
“We live a double life. During the day, I deal with paperwork. At night, I shoot down drones,” said Oleksandr, a lawyer, standing beside his truck-mounted machine gun in a field outside Kyiv. “It’s a strange duality. With time you get used to it.”
But warfare in Ukraine evolves at extraordinary speed and units such as Mriya are struggling to keep up.
Since the summer, Russia has increasingly deployed jet-powered drones that crews say can travel at about 600km/h (373mph), much faster than the original propeller-driven Shaheds, and reach altitudes of up to 10km (6 miles), far beyond the range of the volunteers’ guns.
Ukraine’s interception rate for the new drones is between 50% and 60%.
“In 2023 and 2024, we were shooting them down in batches,” Artem, a 63-year-old military veteran, said proudly. On a good night, he added, a single crew could bring down three or four Shaheds.
Now, his unit had managed to shoot down just one jet drone after it slowed enough to come within range of their guns. “There’s this feeling of helplessness,” he added.
The problem, Artem explained, was that the guns’ sights were designed for slower targets. Jet drones fly so fast that gunners must aim beyond the sight to hit them. “The Shahed no longer fits inside our aiming grid,” he said.
Ukraine’s air defences operate as a layered system, with different weapons matched to different threats. Volunteer machine gun teams work alongside interceptor drones to hunt slower, low-flying Shaheds. More sophisticated weapons, including the country’s scarce US-made Patriot batteries, are needed against cruise and ballistic missiles.
For now, the main answer to the jet drones has been fighter aircraft, including F-16s, which are expensive to fly and put their pilots at risk.
Russia’s introduction of new drones came at an especially acute moment for Ukraine. With its ground offensive making slow progress, Russia has sharply intensified its air campaign, striking Kyiv almost daily in an effort to make the capital unlivable as winter approaches.
In the last week, jet-powered drones have repeatedly struck bridges across the Dnipro in Kyiv, prompting restrictions on several of the city’s main crossings. Russia launched another large-scale bombardment across Ukraine on Wednesday, firing dozens of missiles alongside drones and causing fresh disruption to electricity and water supplies in the capital.
The attacks have upended daily life in a city that, for much of the war, was considered relatively safe compared with those nearer the front. Anti-drone netting, long a familiar sight in frontline towns, has begun to appear around Kyiv, and during the heaviest attacks some people have taken to sleeping in metro stations.
Moscow has also begun sending waves of jet drones throughout the day, a break with years of assaults taking place mostly overnight.
“Every hour, two or three come in,” said Oleksandr, the lawyer, who joined Mriya early last year. His mobile group once deployed from base as drones approached the city, but now spends hours at a time waiting in fields.
“They’re fast and they keep our groups constantly moving. Some days, it feels like Russia has an endless supply of them,” he shrugged.
Mriya’s volunteers are something of a mirror of Kyiv. The crews that the Guardian accompanied included in their ranks an advertising creative director, a man who repairs intercoms, a hand-to-hand combat coach and the former head of a design institute.
The military supplies the units with heavy machine guns, including American-made Browning M2s and Soviet-era DShKs, both designed before the second world war. But the volunteers pay for their own vehicles, fuel and other equipment.
What united them, they said, was that the stakes felt close to home. “If we let a drone through, that means it flies to the city and can kill our families,” said Ivan, a university professor in Kyiv.
Ivan joined the unit after a Shahed struck the courtyard of his home about a year and a half ago. “It badly frightened my family and destroyed my property,” he said. “So I had a personal score to settle as well. I have two children. The more of this filth that is destroyed on the approach to Kyiv, the lower the chance that my children will be hurt.”
When a shift runs into the morning, he teaches his class online from the position, on his phone. Others described volunteering as a way of reclaiming a measure of agency over a war that has left millions of Ukrainians feeling powerless.
“In the city you can’t do anything. People sit in basements, bomb shelters or apartments and wait: will you be lucky or not, will it hit or not?” Oleksandr said. Out on the position, he said, there was at least a chance of shooting one down.
Help, though, may be on its way. Back in the field, Artem pulled out a tablet showing a live map of drones over Ukraine.
Among the moving icons were ones the volunteers have begun to see more often: Ukraine’s new generation of high-speed interceptor drones, designed to hunt down their Russian counterparts.
He pointed to two Ukrainian interceptors travelling at more than 600km/h. Moments later, each brought down a Russian drone and disappeared from the screen.
Across the country, the Ukrainian government and private defence companies have been thrown into a race to build jet-powered interceptors that can match Russia’s latest drones.
“We have to admit that we were caught sleeping by these jet-powered Shaheds,” said Stanislav Hryshyn, a co-founder of General Cherry, one of Ukraine’s largest drone manufacturers, which is developing the new interceptors.
The biggest obstacle, he said, was a shortage of the small jet engines that power them, which Russia sources in bulk from China. Neither Ukraine nor Europe, Hryshyn said, had built the industrial capacity to make them in the quantities required.
Hryshyn estimated it would take three to four months before Ukraine could produce enough interceptors to match Russia’s jet drones.
Even if Ukraine fields thousands of new interceptors in the coming months, any advantage may prove short-lived. Russia has repeatedly adapted its drones, changing their speed, altitude and flight paths in response to Ukrainian defences, and Hryshyn said each new countermeasure invited another innovation.
“It’s a constant race over who gets there first,” Hryshyn said. “A life-or-death race.”

articles.title: 'Will only lead to more slaughter' — bipartisan backlash erupts in US over Trump-Russia diesel deal
articles.body:
'Will only lead to more slaughter' — bipartisan backlash erupts in US over Trump-Russia diesel deal
Editor's Note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
U.S. President Donald Trump's deal allowing Russian diesel exports to American and global markets drew sharp criticism on Oct. 10 from both Democrats and Republicans in Congress, who warned the move could help fund Russia's war against Ukraine.
Trump on Oct. 9 shocked Ukrainians and many in the U.S. when he announced that he would ease sanctions against Moscow by opening up global markets to Russian diesel. He claimed this would alleviate a worldwide diesel shortage, which he attributes to Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries rather than his own decision to attack Iran.
Lawmakers from both major parties argued the move would undermine recently enacted sanctions against Russia, potentially provide Moscow with billions of dollars in revenue, and contradict Congress's efforts to pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war in Ukraine.
Some lawmakers questioned whether the plan would meaningfully lower fuel prices for Americans, which have increased dramatically across the country since the start of the U.S. war with Iran.
Others pointed out that Trump's deal with Putin may even be illegal. In 2022, then-President Joe Biden signed a law prohibiting American imports of Russian energy products, with conditions for lifting the ban tied to an agreement by Russia to withdraw its troops from Ukraine.
"Congress banned Russian energy imports in 2022. (The president) cannot simply ignore that law to buy diesel from Putin," Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, said after the deal was announced.
Trump also recently signed another bill on Sept 18, which paved the way for further sanctions on Russia. Lawmakers claim the new agreement allowing for Russian diesel imports undermines that legislation.
"A few weeks ago, Congress overwhelmingly passed legislation to increase sanctions and tariffs on Russia," Senator Lisa Murkowski, a Republican, wrote on social media, referring to the recent sanctions bill.
"The president should be using those authorities instead of allowing Russia to export diesel, rake in revenues and continue its catastrophic war in Ukraine."
The sanctions bill, named for the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of U.S. aid to Ukraine and sanctions against Russia, allows the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from foreign countries that meet specified criteria within 30 days of the law’s enactment.
The newly announced diesel deal directly contradicts the provisions made in the legislation, Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat, said in a statement on social media.
Trump's deal "will lead to the slaughter of more innocents in Ukraine," he added.
"This agreement with a murdering dictator is a stain on our nation's character, an insult to Lindsey Graham's memory, and directly contrary to Congress's intent in our bipartisan sanctions bill," Blumenthal said.
Senator Gluesenkamp Perez, a Democrat, also criticized the deal, writing on social media that it "undermined" decisions made by Congress.
"It won't actually bring down prices," she said, adding that "we're now funding the war against Ukraine."
"Whose side is Trump on?" Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat, asked on social media. "The entire goal was to choke off Putin's money for the war by punishing countries who were evading the sanctions and buying Russian oil. Does that mean we're sanctioning ourselves now?"
read also
Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick promised that bipartisan legislation blocking all purchases of Russian oil would be introduced in the coming days.
"We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil. ... It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly," he wrote.
Critics of the proposed deal include Congressman Don Bacon, a Republican, who, in a lengthy post on social media stated that although Americans want lower diesel prices, "buying Russian fuel is the wrong answer."
"Now is the time to use those sanctions to squeeze Putin’s war machine," he said. "Not reward a dictator by putting more money in his hands while he continues targeting and killing Ukrainian civilians."
Trump has framed the proposed diesel deal with Russia as a way to lower costs for Americans ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The midterm elections, which will determine which party controls Congress, are set to take place on Nov. 3, and voters are critical of rising oil prices and a general increase in cost of living tied to the war in Iran.
But support for Ukraine remains popular among Americans. A recent Economist/YouGov poll found that 61% of Americans sympathize more with Ukraine, compared to only 3% who sympathize more with Russia.
Before Trump's diesel announcement, U.S. lawmakers had been putting pressure on the administration to enforce the sanctions outlined in the recent legislation before the Oct. 18 deadline.
In a letter shared with the Kyiv Independent and later made public, Shaheen and Republican Senator Roger Wicker argued that Russia's intensified missile strikes targeting Ukraine's civilian population and energy infrastructure, along with new North Korean troop deployments, make immediate economic pressure necessary.

articles.title: More than 50 Iranian army units deployed along borders, commander says
articles.body:
More than 50 Iranian army units deployed along borders, commander says
TEHRAN — Iran has deployed more than 50 combat and support units of its Army Ground Force along the country’s borders, including mobile, rapid-reaction, armored and mechanized brigades, as well as artillery, engineering, missile and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) units, the force’s commander has said.
Brigadier General Ali Jahanshahi, commander of the Islamic Republic of Iran Army Ground Force, said the force had revised its operational plans, restructured elements of its combat organization and strengthened its readiness in response to lessons learned from previous conflicts, including the 12-day war and the conflict Iranian officials refer to as the Ramadan War.
In remarks reported by Mehr News Agency, Jahanshahi said the post-war reforms had prioritized the introduction of precision-strike, smart and network-enabled weapons systems, alongside expanded training programs to enhance personnel proficiency and operational effectiveness.
 
He added that measures to reduce personnel casualties, protect military assets and sustain operational readiness included the construction of extensive tunnel networks, trenches, firing positions and defensive fortifications at military installations.
Large-scale force deployment across Iran
Jahanshahi said that, following the outbreak of the Ramadan War, more than 50 combat and support units had been deployed to border areas across the country.
The deployments extended from Iran’s northwestern and western frontiers to the southwest, east and southeast, as well as the Makran coastline. According to the commander, the redeployment effort involved more than nine million kilometers of road movements, alongside the transport of substantial quantities of ammunition and military equipment by heavy vehicles.
He said the movements were conducted under the surveillance and potential threat of hostile drones and aircraft, with forces repositioned at night to reduce their exposure. Jahanshahi said the deployment had strengthened Iran’s deterrence posture and helped prevent enemy forces from crossing the country’s borders.
He added that Ground Force units remained deployed along the frontiers and maintained operational readiness despite temperatures exceeding 50 degrees Celsius, high humidity and limited logistical facilities.
ounter-infiltration measures and continued weapons production
Jahanshahi said military planners had identified locations that could potentially be used by hostile forces to enter Iranian territory, including disused airfields. Countermeasures had been planned for potential incursions, while intelligence operations had been conducted to improve situational awareness.
He also said domestic military production had continued throughout the conflict and remained ongoing.
According to Jahanshahi, the Army Ground Force, operating alongside other branches of Iran’s armed forces, launched thousands of Arash drones against US military bases in regional countries and targets associated with Israel during the war.
Passive defense measures limit personnel losses
The commander said several Ground Force installations had been struck during the conflict, with military buildings and personnel accommodation among the targets. At one base, he said, 10 barracks buildings were hit. Attacks also caused extensive damage to military infrastructure, destroying hundreds of thousands of square meters of buildings, according to his account.
Jahanshahi attributed the comparatively limited loss of life to the dispersal of personnel and the implementation of passive defense measures. Without those precautions, he said, the number of fatalities could have reached thousands.
Despite the damage, he added, personnel had maintained their positions and continued their missions.
Jahanshahi concluded that the Ground Force’s operational readiness and capabilities had improved significantly compared with the period before the conflict, with equipment production continuing and units maintaining their preparedness for potential threats.

articles.title: While Washington eases up on Russia, Europe hits back harder: EU plans to pass its largest sanctions package on Russia’s war machine in two days
articles.body:
Europe will not loosen its pressure on Russia after the US-Russia diesel deal, EU Foreign Policy chief Kaja Kallas says. She has announced that EU foreign ministers will approve the bloc’s largest set of sanctions against Russia’s war machine since the full-scale invasion on 12 October.
Washington has just eased the pressure on Russia, letting Russian diesel back onto world markets and handing Moscow more money to wage war. This comes as Russian strikes have killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians in two days, 22 of them on Russian President Vladimir Putin's birthday on 7 October.
Moreover, Russia has stepped up its hybrid attacks against Europe, both EU Member States and NATO Allies. It is now the time to tighten sanctions, not loosen them, Kallas says.
“Suspending sanctions on Russian diesel provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war. This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” she claims.
A split with Washington
On 9 October, Trump claimed he had agreed with Putin to put more than 300,000 tons of Russian diesel on world markets immediately.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the deal a weak decision by strong partners, arguing that Russia turns oil-product revenue into weapons against Ukraine's civilians, according to the BBC.
The package aims at the missile chain
On 7 October, EU ambassadors approved the 22nd package of sanctions, with about 1,700 listings, Ukrainian President’s Commissioner for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk notes. It is expected to be formally approved on 12 October. 
This package contains the largest number of sanctions targeting Russia’s defence industry. Of these, 60% were drawn from Ukrainian decrees and proposals. The package includes measures targeting machine tools, Lancet drones, ballistic weapons, and related technologies.
“The core of the package is Russia’s missile programme and electronic components: electronics, capacitors, resistors, and semiconductors. It also covers electronic warfare, shipbuilding, and explosives,” Vlasiuk says.
It took just a few weeks from Ukraine's decision to the European one.
"But we are already working on further measures, including sectoral sanctions targeting energy, the defense industry, finance, and trade,” he stated.

articles.title: Pentagon raises official US death toll in Iran war
articles.body:
Pentagon raises official US death toll in Iran war
The Pentagon has revised its previously underreported tally of US military deaths linked to the war with Iran, raising the official count to 21.
The Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) initially listed 18 US military deaths from hostile and non-hostile causes since the conflict began on February 28. The Washington Post reported last month, citing six US officials, that the database understated the number of deaths. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth called the findings “a complete lie.”
On Friday, the database was updated to include Army National Guard Maj. Sorffly Davius, 46, who died in Kuwait on March 6, and an unidentified Navy member who died by suicide in September.
It also recorded the death of Sgt. Devin A. Seibel, 26, who died in a training accident in Iraq in May. The military, however, did not link the incident to the war with Iran and classified it under Operation Inherent Resolve, the decade-long campaign against Islamic State (IS, formerly ISIS). His inclusion brings the broader number of US military fatalities in the Middle East since February 28 to 22, in line with the figure previously reported by the newspaper.
The updated records also show 865 wounded service members.
Democratic Representatives Adam Smith and Chrissy Houlahan criticized the incorrect count, calling it “an embarrassment” for the military.
“There is no excuse for a mistake of this magnitude,” they said in a joint statement.
Approached by the Washington Post, the Pentagon did not address the changes but said it “continues to maintain a steadfast commitment to the transparent, accurate accounting of all service member casualties.”
Last month, the US Navy acknowledged that eight sailors assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during a ten-month deployment that included the Iran war. The disclosure followed reports of burnout, declining morale, and shortages of food and basic supplies.
Despite US President Donald Trump’s insistence that the campaign has been a success, a Reuters/Ipsos poll in September found that 62% of Americans disapprove of military strikes against Iran.
The conflict has also deepened political divisions ahead of November’s midterm election, with the financial cost and economic fallout drawing scrutiny. US Central Command estimated the bill at $43.6 billion through September 3, according to figures provided to lawmakers and seen by AP.
Trump previously said the war would end immediately after the election, subsequently telling Axios that he faces a “big decision” over whether to resume major attacks to bring it to a close.
In a phone call on Friday, Trump discussed Iran with Russian President Vladimir Putin, who stressed that a diplomatic settlement remains possible and reiterated Moscow’s offer to accept Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium to help resolve the dispute over its nuclear program. Trump welcomed Russia’s diplomatic involvement, according to presidential aide Yury Ushakov.

articles.title: ‘Putin will drag you into the war,’ former Ukrainian foreign minister tells Europeans
articles.body:
KYIV — Russia's Vladimir Putin is preparing for a broader confrontation with Europe amid an uptick in the Kremlin's hybrid attacks on the continent, Ukraine's former Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba has warned.
In an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, Kuleba, who was Ukraine's foreign policy chief from 2020 to 2024, said that Russia's continued war preparations and anti-European propaganda are signs that Putin is planning attacks on other European countries.
"Anti-European hysteria is being fueled in Russia, which I interpret as the preparation for a broader conflict with the rest of Europe," said Kuleba, before adding: "We [Ukrainians] don't have to drag you — Putin will drag you into the war."
Advertisement
European officials say Moscow has upped its hybrid campaign across the continent in recent months, using cyberattacks, sabotage and disinformation to disrupt critical infrastructure and weaken support for Ukraine.
Kuleba said the failed drone attack on the Leipzig airport in Germany in August was a sign of "growing preparation" for an offensive on the continent. "They see how your intelligence operates. They see how your security forces operate. They see how you react and they draw conclusions," he added.
In the aftermath of the incident, the German government concluded that Moscow was responsible for the attack, and ordered a review of security around sensitive locations.
However, Kuleba, who stood down as Ukraine's foreign policy chief in September 2024, does not think Russia is preparing a full-scale offensive beyond Ukraine. In his view, Moscow is more likely to launch an attack on NATO countries involving drones targeting key infrastructure that would test the alliance's unity and preparedness.
"The truth is that Russia does not need 400,000 more people to wage that war. It needs five drones," he said, adding that in the event of an attack, "[Europeans] can call for NATO consultations... can call for restraint. But this will only encourage Putin to make the next step ... He will always have enough drone and missile capabilities."
Kuleba no longer believes Putin can be persuaded to end the war through negotiations. "He's not looking for a solution, for a pause, and there will be no moment when he will start looking for it," he said, concluding: "Putin is a guarantee of war: anyone after Putin is a chance for peace."
Advertisement
According to Kuleba, any attempts at negotiating with Putin, or pushing for peace, are a waste of time. "The sooner we come to terms with reality, the better policies we can develop to address it," he said.
He noted that while Europe’s political culture is based on "a win-win approach" in which both sides can benefit, Putin’s outlook is very different: “For him, a solution that benefits both sides is not the best option. For him, the world works on the principle of victory and defeat. One side has to win and the other has to lose,” said Kuleba.
The former foreign minister also warned that Ukraine would face its worst ever winter as Moscow ups its attacks against civilians in a bid to break their spirit.
In recent months, Russian strikes have hit Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and transport links, including bridges over the Dnipro river, as well as homes and civilian sites such as bus stops, schools, postal depots and internet providers. The attacks have disrupted power, transport and daily life as winter approaches.
On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in a Russian attack on two buses in Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s Donbas region.
Kuleba explained why he believed Moscow has now sharply escalated its airstrikes: “The bombing of cities is a direct consequence of Russia’s failure to defeat Ukraine on the battlefield.” He continued: “The main target of Russian drones and missiles is the Ukrainians’ will to resist — but also the will of Ukraine’s friends abroad to keep supporting it.”
Advertisement
He added:“They don’t just want to turn out the lights in Ukraine. They want to paralyze the country.”
Kuleba described the worst-case scenario in Ukraine as “the collapse of the systems that make life in a big city possible,” such as electricity, water and drainage services.
Could Russia succeed? “I believe Ukraine is too large, too mobile and too adaptable. That’s why I think we’ll get through this winter," said Kuleba.
"The price will be much higher than last year's."
The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet, The Telegraph, and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

articles.title: Ukrainian Drones Strike $50 Million Radar Used by Russia’s S-400 Air Defense Systems
articles.body:
- Category

Ukrainian Drones Strike $50 Million Radar Used by Russia’s S-400 Air Defense Systems
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian 96L6 radar station used by S-300 and S-400 air defense systems, targeting a key component responsible for detecting aircraft, missiles, and drones at distances of up to 300 kilometers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s 15th Separate Artillery Reconnaissance Brigade, known as “Black Forest,” on October 10, the radar was located, tracked, and attacked by Ukrainian drones. The brigade released footage of the operation, identifying the equipment as a 96L6 radar valued at approximately $50 million.
The footage shows a Ukrainian reconnaissance drone following the radar station as it moved toward a deployment position near a wooded area. Once the equipment stopped and deployed, Ukrainian strike drones carried out two attacks, hitting the area around its antenna.
The 96L6 is an early-warning radar operating in the C-band frequency range. It forms part of Russia’s integrated air defense network and provides targeting information to command centers and missile launchers.
The system is designed to detect and track various aerial threats, including fighter jets, cruise and ballistic missiles, and unmanned aircraft. According to its stated specifications, it can detect targets at distances of up to 300 kilometers and simultaneously track as many as 100 objects.
The radar can also operate alongside other detection systems, allowing Russian air defense units to coordinate surveillance and missile engagements across a wider area.
Disabling such equipment can reduce the detection capabilities of Russian air defense formations, particularly those operating S-300 and S-400 missile systems, which depend on radar data to identify and engage incoming threats.
Earlier, a Ukrainian missile strike on Russian command centers in temporarily occupied Donetsk on August 26 killed 20 Russian officers, including seven colonels and six lieutenant colonels. The attack marked the highest confirmed number of Russian officer deaths in a single strike since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Trump tells Ukraine to 'find a new president' as Russia intensifies deadly strikes
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump renewed his direct confrontation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Saturday evening, calling for him to be replaced. The attack came after Zelensky sharply criticized an agreement Trump announced Friday under which Russia would be allowed to export large quantities of diesel to global markets in exchange for the lifting of some sanctions.
Trump had already been asked Friday about Zelensky’s criticism — the Ukrainian leader called the move “a weak decision by strong allies” — but declined to address it at the time. On Saturday, however, he attacked Zelensky just hours after another deadly Russian bombardment, which killed 20 people in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia.
Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump was asked about Russian attacks that have only intensified and that this week killed dozens more civilians in two particularly deadly strikes. Rather than criticize the Kremlin, even indirectly, he turned his anger toward Zelensky.
"I advise (the Ukrainians) to find a new leader who can make a deal, because he actually could have made many deals, but for some reason he makes none," Trump said. “This is a war that should never have started, and I think it’s time for Ukraine to find a new president.”
Trump announced the agreement to release Russian diesel onto global markets after a phone call with President Vladimir Putin, in an effort to bring down fuel prices that have been weighing heavily on Americans ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections.
In his remarks Saturday, Trump also criticized Zelensky for refusing his appeals to halt Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries. Those strikes contributed to a severe fuel crisis in Russia over the summer and forced Moscow — normally a major fuel exporter — to temporarily halt diesel exports in order to preserve supplies for domestic consumers. The move helped drive up diesel prices, alongside another increase caused by the war with Iran.
“We said, ‘You can do whatever you want to Russia. Don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem,’” Trump said. “He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers with diesel fuel, because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel around the world,” Trump said.
“And what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel,” Trump added. “He better damn well stop.”
Zelensky has yet to respond to Trump’s criticism, which appears to mark a return of the severe rift between the two leaders last year. That crisis began with the “shouting summit” at the White House in February, which ended with Zelensky being thrown out after refusing the U.S. president’s demand that he compromise in negotiations with Russia — a demand Trump was then pushing as part of an effort to fulfill his campaign promise to end the war in Ukraine within 24 hours.
That crisis also led to a temporary halt in U.S. intelligence assistance to Kyiv, but the dispute was later resolved and the two leaders patched things up and met several times afterward.
Earlier this year, Trump even praised Kyiv’s campaign of drone attacks on targets deep inside Russia, aimed at making Russian civilians feel the effects of the war and thereby pressuring Putin to seek an agreement to end it.
But those attacks have also targeted oil refineries, contributing to the current surge in global diesel prices. Trump, concerned about the impact on Republicans’ already difficult prospects of retaining control of Congress in the midterms, has been pressing for the strikes to stop.
As early as the middle of last month, Trump announced what he described as an agreement between Kyiv and Moscow under which both sides would stop attacking energy facilities. Neither side confirmed such an agreement, however. Zelensky made clear that he would halt attacks on oil facilities only if he received guarantees that Moscow would do the same.
In recent days, Russia has instead stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian cities, including strikes on energy facilities that have forced Ukraine to announce planned power outages just before the freezing winter. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have also continued without letup.
Trump surprised observers Friday when he announced the agreement allowing Russian diesel exports to the United States and other countries.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said Russia would immediately provide more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia would provide another 3 million tons “within a short period of time,” he added.
Soon afterward, the United States lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Russia itself lifted restrictions Saturday morning that it had imposed over the summer on diesel exports because of domestic shortages caused by Ukrainian attacks.
The agreement marks a significant reversal after years of U.S. pressure on Moscow since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It came only a month after Trump signed a sweeping sanctions law targeting Russia, aimed in part at curbing its ability to profit from oil exports that help finance the war.
Ukraine reacted angrily to the agreement, which was announced as U.S. and Ukrainian representatives were holding talks on the war. Those talks were interrupted after the announcement. Zelensky described the deal as “a weak decision by strong partners” and warned: “Gifts to Putin, such as weakening sanctions, will not end the war. Russia will ‘repay’ concessions on diesel with more terror.”
Hours after the agreement was announced, Russia continued its attacks on Ukrainian cities. In one strike on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, at least 20 people were reported killed, including three children, after glide bombs hit a residential complex.
“Today, Russia said ‘thank you’ for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelensky said. “Last night provided further confirmation that Russia sees every easing of pressure on it as a signal that it can supposedly continue fighting and continue dropping bombs on cities. Different messages need to be sent.”
Images from the scene showed buildings completely destroyed. Authorities said Russia struck several locations in the city simultaneously in the early morning hours.
At least 18 more people were wounded. Reports said one of those killed was a 6-year-old girl. Her grandfather, Anatoly Chumny, was seen crying over her body, which had been covered with a white sheet after rescue workers pulled her from the rubble. Reuters reported that another resident’s leg was trapped in the debris and that he screamed in pain as rescue workers tried to free him.
“If the Russians have money, they will be able to keep fighting us,” said Natalia Malysheva, 49, whose parents were critically wounded in the attack and later died at the hospital after being pulled from the ruins. “How many lives have been lost here? How many homes have been destroyed? How many innocent people have died in the meantime?”
Kyiv was also hit by waves of drones Saturday. Dramatic footage circulated from the city showing a drone exploding at a kindergarten, as a passerby standing nearby ran away moments before the impact.

articles.title: US races Russia and China to build a nuclear reactor on the moon
articles.body:
In 2019, Russia tested a nuclear-powered cruise missile. The test failed, and the missile plunged to the bottom of the White Sea in northern Russia. Shortly afterward, a large explosion occurred near the crash site, causing radiation levels in the area to spike. U.S. intelligence officials assessed that the explosion took place during a Russian operation to recover the missile from the seabed. At least five nuclear scientists and employees of Russia's state-owned nuclear energy company, Rosatom, were killed. Russia quickly denied that the missile was nuclear-powered, but Rosatom subsequently all but acknowledged what had happened.
Now imagine a rocket carrying an actual nuclear reactor to the moon crashing into the ocean. It sounds like particularly dangerous science fiction, but until just a few years ago, the possibility of artificial intelligence taking over the world also seemed like nothing more than science fiction. With the world's major powers locked in a frantic race to install a nuclear reactor in space, such a scenario may be just around the corner.
A dangerous undertaking
About two months ago, NASA asked private contractors to prepare to build a nuclear reactor capable of surviving a journey through space and operating without maintenance near the moon's south pole. The target launch date: December 2030. The goal: to beat Russia, which aims to have a reactor operating on the moon by 2036 as part of a not-so-secret partnership with China. In 1961, President John F. Kennedy challenged America's leading scientists to land a man on the moon before the end of the decade. Now the goal is to have a functioning nuclear reactor on the moon within four years.
Even before sending nuclear reactors to the moon, the United States plans to put humans back on its surface as part of the Artemis program. The third test flight is scheduled for summer 2027, while the crewed Artemis 4 mission is planned for early 2028.
The somewhat dystopian race to install a reactor on the moon is probably inevitable, and it has implications for the entire future of space exploration. For example, a lunar day lasts about 14 Earth days, followed by 14 consecutive Earth days of complete darkness. During that time, solar panels cannot generate electricity, and temperatures plunge to minus 130 degrees. A nuclear reactor provides continuous electricity and heat around the clock, regardless of sunlight. Any ambition to reach Mars, let alone establish habitable conditions there, also requires nuclear energy.
Establishing a base on the moon is critical to the search for resources and the launch of missions into the depths of the solar system. All of this makes control over access to lunar resources essential, and the major powers believe a nuclear reactor is the foundation for achieving these ambitions. But it is a dangerous undertaking.
As in the case of the Russian missile in 2019, debris from a reactor falling back to Earth could scatter radioactive materials, as happened in Canada in the 1970s. An explosion or reactor core meltdown on the lunar surface could also render entire areas of the moon off-limits. All three countries promise that their reactors will remain inactive until they reach the moon, but these days it is difficult to take their leaders at their word, especially when the race is also, of course, a display of nationalist power.
Leading scientists warn that governments are moving too quickly at a time when space exploration has experienced a string of failures over the past six years. Chinese, American and Russian rockets have exploded, and space debris regularly falls back to Earth.
"There will always be a space race going on, and if you enter nuclear power into that mix, then it could take a potentially more dangerous turn,” said Edwin Lyman, the director of nuclear power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists.
A deadline pushed back
When it comes to nuclear power in space, Russia has no rivals. It has launched more than 30 reactors into Earth orbit, primarily aboard Cold War-era satellites in the 1970s and 1980s, and holds the largest stockpile of what is considered the safest nuclear fuel for space missions.
The last space reactor NASA tested, in 2018, used highly enriched uranium, which is lighter and cheaper to launch than other fuels. But its use is dangerous because the material can be turned into a nuclear weapon. That leaves the option of using low-enriched uranium fuel, except that the Americans do not have enough of it and cannot import it from Russia because of a ban imposed in 2024 in response to the war in Ukraine.
To date, the United States has invested more than $20 billion in space nuclear programs. Last month, the Pentagon selected a company called Antares to develop and demonstrate a space microreactor, while NASA is accelerating its timetable out of concern that a Russian-Chinese reactor could effectively establish an exclusion zone on the moon.
Such a move could, in practice, prevent American astronauts and rovers from accessing large areas of the lunar surface. That would itself violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, but international agreements are being violated on a daily basis these days.
Despite the sense of urgency, all the major powers have repeatedly pushed back their target dates, and few experts believe they will meet their deadlines. None of them even has a proven lunar lander capable of delivering heavy, potentially radioactive materials to the moon's unforgiving surface.
There is, of course, the option of international cooperation, as has happened time and again in space exploration. But the current global climate leaves little room for optimism.
"Governments have always achieved more by working together than by competing," Katy Huff, head of the Department of Nuclear Engineering at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, told The New York Times. "Collaborative, team-based science in space has always managed to rise above our fraught international politics."
