articles.title: Trump's diesel deal with Putin: How much, how long, and will It cut prices?
articles.body:
Trump's diesel deal with Putin: How much, how long, and will It cut prices?
TEHRAN - On October 9, US President Donald Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply diesel to the US and global markets, paired with a temporary 6-month US sanctions waiver. The move is aimed at easing record-high US diesel prices weeks before the November 3 midterms. Initial volumes are modest relative to consumption, so analysts expect limited and mostly psychological price effects — unless larger follow-on deliveries materialize and Russian refineries recover.
What exactly was agreed?
Trump said the deal was reached in a phone call with Putin and described it as highly successful. In his words, "vast amounts" of fuel would flow, and he publicly thanked Putin.
Putin confirmed Russia's "readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and world markets."
Operationally, the agreement has two parts:
Physical volumes in phases, as outlined by Trump:
300,000+ tons immediately — roughly 2.25 million barrels
500,000 tons in November
1 million tons shortly after
3 million tons more "in a short period," conditional on the state of Russian refineries
Total nominal volume: over 4.8 million tons.
A legal window to deliver it. The US Treasury's OFAC issued a temporary general license allowing the sale, delivery, offloading and import of Russian-origin diesel. The authorization runs for about six months, until April 7, 2027, covering cargoes loaded during that window.
This is the largest fuel-related sanctions relaxation since the Ukraine war began in February 2022. Previous licenses in the context of the ongoing US-Iran conflict were typically 30-day extensions.
How big is this in market terms?
Put in context, the first shipments are small:
The US consumes about 3.6 to 3.8 million barrels of diesel per day and exports about 1.5 million barrels per day. The first 2.25-million-barrel tranche equals roughly half a day of US consumption.
Global diesel demand is around 30 million barrels per day. The early Russian volumes equal 72,000 to 124,000 barrels per day — a fraction of one percent.
The 800,000 tons expected by end-November equals about 6 million barrels, or less than two days of US use.
That is why most market analysts describe the deal as a redirection of existing flows rather than major new net supply: if Russian barrels go to the US, current buyers of Russian diesel must source from elsewhere, leaving global balances broadly unchanged.
Looking back: how did we get here?
US sanctions history: Since 2022, the US has banned imports of Russian oil and petroleum products and, together with allies, imposed price caps and shipping restrictions to limit Moscow's energy revenues.
Only three weeks before the diesel announcement, Trump signed a sweeping bipartisan sanctions law targeting Russia's oil and gas income. The new diesel license therefore represents a sharp, if temporary, reversal — a pause, not a repeal.
Russia's export position: Russia imposed its own restrictions on diesel exports in July after Ukrainian drone strikes damaged several refineries. The International Energy Agency has estimated Russian diesel output fell by about 30%.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow would begin lifting those restrictions ahead of schedule starting in October, adding that the domestic market remains "fully supplied." Russian officials have framed the US deal as a normal commercial operation that also helps stabilize world markets.
Why US diesel is at record levels: Two overlapping disruptions explain the price spike:
Refinery losses in Russia from the Ukraine war, reducing global diesel availability.
Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz and Middle East refining amid the eight-month US-Iran conflict, which has raised freight, insurance and replacement costs.
The result: US average diesel hit a record $6.53 per gallon on September 22, easing only slightly to $6.28 by October 9, according to AAA. A year earlier it was about $3.68. Futures prices dipped modestly on the announcement, but pump prices did not move.
Trump had already tried domestic tools — including a proposed ban on diesel exports and authorization for off-road, tax-exempt diesel use — before turning to external supply.
Why now? The political calendar
The timing is inseparable from US domestic politics. The midterm elections are on November 3, with fuel prices and inflation ranking as voters' top economic concerns. Farm states such as Iowa have been hit particularly hard by diesel costs during harvest season.
Trump has stated the goal explicitly: lower costs for "farmers, ranchers and truckers" as his top priority. Supporters present the deal as pragmatic — using every available barrel to protect consumers. Critics in Congress, including Democrats Chuck Schumer, Jeanne Shaheen and Elizabeth Warren, as well as some Republicans such as Michael McCaul, argue it contradicts the intent of the sanctions law passed weeks earlier and provides revenue to Moscow while the Ukraine war continues.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it a "weak decision" and a "gift to Putin."
Energy analysts, regardless of political view, converge on a narrower technical point: volumes are too small to transform prices, though they could shave the peak off futures and provide localized relief on the US East Coast — New York-New Jersey and Philadelphia — where Russian-origin cargoes would most plausibly land.
What happens next? Three scenarios
Base case — partial delivery, limited price impact:
Russia delivers the first 1.8 million tons (300k + 500k + 1m tons) while keeping the conditional 3 million tons under review. Global diesel futures ease modestly, US retail diesel falls by cents, not dollars. This is the consensus among analysts at Eurasia Group, CSIS and Columbia University.
Prerequisite: Russian refineries stabilize and Hormuz-related freight costs do not worsen.
Upside case — full delivery plus refinery recovery:
If all 4.8+ million tons arrive in November-December and Russian refineries return toward normal throughput, combined with a seasonal demand softening, US diesel could retreat more meaningfully from record highs. Even then, analysts note, prices would remain far above 2025 levels because Middle East refining and shipping constraints persist.
Downside case — logistics and politics interrupt flow:
Tanker availability, insurance disputes, port restrictions, Congressional pressure, or a new escalation in either Ukraine or the Gulf could delay or shrink deliveries — particularly the conditional 3 million tons. In that case, the price effect would be almost entirely symbolic, while the political controversy would remain.
The key variable to watch is not announcements but loadings: how many vessels actually load Russian diesel in October-November, where they discharge, and whether OFAC extends or narrows the license after April 2027.
Bottom line
The agreement opens a narrow, time-limited corridor in an otherwise sanctions-constrained relationship. Economically, it is best understood as a short-term buffer — potentially helpful at the margins, but not a structural fix for a diesel market strained by two conflicts at once. Politically, it signals that in an election season, energy prices can temporarily outweigh sanctions logic.
Whether drivers feel it at the pump will depend less on diplomacy and more on refineries, tankers and the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: US Lawmakers Draft Bill to Block Russian Oil Purchases
articles.body:
Members of the US Congress are preparing bipartisan legislation to prohibit purchases of Russian petroleum, moving to challenge US President Donald Trump’s commercial agreement permitting Russian diesel imports onto American and global markets.
The legislative initiative, titled the “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act,” is being drafted by Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, with Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska confirming he will join as one of its initial co-sponsors.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The bill aims to establish a statutory ban on purchasing Russian oil and petroleum products, seeking to reverse the administration’s regulatory exemptions and curtail revenues funding the Russian military.
We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil. It will be called the “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act.” It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly. #PeaceThroughStrength
— Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick 🇺🇸 (@RepBrianFitz) October 10, 2026
In comments to Ukrainska Pravda, Bacon criticized the administration’s diesel agreement, characterizing the decision as a grave policy misstep that projects weakness toward the Kremlin while providing financial lifelines to Moscow’s defense sector.
“Allowing the purchase of Russian diesel fuel gives money to the Russian economy and its war machine,” Bacon said.
“A year ago, the president criticized Europeans for purchasing Russian gas. I completely disagree with this decision, and I consider the president’s policy regarding Russia and Ukraine a failure. I and ‘old school’ Republicans, supporters of Ronald Reagan, are deeply disappointed.”
Ukraine Should Keep Striking Russian Refineries, Kellogg Says
Bacon attributed the administration’s decision to domestic political calculations ahead of the upcoming midterm elections, noting that retail diesel prices approaching $6 per gallon have created pressure on voters. However, the lawmaker argued that the transactional approach undermines the nation’s strategic and moral standing.
Writing on X, Fitzpatrick also reaffirmed congressional backing for Kyiv, stating that President Volodymyr Zelensky maintains the overwhelming support of lawmakers and the American public.
“Russia illegally invaded Ukraine, a sovereign and freedom-loving nation, and Russia is squarely to blame for all damage and destruction, to both lives and treasure, that has resulted from Putin’s unprovoked attack,” Fitzpatrick stated.
“We have your back, and we will stand with you until Ukrainian victory is achieved.”
Congressional resistance to the Trump-Putin diesel arrangement
The push for legislative intervention follows Trump’s announcement on Friday, Oct. 9, of a bilateral arrangement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to American and international buyers.
Under the terms announced by Trump following a telephone conversation with Putin, Moscow agreed to deliver 300,000 metric tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter, with prospective deliveries scaling up to 3 million tons depending on the operational status of Russian refineries.
To enable the transactions, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The waiver was enacted only three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Sept. 18, a statute intended to expand secondary sanctions and tariff mechanisms across Russia’s energy, banking, and defense sectors.
The announcement drew condemnation from Ukrainian officials, who noted that the deal coincided with multilateral peace consultations in Miami involving US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. President Zelensky characterized the timing of the Miami talks as a “smokescreen” for bilateral energy concessions.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned that offering economic accommodations to the Kremlin signals Western weakness, arguing that the Russian leadership interprets concessions as appeasement rather than an incentive to negotiate.
Sybiha maintained that only an energy ceasefire – under which Russia halts attacks on Ukraine’s electrical and heating infrastructure in exchange for a pause in Ukrainian refinery strikes – can sustainably reduce fuel costs.
Lawmakers backing the new bill argue that allowing Russian refined hydrocarbons back into Western supply chains directly contradicts allied efforts to starve Moscow’s wartime budget.
The draft statute must be formally introduced in the House of Representatives and pass both chambers of Congress before it can be submitted to the president, setting up a potential legislative confrontation over executive sanctions waivers and energy trade with Russia.

articles.title: ‘Russian diesel for US friends’: Russians react to Trump-Putin deal (PROPAGANDA POSTERS)
articles.body:
‘Russian diesel for US friends’: Russians react to Trump-Putin deal (PROPAGANDA POSTERS)
A series of Soviet-style propaganda posters has appeared on the popular Russian social platform Pikabu following President Donald Trump’s grand announcement of a diesel deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin.
Pikabu is a Reddit-style website where users create entertainment content and share stories, images, and memes. The tongue-in-cheek posters, celebrating a newfound partnership over barrels of fuel, appeared on Saturday in a post titled ‘Morning Propaganda’.
“American, remember! Your enemy is not Russian – the Russian gives diesel! Your enemy is the Green Rat, who bombs your diesel in Russia!” the first poster reads, referring to Vladimir Zelensky, known for his signature green attire and whose surname is derived from the word for ‘green’ in Russian and Ukrainian.
“From Russia with diesel,” the second says, giving a fuel-themed twist to the James Bond movie title. The poster features a Russian couple in traditional dress presenting a barrel of fuel to an American family.
The budding friendship goes a step further in the third image, which features a happy American family and soldiers from both countries shaking hands in front of a Patriot air defense system.
“Is the Green Rat bombing our diesel in Russia?” the caption asks. “Let’s give our Russian friends a Patriot and protect our values!”
The final poster features late US Senator Lindsey Graham, a close ally of Kiev and co-author of the “bone-crushing” sanctions bill that proposed a 500% tariff on countries that import Russian energy. Graham, who died in July, is depicted in anguish amid flames and devils while a tanker labeled “Russian Diesel” approaches New York.
“Lindsey Graham in hell’s writhing – Russian diesel in America’s arriving!” the caption reads.
US President Donald Trump, who has blamed Zelensky for driving up fuel prices for American consumers through his stubborn refusal to halt attacks on Russian refineries, has approved a temporary sanctions waiver allowing Russian diesel exports and sales through April 7, 2027.
Following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, Trump announced that Moscow agreed to supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets “immediately,” followed by 500,000 tons in November and another 1 million tons shortly afterward. Moscow has confirmed that it will ease restrictions on diesel exports sooner than planned, saying the move will benefit the global economy.
Trump struck the deal with Putin after Zelensky ignored a number of requests to stop attacks on Russian refineries, according to Axios. Zelensky was furious and denounced Trump’s move as a “weak decision.”
“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president… I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,” Trump said on Saturday. Ukrainian negotiators left the talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami a day earlier than planned.

articles.title: Washington makes it official: US Treasury license clears sale and import of Russian diesel blocked by sanctions
articles.body:
Washington has put its sanctions on Russian diesel on hold. The US Treasury has authorized the sale, delivery, offloading, and import of Russian-origin diesel fuel, effectively suspending sanctions on that trade until 7 April 2027, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) said on its website on 9 October.
The waiver lets Russian diesel back onto world markets and, Ukraine argues, hands Moscow fresh revenue for its war, which has killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians in two days. Until now, it was unclear whether Washington would roll back the sanctions it imposed on Russia in 2022.
OFAC has issued the measure as General License 135, signed by the office’s director, Bradley Smith, according to the report. It authorizes transactions in Russian-origin diesel that sanctions would otherwise block.
The license sets one limit. It does not permit any debits from accounts at US financial institutions held by Russia’s central bank, its National Wealth Fund, or its finance ministry, the document says.
Trump’s promise of cheaper fuel
On 9 October, US President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, then 500,000 tons in November, and another million tons right after.
Moscow would later send the US up to 3 million more tons, depending on the state of Russia’s refineries, Trump added, framing the deal as a way to bring down energy prices.
Why the volumes fall short
Analysts say the amounts are too small to move prices much. Together, the first tranches would cover about a day and a half of US demand, while US diesel use alone runs near 16 million tons a month. Experts read the move as politics ahead of an election rather than a real shift in the market, pointing out that Trump cited volumes in tons, which look larger than the barrels traders track.
The deal drew fury in Kyiv, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it a weak decision by strong partners. The EU is moving the other way, with ambassadors approving the bloc’s largest sanctions package against Russia’s war machine, due for final adoption on 12 October.

articles.title: Ukraine hit by deadly Russian strikes as ‘thanks’ for Trump diesel deal, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Donald Trump has said Ukraine needs “a new leader”, a day after making a deal with Vladimir Putin to buy large quantities of Russian diesel.
The US president suggested Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war with Russia and blamed him for high diesel prices in the US.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said.
Trump made the comments as Russia launched deadly strikes on civilians in Ukraine, which Zelenskyy said were a “thanks” to Trump for the diesel deal.
The Ukrainian president has expressed outrage at the agreement announced by Trump on Friday, which the US president said was needed to reduce diesel prices, and comes ahead of November’s midterm elections in which fuel costs are a key voter issue.
The deal, which appeared to blindside Kyiv as it was announced while Ukrainian negotiators were in Miami for peace talks, was described by Zelenskyy as a “gift” to Russia’s president.
He said Russia would use the money it raised from the fuel sales to invest in its war and that “any easing of sanctions” would play into Russia’s hands, “allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”.
That prediction was realised hours later, when Ukrainian officials announced that a barrage of Russian strikes on the country’s south-east early on Saturday had killed 20 people, including three children.
“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said on social media on Saturday.
“Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed,” he said.
There were also “large-scale power outages” in the capital, Kyiv, the country’s largest private energy provider said.
Andy Burnham reiterated his “complete solidarity” in a call with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders agreed to meet in person in the coming days to continue talks.
The prime minister said he recognised the past day had been “difficult for Ukraine” and the two talked about the importance of keeping up pressure on Russia, No 10 said.
In stark contrast to Zelenskyy’s open frustration with Trump, a Kremlin readout of Friday’s call between the US president and Putin was glowing, with the Russian news agency Interfax quoting an aide as saying it was “very substantive and friendly”.
“Neither wanted to be the first to hang up,” the Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said of the two leaders. “They hung up simultaneously, literally at the same time.” Zelenskyy has previously said Putin is playing games with Trump.
The diesel deal disrupts four years of western financial pressure on Moscow and leaves Kyiv’s allies in Europe and Nato scrambling to adapt their sanctions plan. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the diesel deal “provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war”.
“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” she said on Saturday. “On Monday, EU foreign ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war.” She was referring to plans to formally add 1,600 new individuals and entities to the EU’s sanctions blacklist.
Major European governments have attempted to balance their diplomatic and trade relationships with a mercurial Trump and their support for Ukraine.
The German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said Berlin “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions”, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering”.
Ulf Kristersson, the Swedish prime minister, expressed “regret” at the US agreement, saying energy revenues were “a vital source of funding Russia’s war of aggression”.
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia “must feel its losses” and has promised to respond. In the Russian-occupied Luhansk region, Ukrainian attacks in the past 24 hours had killed four civilians and wounded five, the region’s Russian-installed governor, Leonid Pasechnik, said on Saturday.
Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to take “de-escalatory steps” in the war but only if Russia did the same.
Russia’s fuel production has become a key point of contention between Zelenskyy and Trump, who has attempted to stop Ukraine from bombing Russian refineries, which he says exacerbates a global diesel shortage. The Ukrainian leader has rejected such requests unless Russia stops attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The Financial Times reported that during the talks in Miami, Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility that US intelligence sharing could be cut off if Kyiv did not halt the strikes.

articles.title: On October 7, Hamas’s goal was not the Nova festival - it was New York - opinion
articles.body:
I never thought I would ever write a book.
At The Jerusalem Post, I wrote more than 10,000 articles, but I don’t think any of them exceeded 4,000 words. How could I ever write 60,000? Some magazine articles I wrote covered six pages, but that’s far from 200 pages.
I had every reason to doubt that I would be able to concentrate and maintain focus for the time it would take.
But when Wicked Son Publishers in New York presented an opportunity and a unique professional and personal situation permitted it, I jumped at the chance.
After more than 20 books in English and Hebrew were written on what went wrong on the military and intelligence battlefronts, I became aware of the glaring need for a book presenting an Israeli insider’s perspective on what went wrong on the media battlefield for Israel and the international Jewish community. After all, every day since Oct. 7 has arguably gotten progressively easier on the military battlefield, while every day since the massacre has gotten progressively harder in the narrative war.
It could also be argued that while most of the lessons from the blunders on the military battlefield that led to Oct. 7 have long been learned and implemented, the media battlefield’s mistakes are still far from being internalized, and they have led in part to the antisemitism that is currently spiraling out of control in America and around the world.
My book reveals that unleashing that overwhelming and no longer shocking hatred of Jews was actually the goal of Hamas head Yahya Sinwar and the Hamas leadership, who were unaware of the Nova music festival taking place 5 km. (3.1 miles) east of the Israel-Gaza border fence.
They were, however, well aware that the Palestinian cause was gradually being forgotten, as the Abraham Accords were about to expand to Saudi Arabia and then to other countries and leave them behind. They wanted to bring the Palestinians to the forefront of the world’s agenda, and no one can deny that they have succeeded beyond their wildest dreams.
Hamas’s political bureau head Ismail Haniyeh said very openly in a speech to the International Union of Muslim Scholars in Doha, Qatar, on January 9, 2024, that Hamas initiated what it strategically called Operation Al-Aqsa Flood to return the Palestinians to the international agenda.
“The world, the international community, and global decision-making circles no longer raised the issue of Palestine,” Haniyeh complained as he justified the attack. “The world began to deal with it as an internal Zionist matter, to be handled in its own way. There were no international resolutions, no conferences, and not even talk of a two-state solution. Such talk was no longer circulating among decision-makers worldwide. The issue became completely marginalized.”
The element of surprise
SO HOW DID they succeed in drawing back the world’s attention? By using what Haniyeh called “verbal jihad” and taking advantage of several assets, which are each explained from behind the scenes in the book.
Their first asset was the element of surprise, which caught both the Israeli government and the American Jewish establishment completely off guard. And Israel was even less prepared for Oct. 7 on the media battlefield than it had been on the military battlefield.
The IDF may have mishandled Oct. 7 completely, and its functioning was briefly limited, but at least it continued to exist. The Israeli government employed no English spokesperson on Oct. 7, nor did it have a consul-general in New York, where most of the international media is based. There was no strategic plan ready to deal with a crisis and media circus of this magnitude.
Hamas, by contrast, did have a strategic plan for the narrative war – formulated by their notoriously brilliant veteran propaganda chief Abu Obeida – which Hamas documents have revealed was prepared well in advance, alongside their military plans. They also had an army of trained journalist loyalists who worked for top international media outlets during the war, due in part to Israel’s decision not to let independent media into Gaza since 2014.
These terrorists, whom the world accepted as journalists, became part of the blood libel machine, funded by the Qataris who maintained an open channel of communication between Hamas and their government mouthpiece Al Jazeera, which was deeply involved in all aspects of strategically broadcasting the war to the world.
This all overwhelmed the leadership of the American Jewish community, which had been concentrating on building bridges with progressive groups to deal with intersectionality but found itself abandoned by purported allies when it needed them most. Jewish college students were nowhere near ready to go on defense in a fight forced on them and certainly not to go on offense.
Just like Hamas had 16 years to prepare for this war while Israel had not one day, anti-Israel groups in the United States and other countries around the world had been preparing for Oct. 7 for decades, with unlimited funding at their disposal. They were an integral part of the strategic plan – and the blood libel machine – and unlike Hamas, Hezbollah, Syria, and Iran, their success has not been halted.
Continuing to spread hatred of Jews and of the State of Israel
They have continued to spread hatred of the Jewish people and the Jewish state, gaining positions of influence and scaring ordinary Jews who had no connection to what was going on in the Middle East, some 12,000 km. away. They exploit their numerical advantage and their head start on social media and AI platforms in what is nowhere near a fair fight.
Sinwar’s goal was to initiate a future multifront war that could succeed after Israel lost the world’s support, and ideally after Iran obtained a nuclear capability. That may appear more unrealistic now because of Israel’s military successes on seven fronts, but if international condemnation of Israel continues making the Jewish state even more isolated, it certainly cannot be ruled out.
That is why the book urges future governments of Israel to make the narrative war a top priority – as this column has repeatedly – which even Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu himself admits openly has not been the case since Oct. 7. It is also why the book offers readers more than 30 tools for fighting for Israel on social media and AI platforms.
Those tools were praised in the book’s endorsements by hasbara (public diplomacy) heroes Natan Sharansky, Michael Oren, Nachman Shai, and Gil Troy, as well as Noa Tishby, who put the book in context in the foreword she wrote.
Because the narrative war has been at the forefront of international headlines lately, Wicked Son advanced its publication by a month, and it went on Amazon on the eve of the massacre’s Jewish calendar anniversary, Simchat Torah. I symbolically – and chillingly – received my first copy from the Pomeranz bookstore in Jerusalem on Oct. 7.
So I really did write a book, and I hope it makes the positive impact it needs to, so there won’t be anything like Oct. 7 ever again – on either the military or media battlefields. ■
The writer is the author of the book The Blood Libel Machine: Exposing the Anti-Israel Hate Network and How to Fight Back, which can be ordered from Pomeranz Books in Israel and Amazon around the world.

articles.title: Once considered “taboo,” Russian assassination plots against European defense executives are escalating as its hybrid warfare grows bolder, intelligence agencies warn – FT
articles.body:
Russia is expanding efforts to target European defense industry leaders as part of a broader campaign of sabotage and hybrid operations aimed at weakening support for Ukraine, the Financial Times reported on 11 October, citing officials from five European intelligence agencies.
The warnings come amid a wider increase in Russia-linked sabotage and other covert operations targeting European defense companies and critical infrastructure. Moscow is expanding its so-called hybrid warfare campaign against European countries as they continue to support Ukraine, using covert networks, intimidation, and suspected sabotage to undermine security and deter further assistance to Kyiv.
The FT reported that assassinations of civilian targets in Europe, once considered "taboo" even within Russian intelligence services, are becoming an increasingly prominent part of the Kremlin’s plans.
Russian operatives target defense industry leaders
European intelligence officials told the FT that Russian operatives are targeting chief executives and senior employees at defense companies, including smaller firms manufacturing drones and drone components.
The campaign comes as Russia seeks to undermine European backing for Ukraine amid a battlefield stalemate and mounting pressure on the Russian economy.
The warnings have prompted defense companies to strengthen security around senior executives. Some have increased personal protection, while others have relocated production sites in response to suspected Russian threats, according to the FT.
Germany's domestic intelligence service, the BfV, has stepped up contact with employees and management at German defense companies and recommended that some use privately contracted close-protection teams, an agency official told the newspaper.
BfV chief Sinan Selen warned German lawmakers that Russia was deliberately planning acts of violence against individuals through state or state-controlled actors. He said the operations were evolving in their targets, methods, and use of organized crime networks.
Russia adapts its methods to carry out attacks
According to the intelligence officials cited by the FT, Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, has adapted its methods by working more closely with criminal groups and dividing surveillance, logistics, planning, and execution among different operatives.
Officials said some plots had been disrupted, while other cases involved surveillance of targets at home and at work.
The campaign's intended effect extends beyond any individual attack. One European intelligence official told the FT that the threat is psychological, designed to make people reconsider doing business with Ukraine.
Although some Russian operations remain amateurish and have been detected early, the resulting uncertainty forces companies to devote more resources to security. Smaller firms, which may have fewer resources to protect their personnel and facilities, could be particularly vulnerable.
Plot against Rheinmetall CEO raised alarm in 2024
European defense executives have been on heightened alert since 2024, when US and German intelligence agencies uncovered a Russian plot against Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger, a prominent advocate of supplying weapons to Ukraine.
Papperger has said he now receives round-the-clock protection from private security personnel and police.
The FT reported that European intelligence agencies now view threats against defense industry leaders as part of a broader effort to disrupt the production and supply of weapons to Ukraine, rather than isolated plots against individual executives.

articles.title: Dozens reportedly injured in Yemeni Houthi attack at Riyadh airport
articles.body:
The latest attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital of Riyadh killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others, civil aviation authorities said early on Sunday, with some in a critical condition. A Saudi-led coalition blamed Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen.
A missile struck a King Khalid international airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorised to speak to the media.
A Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals.
The US president, Donald Trump, said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen. “We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, called the attacks “reprehensible” and said “they must stop now”.
One witness at the Riyadh airport reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded.
“I was on gate 403,” at the domestic terminal, the witness told the Agence France-Presse news agency. “I saw [gate] 401 hit, I saw injured [people] in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”
The relative of one injured person said they had been wounded in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass and taken to hospital.
A projectile also fell near the King Fahd international airport in Dammam, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis. The Dammam airport has become an important alternative to Riyadh amid the recent spate of attacks.
There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sana’a international airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
Schools in Riyadh will move to remote learning for a week, according to the education ministry, following the deadly attack.
Saturday’s incident comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis on the kingdom. The airport has already been attacked twice this week, leaving four people dead and others wounded, and badly damaging an aircraft.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.
The attack came as forces allied to the UN-recognised government in Yemen claim to have mounted a successful offensive to retake the Bab al-Mandab strait from Houthi rebels, but accounts vary as to whether the push has been repelled.
A Houthi spokesperson said forces from the Saudi-backed government based in Aden “were targeted with a large number of ballistic missiles, artillery support and heavy weapons, resulting in the destruction of more than 22 armoured vehicles and the killing and wounding of dozens, including a number of commanders.
“More than 30 ambulances arrived in Aden to transport the dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations.”
By contrast, the Saudi ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed al-Jaber, said: “Blessed Friday and victory for every Yemeni and Arab. Bab al-Mandab has been cleared of the remnants of the Houthi terrorist militia.”
The exposed 5 sq mile (13 sq km) Perim Island straddles the strait, acting as a lookout point for all traffic from the Red Sea into the Gulf of Aden and towards the Indian Ocean. Aidarous al-Zubaidi, the president of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), one of the main political forces in the south of Yemen, claimed the island and coastal area had been recaptured from Houthi hands.
An official military spokesperson for the UN-recognised government forces qualified the claim, saying only half the area had been recaptured so far. Waddah al-Dabish said newly established Houthi defensive lines had been broken on the land next to the strait, leading to the death of thousands of Houthi fighters.
It is thought that as many as 500 Houthi fighters are stationed on the island, and Saudi Arabia is desperate to be able to report that the strait has been reclaimed to show that the land counteroffensive it launched at the beginning of the week is advancing.
The report came as the United Nations’ special envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, admitted to the UN security council in New York that Yemen – one of the poorest countries in the world – had lapsed back into full-scale war and said the first victims would be women and children.
The Houthis seized control of the strait two weeks ago and said no Saudi-linked commercial traffic would be permitted to go through the narrow waterway. The Houthis are waging a war to remove Saudi influence from Yemen, and have been mounting missile attacks on Riyadh in support of this objective.
There have been previous premature reports of military breakthroughs by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government since it launched its counteroffensive at the start of the week, but the recapture of the land by the strait and Perim Island (also known as Mayyun Island) is a military prize western governments desperately need.

articles.title: Trump: Putin Wants Ukraine Deal, Praises Russian Oil Supplies
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said that Russian President Vladimir Putin expressed a strong desire to reach a settlement to conclude the war in Ukraine during a telephone conversation between the two leaders on Friday.
Speaking to journalists on Saturday, Oct. 10, Trump stated that Moscow is seeking a negotiated outcome, while asserting that President Volodymyr Zelensky has been unwilling to finalize an agreement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I think that Russia would like to make a deal, and we’ve had it back and forth, but Russia would like to make a deal,” Trump told reporters.
“This is something that could have been solved many times, but for whatever reason, Zelensky does not want to make a deal.”
Asked specifically what Putin communicated during their bilateral call, Trump stated that the Russian leader expressed a commitment to ending hostilities.
“He’d like to see a settlement. President Putin would like to see a settlement strongly,” Trump said.
Trump also commended Putin for releasing Russian oil onto international markets, describing the shipments as a positive contribution to lowering global energy costs.
“And look, he is freeing up a lot of oil for the world, okay? A good thing,” Trump added. “And by the way, at a very low price.”
Calls for Ukrainian political change
Trump’s remarks to reporters followed his announcement on Friday of a bilateral commercial diesel agreement reached with Moscow, under which Russia agreed to deliver over 1 million metric tons of diesel fuel to American and international buyers through 2027.
US Lawmakers Draft Bill to Block Russian Oil Purchases
Speaking roughly a month ahead of the US midterm elections as retail diesel prices in the US approached $6 per gallon, Trump reiterated sharp criticism of Zelensky, accusing the Ukrainian leadership of compounding energy pressures for American farmers and transportation networks through deep-interdiction strikes against Russian oil refineries.
“He wants to make problems for the world, for our farmers with diesel,” Trump said. “Zelensky could have settled this war many, many times, but he chooses not to. I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
The US president’s calls for a leadership transition in Kyiv drew a rebuttal from Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, who affirmed on Sunday that only the Ukrainian electorate holds the legal and sovereign authority to determine national governance during wartime.
Sybiha stated that external criticism only demonstrates that Zelensky is performing his duties effectively, emphasizing that the Ukrainian head of state retains broad public support.
To facilitate the Russian fuel shipments, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The waiver was granted three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which established mandatory statutory sanctions and tariffs on purchases of Russian petroleum.
The agreement was announced while Ukrainian negotiators were engaged in multilateral consultations with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami.
Zelensky described the Miami talks as a “smokescreen” for bilateral economic concessions to the Kremlin, noting that granting Moscow market access generates revenues that sustain Russian military operations.
Under the administration’s proposed diplomatic framework, Washington has asked Kyiv to halt drone attacks on Russian refineries to stabilize energy benchmarks. However, the proposal does not include a binding condition requiring the Russian military to suspend missile and drone strikes against Ukraine’s power and heating infrastructure.
Ukrainian officials have stated that Kyiv will not suspend its asymmetric interdiction campaign against Russian refining installations without an enforceable, mutual energy ceasefire that protects Ukrainian utilities ahead of winter.

articles.title: Missile strikes Riyadh airport terminal, leaving multiple people wounded
articles.body:
Riyadh’s international airport in Saudi Arabia was struck Saturday night by a missile launched by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, two days after another deadly attack on King Khalid International Airport. The attack marked the deadliest strike in a Gulf Arab country since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in February, and came as President Donald Trump said Washington could join Saudi military strikes against the Houthis, although no decision had been made.
A regional official familiar with the details told The Associated Press that the missile struck an area housing passenger Terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights, and that there were “many casualties.”
Saudi aviation authorities later said at least 12 people were killed and 309 wounded in the attack.
According to the statement, those killed included an American citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian, a Palestinian, a Sudanese national, two Bangladeshis and four Saudis.
Reports said the airport was evacuated and numerous ambulances were dispatched to the scene. Saudi authorities deployed heavy security at the complex and warned against circulating any footage of the Houthi attacks. So far, no footage from the airport has been released.
The New York Times cited two Western officials and one Arab official, all speaking anonymously because they were not authorized to discuss the attack publicly. Earlier, a medical source at a Riyadh hospital told AFP that at least two people had been killed, identifying one as an Egyptian crew member working for a Saudi airline and the other as a Palestinian carrying Egyptian travel documents.
Saudi authorities initially confirmed injuries without providing a casualty toll. The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said it was still assessing the damage at the airport and announced the temporary suspension of operations. Incoming flights were diverted, departures were delayed or canceled and passengers were evacuated as emergency crews responded.
The missile struck the complex housing the airport's domestic terminals, triggering panic among passengers and staff. Witnesses described hearing an explosion and seeing injured people near boarding gates. Foreign embassies urged their citizens to avoid the airport and surrounding areas.
Senior Houthi official Mohammed al-Bukhaiti claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack, saying it was retaliation for Saudi strikes in Yemen, including attacks he said had targeted civilian infrastructure. He argued that the protections afforded to civilian facilities should apply equally in Yemen and elsewhere, citing airports, seaports, hospitals, markets and venues for weddings and funerals.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said later Saturday in a statement that a projectile had fallen near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam. The airport, in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Region, has become an important alternative to Riyadh airport following the spate of attacks on the capital.
The attack in Riyadh came just two days after another deadly Houthi assault on the airport. Saudi authorities said three Saudi citizens, including an airline pilot, were killed in Thursday's strikes, which also damaged an aircraft belonging to the national carrier Saudia.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure in recent weeks, seeking to disrupt air traffic and increase pressure on Riyadh. The group has warned international airlines against flying through Saudi airspace, declaring much of it a military operational zone.
The repeated attacks also threaten Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's efforts to transform Riyadh into a major international business and travel hub, with high-profile international events scheduled in the Saudi capital in the coming weeks.
Trump weighs joining Saudi strikes
Asked Saturday whether the United States would join Saudi Arabia's military campaign against the Houthis, Trump said the administration was considering the possibility.
"We may. We're going to look at it," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "We move very quickly."
Trump said Washington had only recently learned of the latest attack and would decide how to respond. His comments raised the possibility of more direct American involvement in a conflict that has intensified across Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
Saudi warplanes have been conducting airstrikes against Houthi targets in Yemen in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which has launched a major counteroffensive aimed at retaking territory captured by the rebels.
The Houthis say Yemen has been subjected to hundreds of Saudi airstrikes in recent weeks, including attacks that they claim have killed children and other civilians. The Saudi bombing campaign and the Houthis' attacks on civilian aviation facilities have intensified the conflict on both sides of the border.
The renewed fighting has centered on the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and serves as a vital maritime passage for international commerce and energy shipments.
The Houthis seized significant stretches of Yemen's western coastline during a rapid offensive last month, threatening maritime traffic through the strait. Saudi-backed government forces subsequently launched an operation known as Yemen Dawn, seeking to reverse those gains.
Government forces have claimed progress in recapturing territory around the strait, while the Houthis have disputed some of those claims and said they repelled attacks. Heavy fighting has also continued in areas around Taiz, with both sides reporting casualties.
Pakistan and Turkey drawn into Saudi defense efforts
The escalation has also placed renewed attention on Saudi Arabia's defense cooperation with Pakistan and Turkey, which signed a trilateral agreement in Mecca in August.
The three countries agreed to implement collective defense arrangements and deploy military capabilities to Saudi Arabia in response to the growing threat.
Pakistan, however, has emphasized that its role is defensive. Islamabad has said its forces will not cross into Yemen to carry out offensive operations against the Houthis, although they may assist in protecting Saudi territory and sovereignty.
Turkey has also framed its involvement within the trilateral defense arrangement, while Saudi Arabia continues its military campaign in support of the Yemeni government.
First published: 19:05, 10.10.26

articles.title: Only Ukrainians Decide Leadership, Sybiha Says
articles.body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha responded on Sunday, Oct. 11, to statements by US President Donald Trump suggesting that Ukraine should elect a new president, affirming that only the Ukrainian people hold the authority to determine their national leadership.
Writing on X, Sybiha emphasized that President Volodymyr Zelensky maintains the confidence of the Ukrainian public as he leads the country during wartime.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“President Volodymyr Zelensky leads our nation in a time of war – a war for independence, freedom, and dignity,” Sybiha stated. “He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support.”
Sybiha’s remarks followed comments made by Trump to reporters on Saturday, in which the US president argued that Zelensky had passed up opportunities to negotiate an end to the armed conflict with Russia and suggested that Ukraine should replace its leadership.
President @ZelenskyyUa leads our nation in a time of war — a war for independence, freedom, and dignity. He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support.
— Andrii Sybiha 🇺🇦 (@andrii_sybiha) October 10, 2026
Trump’s remarks and calls for political change
Speaking to journalists roughly a month ahead of the US midterm elections, Trump criticized the Ukrainian head of state for not finalizing a negotiated settlement with Moscow.
“Zelensky could have settled this war many, many times, but he chooses not to,” Trump told reporters. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
Trump additionally faulted Ukraine’s long-range drone strikes against Russian oil refineries, claiming the operations have contributed to elevated retail fuel prices internationally. The comments came as domestic diesel prices in the United States approached $6 per gallon.
There Will be no Breakthrough in Peace Talks, - Stefan Korshak
“He wants to make problems for the world, for our farmers with diesel,” Trump added.
The public criticism echoed prior statements made by Trump throughout 2025 calling for national elections in Ukraine. American billionaire Elon Musk subsequently backed Trump’s statements on Saturday, writing on X that Zelensky had “gone too far.”
The diplomatic friction between Washington and Kyiv follows Trump’s announcement on Friday, Oct. 9, of a commercial diesel agreement reached with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Under the framework announced by the White House, Moscow agreed to deliver 300,000 metric tons of diesel fuel immediately, with scheduled deliveries scaling up to 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons in subsequent phases through 2027.
To facilitate the shipments, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The waiver was granted three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which aimed to establish statutory penalties across Russia’s energy, banking, and defense sectors.
The announcement occurred while a Ukrainian delegation was participating in multilateral security consultations with US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami. Zelensky described the Miami session as a “smokescreen” for bilateral economic concessions to the Kremlin.

articles.title: Trump’s diesel deal with Putin draws calls for EU resolve
articles.body:
- Urgewald urged European leaders not to weaken Russian energy sanctions after Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Putin on Oct. 9.
- The U.S. Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel through April 2027, days before the Graham Act’s Oct. 18 implementation deadline.
A German environmental and human rights group has urged European leaders not to weaken sanctions on Russian energy after President Donald Trump announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply diesel fuel to the United States and global markets, a week before a new U.S. sanctions law on Russia reaches its first implementation deadline.
Urgewald said Europe should keep its restrictions on Russian liquefied natural gas, or LNG, and on the shipping, insurance and professional services that support Russia’s energy exports, regardless of the shift in Washington.
“Trump’s deal with Putin is an affront to the civilised world. While Russia continues its assault on Ukraine, he is handing Moscow a fresh energy lifeline. With just over a week until the Lindsey Graham Act’s implementation deadline, this deal undermines the pressure Congress intended to impose,” said Alexander Kirk, sanctions campaigner at Urgewald.
“This is Europe’s Churchill moment. European leaders must stand firm against aggression. Washington’s retreat must not become an excuse to weaken European sanctions or reopen the door to Russian energy. There must be no watering down of restrictions on Russian LNG or the shipping, insurance and professional services that keep this trade moving,” said Kirk.
Trump announced the deal on Oct. 9 after a phone call with Putin. In a post on Truth Social, he said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons after that. He later said Russia could deliver about 3 million more tons depending on the condition of its refineries. The Kremlin said the call, which lasted about an hour and a half, covered large-scale economic initiatives including fuel supplies.
The same day, the U.S. Treasury Department issued a general license that temporarily waives sanctions on Russian diesel through April 2027. The White House has presented the move as a way to bring down fuel prices, which have surged worldwide since the start of the war with Iran and as Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries forced Moscow to restrict diesel exports. Trump publicly thanked Putin for the agreement. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned it, and some energy analysts said the deal helps Russia sell off summer-grade diesel it no longer needs before winter.
The timing has drawn attention because of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Trump signed on Sept. 18 after it passed the Senate 86-11 and the House 262-159. The law requires the president to impose many of its measures by Oct. 18, including sanctions on Russian state-linked companies and banks, action against “shadow fleet” tankers carrying Russian oil, and tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the largest buyers of Russian crude and gas. It also allows the president to waive measures by certifying to Congress that a waiver is in the national interest.
The White House has not said whether the diesel deal will affect how it implements the Graham Act, and neither Washington nor Moscow has released the terms of the fuel agreement, including pricing or which buyers will receive the diesel. European Union officials have not publicly said whether the U.S. move will change their own sanctions timeline on Russian energy.

articles.title: Trump tells Ukraine to replace Zelenskyy in Russia diesel deal spat
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to "get a new leader" following Volodymyr Zelenskyy's criticism of Washington’s decision to ease Russian diesel sanctions, as Trump faces surging fuel prices ahead of midterm elections.
Trump, whose Republicans face dim prospects in next month's vote partly because of soaring energy costs, defended a deal allowing more Russian diesel onto global markets after saying Vladimir Putin strongly wanted to reach a settlement in Ukraine.
Trump accused Zelenskyy of blocking a deal with Moscow and ignoring instructions not to strike Russian refineries, while Kyiv and its European allies warned that easing pressure on Moscow would help fund the Kremlin's war.
Meanwhile, the latest Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least 21 people, including children.
Trump announced Friday that he had spoken to Putin and agreed Russia would release large amounts of diesel into global markets.
Ukraine and its European allies expressed dismay, with Zelenskyy telling reporters Friday it was a "weak decision."
Asked about the criticism, Trump said Zelenskyy had disobeyed his orders not to strike Russian refineries and that the attacks risked worsening fuel shortages linked to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
"He better damn well stop," Trump said.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals that, for some reason, he never does," Trump said.
Trump later said Putin was interested in ending the war.
"Russia would like to make a deal ... but for whatever reason, Zelenskyy does not want to make a deal," he told reporters.
"President Putin would like to see a settlement, strongly."
The U.S. president also criticized Zelenskyy for not holding an election since Russia's 2022 invasion.
"I think he should have an election and he could have settled this thing many times," Trump said.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said lifting sanctions on Russian diesel would only help sustain Russia's war effort.
"This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't," she wrote online.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham reiterated his "complete solidarity" with Zelenskyy in a call.
Downing Street said Burnham also pledged that Britain would "strengthen its sanctions on Russia."
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga also backed his president. "He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide," he said in a post on X.
On Saturday, a Russian glide bomb attack on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia killed 20 people, including three children, according to Ukraine's state rescue service.
"Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Zelenskyy said in a post on X.
A Russian drone attack in the central Dnipropetrovsk region killed an 11-year-old boy, regional officials said.
Russian strikes also caused widespread power cuts in Kyiv.
Russia's Defense Ministry said it had hit a "data center" used by Ukraine's military.
The diesel deal was announced as U.S., Ukrainian and European officials met in Miami in a renewed bid to end the conflict.
Ukraine's delegation was headed home on Saturday, an aide to Zelenskyy said.
U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said on X the talks involved "the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO."
He described the discussions as "constructive" and focused on ways to "de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace."
The Kremlin said Saturday that Trump had conveyed his ideas about how to de-escalate the war to Putin during a phone call Friday.
Putin received the proposals "with understanding," the Kremlin said, without elaborating.
Russia, which launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, now occupies roughly one-fifth of Ukrainian territory.

articles.title: Russia steps up assassination attempts targeting defence company executives in Europe, FT says
articles.body:
Russia steps up assassination attempts targeting defence company executives in Europe, FT says
European intelligence services have warned executives at defence companies across Europe that Russia is stepping up attempts to assassinate them in an effort to intimidate Ukraine's partners.
Source: Financial Times, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Representatives of five different European intelligence services said the Kremlin has ordered an expansion of sabotage and hybrid operations in Europe to significantly weaken support for Kyiv in the coming months.
Intelligence officials say the killing of European civilians, once considered taboo even for the Russian secret services, is becoming an increasingly important part of these plans.
According to the warning, Kremlin agents could target executives and other senior employees at defence companies. Executives of smaller companies are also at risk, particularly those involved in manufacturing drones or their components.
A representative of Germany's Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) said the agency has significantly stepped up its engagement with employees and executives at German defence companies, including recommending that they hire private close-protection teams.
"Russia is engaged in the deliberate planning of acts of violence against individuals by state or state-controlled actors. We are observing a further development of these actions in terms of the targets, the methods and the actors involved, including the use of organised crime structures," BfV head Sinan Selen warned German lawmakers.
Several defence company executives told the Financial Times that they have stepped up their personal security over the past six months on the advice of the government's security services. Others said they took such measures only when travelling abroad.
Responsibility for potential assassination attempts is largely attributed to the GRU, Russia's military intelligence agency .
According to intelligence sources, Russian officers are increasingly working with organised crime groups, using cross-border agent networks and dividing intelligence gathering, logistics, planning and execution among different cells or individuals, rather than relying on "disposable" agents recruited online for money.
In some cases, active plots have already been uncovered and thwarted. In others, suspicious activity has been observed, including surveillance of individuals' daily routines at home and at work.
"The main goal from the Russian perspective is still psychological. Just by making people feel they might be a target, they are having their effect. They want individuals to think twice before doing business with Ukraine," one intelligence official said.
Background:
- Executives at Europe's largest arms manufacturers have been on heightened alert since early 2024, when US and German intelligence services uncovered a Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger, CEO of German company Rheinmetall.
- In January 2025, NATO officially confirmed that Russia had intended to kill Papperger.
- In early August, a Russian couple were detained in Sweden after setting up camp near a property where a person under personal protection lived. It later emerged that the person in question was Micael Johansson, CEO of the Swedish defence company Saab.

articles.title: Australia keeps Russian fuel out even as US opens its market: “We do not want Vladimir Putin to benefit from this war in Middle East”
articles.body:
Australia has no need to buy fuel from Russia, despite US President Donald Trump’s move to bring Russian diesel back to world markets. Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen says that imports from Russia will remain banned to ensure the country does not benefit from its invasion of Ukraine, Bloomberg reports.
Trump has agreed with Russia's President Vladimir Putin to release Russian diesel onto global markets, a move Ukraine says funds a war that has killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians in two days.
“We don’t need or want Russian fuel in Australia. We do not want Vladimir Putin to benefit from this war in the Middle East. What the United States does is a matter for them, but we won’t be changing our approach,” Bowen said.
The deal Australia is turning down
Trump announced on 9 October a series of cargoes beginning this month totaling about 13.5 million barrels of Russian diesel. The release upends years of sanctions, as the White House looks for ways to tame soaring fuel prices before the US midterm elections.
Bowen draws a clear line between that approach and Australia’s. What the US does is its own affair, he stresses, but Canberra will maintain its arrangements with trading partners to keep Russian fuel out of the market.
Enough fuel to hold the line
Australia can hold out without Russian supply, Bowen argues. The country has 43 days’ worth of petrol, two days more than a week earlier, and 31 days’ worth of diesel, one day less, he notes.
He adds that Australia stays in close contact with domestic refiners to keep them running at full capacity. The stance lets Canberra wait out high prices rather than buy fuel that would send money to Moscow.
Australia’s fuel costs have stayed high since the war between the US and Iran disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the route that normally carries about a fifth of the world’s oil and gas.

articles.title: Russian army strikes Sloviansk and Kyiv as Ukrainian drones hit third Yandex data centre
articles.body:
Russian forces struck two apartment blocks in Sloviansk, injuring four, and hit warehouses in Kyiv. Overnight, Ukrainian drones targeted Yandex's data centre in Vladimir, causing major service outages but no casualties.
On the morning of 11 October, the Russian army struck two blocks of flats in Sloviansk in the Donetsk region.
"At this point, four people are known to have been injured", said the city's mayor Vadym Liakh. "Everyone is receiving medical treatment".
There may be people trapped under the rubble, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Warehouses are on fire outside Kyiv following an overnight Russian attack. Storage facilities at an industrial plant in the Bucha district of the Ukrainian capital caught fire, and firefighters are still working to extinguish the blaze.
A paramedic and a driver were injured when a Russian drone hit an ambulance in the Sumy region. According to the head of the regional military administration, Oleh Hryhorov, the medical workers managed to get out of the damaged vehicle on their own.
Emergency power cuts were introduced on Sunday in several regions of Ukraine because of the difficult situation in the energy sector caused by Russian shelling, the press service of the national energy company Ukrenergo said.
Previously published schedules for hourly power cuts are currently not in force. The emergency outages will be lifted once the situation in the power system stabilises.
Ukrainian drones hit Yandex, third data centre targeted
Overnight into Sunday, Ukrainian drones attacked Russian technology giant Yandex's data centre in Vladimir, east of Moscow in the third reported attack on the firm in days.
The company said the centre's infrastructure had been damaged and its operations completely halted. According to the latest information, there were no casualties in the attack.
Yandex added that it is continuing to assess the state of the infrastructure and cannot yet say how long repairs will take. This is already the company's third data centre to be attacked in October.
Yandex, often dubbed "Russia's Google", runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as food-ordering and taxi apps used by tens of millions of people.
Governor Aleksandr Avdeyev confirmed (source in Russian) the UAV attack in Vladimir and the ensuing fire. He said residential areas had escaped destruction. Residents of the houses closest to the attack site have begun to be evacuated.
In Vladimir, two substations supplying electricity to 5,000 residents were switched off. An hour later, the governor said that 80% of the power supply had been restored and heating and water supplies were back to normal.
Preliminary reports suggest that a supercomputer housed at the Vladimir data centre was damaged. An identical machine is located at the Yandex data centre in Ryazan that was also targeted.
Taxi and navigation disruption
In the wake of the attack, users experienced widespread disruptions to the company's services. People were unable to order taxis in Moscow, St. Petersburg, Perm, Krasnoyarsk, Vladivostok, Ulan-Ude, Yekaterinburg and other Russian cities.
"I can't get anything to work at all", said Yevgeny, a 69-year-old sitting behind the wheel of a Yandex-branded taxi near Moscow.
"I've never seen anything like this before. It hasn't happened in the last five years. Now I don't know what to do", he said.
Similar problems were reported in Serbia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia. Drivers say they cannot log into the app or are facing navigation failures, while passengers see no available cars. There have also been reports of outages across many of the company's other services.
On 9 October, drones attacked (source in Russian) Yandex's data centre in Kaluga. On the morning of 8 October, the Ukrainian armed forces struck (source in Russian) a Yandex data centre near Ryazan. After that, malfunctions began in the internal systems of major Russian companies. Websites of major Russian media outlets also stopped loading.
Ukrainian monitoring channels reported strikes on Sunday on a movable railway bridge (source in Russian) in Rostov-on-Don, near the Black Sea. The regional authorities have not yet reported it.
In early October, Russia repeatedly carried out (source in Russian) strikes on key bridges in Kyiv. According to The Telegraph, against the backdrop of military setbacks, Putin decided to switch to attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure and the bridges in Kyiv.
The crisis centre of the Krasnodar region reported that "fragments of drones" had fallen on the grounds of Sochi airport. A fire broke out in one of the administrative buildings, with no casualties. Debris also fell in a residential area.
Russia's Defence Ministry said that overnight air defence forces had shot down 479 Ukrainian drones over 17 regions of Russia and the annexed Crimea.

articles.title: EU imports record 12.18 million tons of Russian Arctic LNG in nine months, 9.5% more than year earlier — research group
articles.body:
Europe keeps buying record amounts of Russian gas even as it plans to punish its war machine against Ukraine. The EU ports took in a record 12.18 million tons of Russian liquefied natural gas from January to September, 9.5% more than in the same period of 2025, according to a study by the German group Urgewald based on Kpler tracking data.
Europe spent about 7.88 billion euros on that Russian gas in nine months, revenue that helps fund a war Russia wages with daily missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities. The flow continues even as the EU prepares its largest-ever package of sanctions against Russia’s military industry.
The gas comes from Russia’s Yamal project, which sent 167 cargoes to EU ports over the nine months, roughly one every 1.6 days. Europe took 85% of the project’s recorded deliveries by volume, remaining by far its biggest market, Urgewald reports.
Europe’s share grew even as Yamal’s worldwide deliveries fell 1.3%, so the EU absorbed a larger slice of Russia’s Arctic output. In September alone, EU ports received 792,440 tons worth an estimated 818 million euros, nearly three-quarters of it going to France.
Washington could pull the plug by 18 October
The imports run up against a looming US decision. The Trump administration has until 18 October to complete its first review under the Lindsey Graham sanctions act, signed into law on 18 September, which allows Washington to sanction this gas trade at any time, the group notes.
However, after the US allowed Russian diesel to enter the US and global market, the decision will likely remain stalled.
Originally, the law covered Yamal’s leadership, foreign vessels that knowingly carried Russian LNG, and foreign ports that serviced US-sanctioned ships. Yamal depends on specialized Arc7 ice-class tankers and on nearby European ports where they can unload and quickly return, so closing that route would make the Arctic trade far harder to sustain.
Europe’s own ban is still months away
The EU’s measures so far have barely dented the trade. A ban on short-term LNG contracts took effect in April and has had no visible effect, while the full import ban under long-term contracts only starts on 1 January 2027, Urgewald says.
Every month of largely uninterrupted trade means more revenue for Russia while Ukraine suffers daily attacks, sanction campaigner Sebastian Rötters says. The next EU package should close the remaining loopholes, above all those keeping the Arc7 tanker fleet running.

articles.title: Ukraine ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Russia stops attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukraine ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Russia stops attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure – Zelenskyy
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine is ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries, provided Russian forces stop attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)
Quote: "The real cause of the war in Europe is Russia and Russia alone. It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so. Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure. Any de-escalation steps must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees."
Details: Zelenskyy stressed that any de-escalation measures must be mutual and backed by genuine guarantees.
Meanwhile, the president reported that, in the past week alone, Russian forces had launched around 1,450 guided aerial bombs, 75 missiles of various types and more than 1,640 attack drones at Ukraine, around 60% of which were jet-powered.
Background:
- On 9 October, US President Donald Trump said he had had a "highly successful discussion" with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin and reached an agreement on lifting sanctions on Russian diesel fuel.
- Zelenskyy strongly criticised Trump's actions, describing the easing of sanctions as an "absolutely terrible" move. He stressed that this "birthday present for Putin" will provide Russia with billions more to continue the war.
- Zelenskyy said Ukraine's negotiating team in the US had been used as "cover" while Trump and Putin reached agreements on fuel supplies.
- Yuri Ushakov, an aide to the Russian leader, stated that in a phone call with Trump, Putin rejected the possibility of peace talks, stressing that Russia will continue military operations until it has achieved "all its objectives".
- It was reported that negotiations in Miami between representatives of the US, Ukraine, European countries and NATO on ways to de-escalate and end the war had ended earlier than planned.
- On 10 October, Dmytro Lytvyn, the president's communications adviser, stated that the Ukrainian delegation that took part in the negotiations in the US is already on its way home.
