articles.title: US Envoys Witkoff, Kushner May Visit Russia Soon
articles.body:
US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner may visit Russia in the coming weeks following a phone conversation between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, Russian state news agency TASS reported.
Citing Russian sources, TASS reported that the trip could take place within the next two weeks, although specific dates have not yet been finalized.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A source confirmed the likelihood of another visit by the US representatives, noting that technical details and schedules remain subject to bilateral coordination.
The reports of prospective travel follow a telephone conversation on Friday, Oct. 9, between Trump and Putin.
Following that call, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told Russian state media that Putin reiterated Moscow’s intent to sustain military operations until all Kremlin objectives are fulfilled, rejecting the resumption of formal peace negotiations.
Ushakov claimed that Trump instructed American officials to relay the diplomatic positions articulated by Moscow directly to the Ukrainian government.
Diplomatic outreach following Miami consultations
The prospective trip follows multilateral consultations convened by the US in Miami on Friday, Oct. 9. The six-hour session brought together Witkoff, Ukrainian negotiators, and representatives from Britain, France, Germany, the European Commission, and NATO to discuss prospective security arrangements and measures to protect Ukrainian energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
‘I Love the Smell of Russian Gas’: Controversial Polish Politician Backs Nord Stream
While Witkoff described the discussions on social media as “constructive” and aimed at exploring avenues to conclude the armed conflict, the talks concluded without an announced breakthrough.
European and Ukrainian officials have expressed skepticism regarding Moscow’s willingness to engage in substantive de-escalation.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned on Friday that offering economic or diplomatic concessions to Moscow projects weakness, arguing that the Russian leadership interprets accommodations as appeasement rather than incentives for peace.
Witkoff and Kushner previously traveled to Moscow and Kyiv in September to meet with senior government officials, as the Trump administration formulated proposals to address the diplomatic impasse.
The prospect of renewed direct contacts in Moscow coincides with debate surrounding Trump’s announcement of a bilateral commercial agreement permitting Russian petroleum shipments into American and global markets.
Under the arrangement announced by Trump on Friday, Russia agreed to supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel fuel immediately, with 500,000 tons scheduled for November and 1 million tons thereafter, potentially scaling up to 3 million tons depending on the operational condition of Russian refineries.
The US Treasury Department subsequently issued a temporary general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The sanctions waiver was granted three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which aimed to expand statutory penalties across Russia’s energy, banking, and defense sectors.
Ukrainian officials, including President Volodymyr Zelensky, criticized the timing of the commercial arrangement while peace delegations were actively negotiating in Miami, cautioning that permitting Russian fuel exports generates revenues that sustain Moscow’s wartime budget.

articles.title: Deadly attack on airport in Saudi Arabia's capital kills 12
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Deadly attack on airport in Saudi Arabia's capital kills 12 people and injures over 300
Saudi Arabia on Sunday extended the closure of the country's main international airport, according to an online flight tracker, a day after a missile attack on the facility killed 12 people from several countries and left more than 300 injured in a major escalation of the war between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom.
A Saudi-led coalition blamed Saturday afternoon's attack on the Houthis. It was the latest of several in the past week at King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, and marked the deadliest attack in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia is the world's top oil exporter, and the attacks have sent up oil prices and rattled markets.
Following the attack, US President Donald Trump said Saturday he was weighing whether the United States would join Saudi strikes against the rebels.
Airport operations were suspended Saturday. Authorities later extended the closure until at least 9PM. Sunday, according to Flightradar24.
Also on Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said 91 Yemenis were killed and 168 injured by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks. It said 60 percent of those killed were women and children.
Mix of nationalities killed at Saudi airport 
The attack struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorised to speak to the media.
The Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said several hospitals were treating the injured.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged in a social media post that an American citizen had been killed in the attack, which he condemned.
The Egyptian man was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flybas, according to the Egyptian state-run Al-Qahera New television.
Trump said he would consider joining strikes against rebels.
The attack is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies, including the United States, to provide military support for the kingdom, which has seemingly tried to avoid all-out war with the Houthis.
Shortly after the attack, Trump said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the rebels. "We may. We're going to look at it," he said. "We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."
Trump said later Saturday that he planned to speak with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Asked if the US might get involved, Trump responded, "We'll find out."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed them for the attack, calling it a "fully-fledged war crime" and vowing a firm response. The airport has no military facilities.
There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier on Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot.
The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.
For Iran, the fighting puts pressure on a key US ally
Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the war on Iran. Now the rebels are a way for Tehran to apply pressure on a key US ally.
The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015 when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the internationally recognised government.
Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas.
Now fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea.
Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defence support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the US has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.
The Houthis this week warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theatre for their military operations.
Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group, and Pakistan International Airlines suspended flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.

articles.title: After RAF Fairford incident, how big a threat to the UK is Iran?
articles.body:
Britain may have been only peripherally involved in the bombing of Iran that Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu started, but in the past fortnight it has become clear that Tehran wants to pose a threat inside the UK in response.
In the aftermath of the confused incident near RAF Fairford, western officials are weighing up whether to warn publicly that Iran now has US military targets in Europe on its mind, such as the air force base in Gloucestershire.
That could come even though there remains British scepticism about Iran’s capability to pull off a drone raid on a secure facility far from Tehran.
What is already accepted by MI5 is that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has sought to coordinate and promote the targeting of the Jewish community in the UK and Europe, starting from March with a string of arson attacks directed at synagogues and similar sites.
That is itself a significant step up from the regime’s longstanding campaign of assassination plots and threats against critics overseas, tasks the IRGC has traditionally hired criminal gangs to carry out.
Exactly what happened at RAF Fairford remains unclear, though Iran may have gained something from it for very little. A week later, last Sunday, a worried US decided to withdraw the 12 B-1 bombers it had stationed there, with leaks to US media suggesting there was a fear of a Ukraine-style drone attack.
What is known is that five men from London drove up in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September, one of whom called 999 as they did so. All five were arrested in Whelford, a village next to the airbase, only to be released on police bail a day later when no explosives were found or discernible plot discovered.
Two more men have been arrested on suspicion of terror offences, and released on police bail. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, has said there were “strong indications” Iran played a part, and on Thursday the Met police chief, Mark Rowley, said “you will see more progress on this investigation”.
RAF Fairford is an exposed site, with plane spotters easily able to get up close enough to photograph and track the forward-deployed US B-1 and B-52 bombers, which with permission from the former prime minister Keir Starmer were taking off to make attack runs into Iran in the spring and early summer.
“Iran has a track record of planning and carrying out attacks especially on opponents of the regime in the UK. Given the use of Fairford by US bombers, it’s only prudent to assume that they would see an interest in attacking a wider range of targets, whatever their involvement in the Fairford incident,” said Lord Ricketts, a former UK national security adviser.
Dr Antonio Giustozzi, a terrorism specialist with the Royal United Services Institute, suggests the drive to the village was “a feint” where individuals, who may have been unwitting, were sent “to hint at what could happen”. But he is sceptical that Iran could pose a real military threat to Fairford or elsewhere.
As for attacking Fairford, piloting first-person view drones of the type used in Ukraine is a skill requiring several days if not weeks of training, while an operation on an airbase would probably take months to prepare. “I doubt that Iran could bring in military-grade explosive to the UK; the last people to do so were the IRA,” Giustozzi said.
A genuine attack on RAF Fairford or similar would almost certainly be a one-way mission ending in capture or even death, which it would be it hard to recruit for. But despite the low risks, the US chose to withdraw the B-1 bombers, which cost $300m (£225m) each, as a precautionary move. It was “an operational decision to reduce the risk”, Rich Knighton, the head of the UK armed forces, said on Thursday.
This week, a US congressional research report counted that 81 US military planes, helicopters or drones had been destroyed or damaged in the Iran war, including several struck on the ground at bases in Saudi Arabia and Jordan, a reminder that Iran fought back more effectively than the US acknowledged. The value of lost aircraft and air defence systems is estimated at $1.9bn and $3.3bn respectively.
Meanwhile, Trump, desperate to lower oil prices, has set back any future attack on Iran until after the US midterm elections in early November. But regardless of other justifications for the US withdrawal from RAF Fairford, and the police investigation – which has yet to lead to any charges – the wider Iran threat in the UK is now elevated.
A week ago, two Iranian nationals, Salam Ahmadyan from Liverpool and Rahman Salehi from Salford, were charged with terror offences, accused of trying to target the Jewish community in Manchester with a homemade chlorine powder bomb.
Prosecutors told a magistrates court on Saturday the pair were in contact with a third party, believed to be in Iran, who directed them and sent them “instructions on how to prepare an explosive device”. A trial at the Old Bailey has been scheduled.
Early in May, the US indicted Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, 32, an Iranian-Iraqi dual national, accusing him of promoting and coordinating 18 arson and other low-level terror attacks against Jewish and US sites in the UK and Europe during March and April 2026. He was, the US authorities said, a commander with Kata’ib Hezbollah, an Iraqi group long backed by the IRGC.
The following month, in a Manhattan courtroom, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty and said he was “a prisoner of war”. He faces a terrorism trial, accused in one instance of participating in an arson attack on a synagogue in London via a FaceTime video call. Though nobody was killed in the campaign, al-Saadi is accused of telling an associate that he was engaged in “psychological warfare”.
The group al-Saadi is accused of running, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia (HAYI), also claimed credit for the firebombing of four Jewish community ambulances in north London in postings on social media. Four people pleaded guilty to arson in the case in August, in an attack that caused an estimated £1m of damage. Sentencing and a full airing of the facts in court are not due until next year.
Jonathan Hackett, a former US marine and intelligence specialist, says the threat in the UK and Europe will endure because Tehran believes it serves a purpose, though it will alter depending on who becomes responsible after al-Saadi. “The psychological effects alone are certainly important; the goal is to create a wedge between the US and its allies,” he added.

articles.title: Russia spending huge sums on production of jet-powered drones – military spox
articles.body:
Russia spending huge sums on production of jet-powered drones – military spox
Air Force spokesman Yuriy Ignat said this in a televised interview, answering a question about whether there are grounds to believe that Russia’s capacity to produce jet-powered drones is ultimately limited, Ukrinform reports.
“The issue here is capacity. It is about producing them, and about the fact that Russia has the money to manufacture these expensive drones. The drones are not cheap; they have a jet engine, which is one of the most expensive components. And the enemy is spending huge sums on these systems,” Ignat said.
He noted that considerable work is currently underway on jet-powered UAV interceptors.
“You can see that other systems, such as the ‘Turrets,’ are also appearing. We are also counting on an aviation component which – I will not disclose the details – could also strengthen the protection of our skies against this threat,” the spokesman said.
He stressed that assistance from Ukraine’s partners is extremely important.
“We have air defense personnel who, under limited conditions, can … do anything. The only thing we lack is the equipment, because the enemy is increasing its capabilities. Every month, the number of jet-powered UAVs used against Ukraine is increasing, as is the number of ‘Banderols,’” Ignat said.
The spokesman explained that despite having the best human resources – experienced people who are dedicated to their work and defenders of the skies – Ukraine simply needs the appropriate equipment.
Speaking about increased production of surface-to-air guided missiles and air-launched missiles in Europe, he said that any quantity of air-defense equipment that a particular country can provide is extremely important for Ukraine, especially now.
“And, of course, I have already said that Russia has the ability, in economic terms, to manufacture expensive UAVs and expensive missiles. This, of course, also involves sanctions and so on. Ukraine is, so to speak, doing its homework. These are our long-range sanctions; these are Russian oil refineries going up in flames, so that [the Russians] can sell less diesel fuel, and so on,” Ignat said.
The spokesman noted that Ukraine would also like to see an adequate response from its partners and stronger sanctions pressure on Russia in order to reduce Russia’s ability to produce offensive weapons.
As reported, Yuriy Ignat said that the Russians are currently increasing the resolution of cameras on their UAVs and using high-quality materials in them.

articles.title: ‘Better Damn Well Stop’ – Trump Lambasts Kyiv’s Refinery Attacks, Calls for New President in Ukraine
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump defended his diesel deal with Russia, criticized Kyiv’s strikes on Russian refineries, and called for a new president in Ukraine – all a day after he announced the diesel deal on Friday.
Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Trump defended the deal he struck with Russian President Vladimir Putin, and slamming President Volodymyr Zelensky for allegedly wanting to create problems
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“He wants to make problems for the world, for our farmers with diesel,” Trump said, about a month before the US midterm elections, as diesel soars above $6 a gallon.
On Friday, as the Ukrainian delegation met with Trump’s envoys in Miami, Trump announced the deal in Washington after a phone call with Putin, the result being Moscow will “immediately supply” over a million tons of diesel to the world market through 2027.
Zelensky described the delegation’s visit to Miami as a “smokescreen.”
Trump then criticized Zelensky on Saturday, claiming he had chances to “settle this war” but “chooses not to,” before reiterating his 2025 calls for Zelensky’s removal.
“Zelensky could have settled this war many, many times, but he chooses not to,” he told reporters. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
The US has sought to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine since Trump’s return to office in 2025.
Putin’s Vile Chess
While Kyiv has proposed freezing the frontline, Moscow has maintained maximalist demands that amount to Kyiv’s capitulation, including ceding Ukraine’s Donetsk region that Russian forces have failed to capture. Recent Ukrainian advances have also reversed much of Moscow’s 2026 gains.
The diesel deal also came a week before Trump is supposed to enact the recently passed Russian oil sanctions, which would impose 100% tariffs on countries buying Russian oil.
Trump has previously pinned the blame for rising diesel prices on Ukrainian strikes instead of the war in Iran, and prematurely announced a bilateral energy truce between Kyiv and Moscow, where Kyiv said it agrees if Russia stops striking Ukraine’s energy grid, whereas Moscow called Trump’s statement a “good idea” without elaboration.
Energy remains paramount for both sides in the ongoing war. Ukraine’s refinery strikes have forced Russia to ration fuel and cut into its oil revenue, targeting a key source of Moscow’s war chest, while the Kremlin is betting that multiple winters of extensive blackouts will soon break Ukraine.
Under the latest deal, Kyiv is being asked to stop striking Russian refineries, while Washington makes no reciprocal demand that Moscow stop targeting Ukraine’s energy grid.
Kyiv has reportedly vowed not to relent and would keep striking Russian refineries, according to unnamed officials cited by the Financial Times.

articles.title: Houthis defiant after deadly Riyadh airport strike: ‘We’ll keep attacking, don’t fly there’
articles.body:
Yemen's Houthi rebels vowed Sunday to continue enforcing their declared air blockade of neighboring Saudi Arabia, hours after a Houthi missile exploded at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, killing 12 people and wounding 309. 
The rebels renewed their warnings to airlines and passengers as the Saudi capital's main airport remained closed following the unprecedented attack. In an official statement Sunday morning, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned airlines, airport employees and passengers against using Saudi airports or airspace, saying they "serve as theaters of operations for our forces."
In his statement, Saree declared that the Houthis remained determined to enforce the rules they had announced: "Airport for airport, blockade for blockade and escalation for escalation, until our objectives are achieved." He also accused Saudi Arabia of bearing responsibility for the consequences of any failed attempts to intercept missiles launched by the Houthis, urging the public to take the group's warnings seriously. Saree said the Houthis regarded all areas of Saudi Arabia as potential theaters of military operations, except Mecca and Medina, Islam's two holiest cities. His comments followed accusations by Riyadh last month that the Houthis had fired a missile toward Mecca, the destination of the annual Muslim pilgrimage and home to the Kaaba, one of Islam's most sacred sites. The accusation portrayed the rebels as threatening Islam's holy places.
Hours after Saturday's missile attack, flight operations at King Khalid International Airport remained suspended. A source in the Saudi aviation industry told AFP on Sunday morning that the airport was still shut. Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 reported on X that the closure had been extended by another 24 hours, until midnight between Sunday and Monday, Israel time.
According to reports from Saudi Arabia, the Houthi missile exploded in the area housing Terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights. The dead reportedly included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, an American, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Sudanese and a Palestinian. Many of the 309 people wounded were reported to be in serious condition. Reports Sunday morning indicated that hospitals in Riyadh remained filled with casualties from the attack. The strike was the deadliest attack on any Gulf Arab country since the war with Iran began in February.
According to Western sources, information collected following the attack indicates that the missile struck without any advance warning and that no sirens sounded before the impact. The deadly attack came just two days after an earlier Houthi strike on the same airport, in which at least one passenger aircraft, empty at the time, was hit. Three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed in that attack. Several additional attacks targeted airports in Riyadh and the southern Saudi city of Abha earlier last week, killing three more people. The series of attacks marks a new peak in the escalating confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, which has intensified in recent weeks alongside renewed fighting inside Yemen between the rebels and forces loyal to the internationally recognized Yemeni government. Saudi Arabia has supported those government forces with extensive airstrikes on Houthi-controlled territory.
On Saturday, President Donald Trump said the United States could join the fighting and assist Saudi Arabia in conducting strikes against the Yemeni rebels, although he emphasized that no decision had yet been made. Trump subsequently described the Houthi attack on Riyadh as "a terrible thing" and "unacceptable." United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres expressed "deep shock" over the airport attack Sunday morning. Germany also condemned the strike, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described it as "a dangerous escalation."
The Houthis have intensified their attacks on Saudi cities in recent days, increasingly targeting airports as part of a campaign to disrupt the kingdom's aviation industry and effectively close its skies. The rebels say the campaign is retaliation for Saudi airstrikes against Houthi positions in Yemen. At the beginning of last week, the Houthis warned international airlines not to operate in Saudi airspace, declaring it an operational zone for attacks against the kingdom. They said they would not accept responsibility for the consequences if airlines continued to fly there.
The renewed confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia began in July, ending a four-year lull in Yemen's civil war. That conflict erupted in 2014, with Riyadh subsequently intervening in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government. The latest escalation began after the Houthis attempted to break the air blockade imposed on them by Saudi Arabia, against the backdrop of an intensifying war involving Iran, their regional ally. Last month, the Houthis launched a rapid territorial offensive, capturing strategic coastal areas in southwestern Yemen overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The territorial gains strengthened their position along one of the world's most important maritime shipping routes. The Houthis had already demonstrated their ability to attack shipping in the Red Sea using long-range missiles and drones, but their advances on the coast gave them tighter control over movement through the strategic passage. Bab el-Mandeb links the Red Sea and Suez Canal shipping route between Europe and Asia, carrying approximately 12% of global trade.
Its strategic importance, particularly for Saudi Arabia, has increased dramatically because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula during the war with Iran. Early last week, Yemeni government forces aligned with Riyadh launched a major ground offensive aimed at driving the Houthis from their newly captured territory and regaining control of Bab el-Mandeb. Saudi Arabia has provided extensive air support for the operation, including heavy bombardment of Houthi-held areas. Reports indicate that pro-Saudi forces have advanced in the area surrounding the strait, although the extent of those gains remains unclear. The Houthis dispute claims by Yemen's internationally recognized government that its forces have already recaptured Bab el-Mandeb, leaving control of the vital waterway contested as the fighting escalates on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula.

articles.title: Major Saudi conferences to proceed despite deadly airport attack
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Major Saudi conferences to proceed despite deadly airport attack
The organisers of two major Saudi energy and investment conferences said their events will go ahead this month and reassured visitors on security, after missile attacks on Riyadh's airport left four people dead and an airliner heavily damaged this week.
The attacks led to widespread flight disruptions, with people taking land routes or circuitous alternative flights. The UK, France and Germany have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh.
Riyadh is sticking to plans to convene global events and trying to draw in investment even amid escalating war with the Iran-backed Houthis in neighbouring Yemen that has seen the kingdom attacked dozens of times over the past weeks.
Organisers of the World Petroleum Congress, set to host top global oil executives and policymakers from Sunday to Thursday, said it would proceed as planned with foreign leaders and ministers in attendance, an email sent to delegates said.
"Your comfort is our priority," it said, noting that alternative routes to Riyadh, including via a four-hour drive from Dammam on the kingdom's eastern coast, were available.
Italian Energy Minister Gilberto Pichetto Fratin on Friday said he would not fly to Riyadh for the International Energy Forum Ministerial Meeting, an event on WPC's sidelines, but would participate via video link.
The Future Investment Initiative, launched by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman as the kingdom's flagship investment conference a decade ago, would also proceed as planned from 26-29 October, organisers said.
"Safety and well-being remain our highest priority," a statement attributed to FII CEO Maha Al Saud said.
"Comprehensive security measures will be in place at Riyadh's airports, our conference venues and official hotels, with coordinated arrangements for participants' transportation," it said.
Chief executives of some of the world's biggest financial institutions such as JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon and Citi's Jane Fraser were on the list of expected attendees. Citi and JPMorgan did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Houthis have said airliners should avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group earlier this month.
Germany's Lufthansa has suspended Riyadh flights through 16 October while Gulf carriers Etihad Airways and Flydubai have cancelled flights to and from the Saudi capital scheduled for 10 October.
Saudi Arabia has responded to Houthi attacks with a wave of strikes on missile launcher sites, vowing to protect the kingdom, and says it has intercepted many ballistic missiles fired by the group.

articles.title: Ukrainian Armed Forces strike on Russia’s missile disposal center may have affected the Kremlin’s strategic programs - Defense Express
articles.body:
Ukrainian Armed Forces strike on Russia’s missile disposal center may have affected the Kremlin’s strategic programs - Defense Express
Kyiv • UNN
The strike on the missile disposal center in the Nizhny Novgorod region may have affected Russia’s arsenal and space projects. The extent of the damage is unknown.
Ukrainian forces struck the Center for the Elimination of Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles in the area of Syrovatikha, Nizhny Novgorod Region, Russia, overnight on October 9. Despite its name, the facility may have played an important role not only in disposing of old missiles, but also in supporting Russia's strategic missile arsenal and ensuring space programs. This is stated in an analysis by Defense Express, reports UNN.
Details
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the enterprise was involved in the production chain for explosives and rocket fuel components. The center was established in 1991 on the basis of a military unit that had previously been engaged in the neutralization and dismantling of missiles.
In the 1990s, the facility disposed of intercontinental ballistic missiles that remained in Russia after the collapse of the USSR. In total, 448 missiles of the R-36 and UR-100N UTTKh types were eliminated there במסגרת international strategic arms reduction agreements.
How the center is connected to the "Satan" missiles and satellite programs
Later, the enterprise acquired additional functions, including maintaining the technical condition of R-36M missiles, known as "Satan" or RS-20 "Voevoda." According to estimates cited by Defense Express, as of 2024 Russia had 34 such missiles.

Although the program was officially closed in 2015, the enterprise continued to participate in supplying liquid-fuel components for other launch vehicles.
Analysts note that such technologies are significant for Russian satellite projects, including "Bureau-1440" and "Yamal," which are viewed as attempts to create their own satellite communications systems similar to Starlink.
Defense Express emphasizes that the strike on this facility is important given its possible role in Russia's rocket and space industry. At the same time, the extent of the enterprise's damage and the actual impact of the strike on Russian programs remain unknown.

articles.title: ‘Stab to the heart’: arrest of German ex-spymaster sparks calls for reform
articles.body:
The ex-spymaster August Hanning once criticised Germany’s own intelligence services as “vegetarians” among prowling carnivores, demanding broader powers to keep the country safe in a treacherous world.
Often described as a “godfather” of Germany’s 21st-century security architecture, Hanning is now charged with treasonous espionage and handing state secrets to a foreign power in one of the most spectacular alleged intelligence breaches of the postwar period.
If true, Hanning may have irreparably damaged Germany’s global security cooperation while exposing grievous internal vulnerabilities, in a tale ripped from a far-fetched political thriller.
“This is an incident that has the potential to escalate into a genuine national scandal,” said Konstantin von Notz, a Bundestag member who sits on the parliamentary intelligence supervisory committee.
Von Notz warned of a “devastating” loss of trust among partner countries “whose support we cannot do without in the current extremely tense security situation”.
Tuesday’s scenes from a small town in Germany staggered even seasoned spy watchers: masked commandos led Hanning from his estate in his birthplace, Nordwalde, to a black police van, his familiar bespectacled face framed by neatly combed white hair. His expression was calm and focused, his wrists without handcuffs.
The detention of the 80-year-old, who ran the federal foreign intelligence service (BND) from 1998 to 2005, marked a first in a western democracy given his previous rank, according to experts.
Federal prosecutors believe Hanning ran his former chief of staff, identified only as Manfred D, as a mole at the BND, paying him to spirit out nearly 2,000 documents, at least some of them classified, over 12 years.
He then allegedly exploited the intelligence for clients of the private consulting firm he launched after retiring – a legal business model that drew fierce criticism over the course of a tumultuous week.
Hanning is in pretrial detention and has, through his lawyers, denied passing on confidential documents to foreign powers. If convicted, he could face 10 years in prison.
Many of the compromised files are believed to have been briefing papers prepared for top officials including the chancellor.
The former BND vice-president Arndt Freytag von Loringhoven described the material as the “crown jewels of the BND”, telling Der Spiegel magazine they were “the most important assessments that a BND president provides”.
The explosive case sent allied secret services scrambling to assess the possible damage. A western official told Reuters that US foreign intelligence was included in documents stolen from the BND. The CIA has not commented on the case.
Luca Manns, managing director of the Intelligence Services Research Unit at the University of Cologne, called the case a “stab to the heart” of the BND, causing incalculable damage to allied cooperation.
“It won’t be an abrupt break,” Manns said, predicting a “creeping erosion of partnerships”.
The suspected betrayal could be corrosive within the agencies as well as in public perception, said Dieter Bacher, a historian at the University of Graz in Austria specialising in secret services.
“When the former head of a service does something like this, the implications are, of course, enormous,” he said. “A loss of trust is certainly inevitable. As information from partner services was apparently also involved, the impact on agency ‘business’ is all the greater.”
The news broke in a week in which Germany’s intelligence service directors had testified to parliament about the heightened threat posed by powers including Russia and China.
The BND chief, Martin Jäger, a former ambassador to Ukraine, warned of a possible violent conflict with Moscow, accusing the Kremlin of mounting a “shadow war” of hybrid and drone attacks.
“We sincerely want to be Germany’s first line of defence,” he said.
Jäger was reportedly already aware of Henning’s impending arrest at the time of his testimony, which came weeks after a foiled drone bomb attack that Berlin has blamed on Moscow.
Russia does not appear to be the recipient of Hanning’s alleged activities, according to reports, at least not directly.
Der Spiegel named Azerbaijan and China among the possible clients, claims not confirmed by authorities. Baku has denied involvement, although Hanning served on the board of the German-Azerbaijani Forum “fostering ties” with the authoritarian-run key energy transit country.
Hanning’s primary motive may have been financial.
He sat on the board of failed Latvian bank PNB Banka, which was declared insolvent in 2019. Bild newspaper said Hanning and another member of the supervisory board – reported to be the former Nato secretary general Anders Fogh Rasmussen – were held liable for up to €4m.
Bild reported that Hanning’s pension had been confiscated to service the debt.
The secret services are facing a reform drive long held back by sensitivities over abuses under the Nazi and communist dictatorships. A law due to pass parliament this year would lift many of the restraints imposed during the postwar period.
Manns warned against any call to stop the measures in light of the Hanning case, saying it would “play into the hands of our opponents, who want a weak German foreign service”.
Hanning was the face of German intelligence during a turbulent period of the post-cold war period, overseeing anti-terror strategy after the 9/11 attacks which were planned in part by a cell in Hamburg.
Investigators only learned of his alleged criminal activities while gathering evidence in a separate child kidnapping case involving a steakhouse restaurant dynasty, which he is accused of abetting using his Israeli intelligence contacts.
The treason charges have sparked a range of troubling questions. Were there other moles? How could his espionage have gone undetected so long? Was the classified information passed to third parties? And who will still trust Germany’s intelligence agencies?
The charges against Hanning are hardly the first scandal to rock the country’s secret services in recent years, with high-profile cases involving spying for Russian intelligence and the CIA.
More broadly, the former head of the domestic intelligence service, Hans-Georg Maaßen, has allied himself with hard-right groups and causes, raising doubts about the neutrality of the agency on his watch.
And the former chancellor Gerhard Schröder, once a Social Democratic stalwart and respected economic reformer, has shocked Germans by taking on a string of lucrative Russian corporate jobs since leaving office in 2005 while becoming a close friend of Vladimir Putin, even attending the Kremlin strongman’s 74th birthday celebrations in Moscow this week.
And with the far-right, pro-Russian party Alternative für Deutschland on the brink of power in a German state for the first time since the second world war, authorities are racing to restrict its access to sensitive intelligence.
With criticism mounting of the legions of former senior German officials who cash in on work relating to their previous activities, Von Notz and Manns joined a chorus calling for a lifelong lobbying ban for high-ranking intelligence officers.

articles.title: Japan Ordered Ukrainian Interceptor Drones From SkyFall
articles.body:
The Japan Ministry of Defense has signed a contract to purchase interceptor drones from the Ukrainian company SkyFall.
This was announced by Japanese Defense Minister Shinjirō Koizumi.
He noted that the ministry is currently working to ensure their delivery as soon as possible.

articles.title: Five Russian bombs kill 17 in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia next day after Trump lets Russia ship first 300,000 tonnes of its diesel
articles.body:
A Russian air strike with guided bombs on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia has killed at least 17 people, including three children, according to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has tied the attack to a US decision to let Russian diesel reach world markets without demanding Moscow halt its strikes on Ukraine first.
On 9 October, President Donald Trump said that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to the US and global markets, a further 500,000 tonnes during November, and 1 million tonnes immediately thereafter. The move has already drawn criticism from US lawmakers in both parties.
“Today, Russia expressed its gratitude for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five guided aerial bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram.
Zelenskyy vows to keep hitting refineries
These figures were accurate at the time the post was written. Later, the State Emergency Service reported that the death toll had risen by two. Meanwhile, Zelenskyy stated that Ukraine would not stop striking oil refineries that bring additional revenues for the Kremlin, which spends them on the war.
“There will be responses to Russian attacks. Thank you to everyone who is helping,” Zelenskyy concluded.
According to Zelenskyy, two of the injured are in critical condition, and doctors are fighting to save their lives. Information is also being verified regarding another 12 people who may have been at the strike site.
“Thirteen of our regions came under attack overnight. Residential buildings, infrastructure, and railway facilities have been damaged,” the Ukrainian leader said.
More pressure on Kremlin
Zelenskyy stressed that the latest Russian strikes further demonstrate the need to increase pressure on Russia. In his view, easing restrictions is interpreted by the aggressor as a signal that it can continue the war and attack Ukrainian cities.
“This night provided yet another confirmation that Russia interprets any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly continue fighting and that it can supposedly drop bombs on cities,” he emphasized.
He also noted that Ukraine’s long-range strike capabilities are inflicting such losses on Russia and stressed that Ukraine would respond to Russian attacks.

Putin Reportedly Unable to Land in Moscow as Drones Paralyze Russia’s Capital
Russian leader Vladimir Putin was reportedly unable to land in Moscow on October 9 as a large-scale drone alert paralyzed the capital’s airports, forcing a presidential aircraft returning from Turkmenistan to divert to St. Petersburg. However, it remains unclear whether Putin himself was aboard the diverted plane.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The New York Times on October 9, flight-tracking data from Flightradar24 showed several Russian government aircraft approaching Moscow during widespread airspace restrictions. Some circled near the capital, while others were redirected to alternative airports.
The disruptions followed reports of drones and balloons approaching Moscow, prompting authorities to temporarily suspend flights at all major airports serving the city for several hours.
Among the affected aircraft was an Il-96 presidential jet with registration number 96025. According to flight-tracking records cited by The New York Times, the aircraft departed Turkmenbashi after two other government planes but was unable to complete its scheduled arrival in Moscow.
Instead, the aircraft diverted to St. Petersburg before continuing to the Russian capital later. Putin had previously been photographed disembarking from the same aircraft during his visit to Turkmenistan, where he attended a Commonwealth of Independent States summit.
The Russian Telegram channel Novaya Ploshchad reported that four aircraft belonging to Russia’s Special Flight Detachment, including three returning from Turkmenistan, were forced to perform holding maneuvers near Moscow.
According to the channel, such a disruption involving government aircraft returning from an international visit had not occurred since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
However, it remains unclear whether Putin himself was aboard the aircraft diverted to St. Petersburg. Russian authorities have not officially commented on the incident or confirmed which aircraft carried the Russian leader back to Moscow.
As The New York Times noted, Putin has access to several Il-96-300PU aircraft equipped to function as airborne command centers, including during a nuclear emergency.
Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned on September 1 that Russian airspace was becoming increasingly unsafe for aviation due to ongoing drone activity. He said the war launched by Moscow was effectively closing its own skies, even as Russian authorities failed to adequately warn international airlines about the risks.

articles.title: Airport Strike Kills 12, Saudi Coalition Vows ‘Decisive’ Response
articles.body:
The deadliest strike on Saudi soil in more than a decade killed 12 people at Riyadh’s international airport and wounded hundreds, prompting the Saudi-led coalition to vow on Sunday a decisive response against Yemen’s Houthis.
The coalition blamed the Iran-backed group for the strike on King Khalid International Airport, describing it as a “full-fledged war crime” that a diplomatic source attributed to a missile.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The attack came during an unprecedented wave of Houthi strikes on the kingdom since a truce in the group’s long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.
The spiralling violence has raised the possibility of a wider escalation, with US President Donald Trump signalling Washington could join military action against the fighters.
One passenger told AFP they witnessed a strike in the airport’s domestic terminal.
“I was on gate 403,” the witness said. “I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”
Four Saudi citizens were among those killed in the attack, as well as two Bangladeshis, one US citizen, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese, the kingdom’s civil aviation authority said in a statement.
It said some of the 309 wounded were in serious condition.
Operations at the airport were suspended following the attack and authorities said damage assessments were ongoing.
US Destroys 3 Iranian Tankers After Warships Attacked in Gulf
The attack prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors to deal with the “serious emergency situation”, a medical source said.
Two doctors told AFP that several pilgrims headed to Mecca were among the wounded.
Schools in Riyadh switched to remote learning for the second time in a month.
Parents in the capital received emails Sunday seen by AFP, citing an order from the education ministry, saying “all schools in Riyadh will switch to distance learning for the entire week”.
- ‘War crime’ -
“The cowardly terrorist attack by the Terrorist Houthi Militia... which resulted in deaths and injuries among civilian passengers and airport staff, constitutes a full-fledged war crime,” coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Malki said in a statement on X.
Earlier, the coalition said it had intercepted missiles targeting Saudi Arabia and destroyed launch platforms.
The Houthis claimed a series of attacks targeting the airport on Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not immediately take responsibility for any new strikes on Saturday.
Saturday’s attack was the deadliest in the kingdom since May 2015, when a suicide bombing by the Islamic State (IS) jihadist group killed 21 worshippers in a Shia mosque in the eastern Qatif governorate.
The civil war in Yemen flared back to life in July after a four-year, UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen’s government militarily since 2015 and is now being drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbour’s conflict.
Asked on Saturday whether he had changed his mind about joining Saudi strikes on the group, Trump said: “We may.”
He said he would be speaking with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, calling what happened in the kingdom “not acceptable”.
US media outlets have reported that previous Saudi requests for US military assistance in dealing with the Houthis have been rebuffed.
- Precautions -
The US, Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia warned their citizens to avoid the airport.
A senior Western diplomat told AFP that several embassies were banning their staff from using the airport “over the next week”.
Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the “heinous attack” and reaffirmed Islamabad’s commitment to Saudi Arabia’s security under their defence pact.
The latest attack came on the eve of Saudi Arabia’s high-profile convention and entertainment season, which begins this month.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas the group captured last month around the Bab al-Mandab strait, military sources told AFP.
The Yemeni government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis.
The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab al-Mandab area -- a key chokepoint for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping -- but claimed to have repelled them.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

articles.title: Kremlin launches hunt for top executives at European defense companies — FT
articles.body:
Kremlin launches hunt for top executives at European defense companies — FT
According to Ukrinform, the report was published by the Financial Times.
The Financial Times spoke with representatives of five European intelligence agencies, who warned that executives and other senior officials at defense companies have become targets of Kremlin agents.
The newspaper also noted that plots targeting civilian sites in Europe—actions previously considered off-limits even for Russian intelligence services—are becoming part of these plans.
According to the sources, Moscow has also set its sights on executives at smaller companies, particularly those involved in manufacturing drones or their components.
A senior European intelligence official told the FT that the threat to both property and people in Europe had increased.
Several defense industry executives told the newspaper that they had stepped up their personal security measures over the past six months, following specific recommendations from government security services.
Others said they take such precautions only when traveling abroad.
The report states that Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, is largely responsible for these operations.
Intelligence officials said a key feature of Russia's approach was that the campaign did not necessarily require actual assassination attempts to achieve its intended effect.
A European intelligence official concluded that Russia's main objective remained psychological, as making people feel that they could become targets was enough to achieve the desired effect. The official added that Russia wanted people to think twice before doing business with Ukraine.
As Ukrinform previously reported, in 2024, the United States and Germany thwarted a Russian plot to assassinate the CEO of Rheinmetall.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia extends Riyadh airport closure after deadly strike
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia extends Riyadh airport closure after strike kills 12
Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport will remain closed until at least midnight local time on Sunday following a strike that killed 12 people and injured 309 others, the latest in a series of deadly attacks on the Riyadh transport hub.
The closure was extended until midnight local time on Sunday, according to a notice to air missions, or NOTAM, issued by Saudi aviation authorities. Flights have been cancelled or diverted while officials assess damage to the airport.
The Saudi-led coalition blamed Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis for Saturday’s attack. The dead included four Saudis, two Bangladeshis and one person each from the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt. Some of the injured remain in critical condition, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree renewed the group’s warning on Sunday against using Saudi airports. His statement, which exempted Mecca and Medina, described other airports as "potential targets and sites for operations by our forces" and urged airlines, airport workers and travellers to take the warning seriously.
The statement also said Saudi Arabia "bears responsibility for any failed interceptions".
Earlier attacks on the airport this week killed four people and damaged a Saudia aircraft on the ground, according to Saudi authorities. The repeated strikes have made the protection of passengers and airport staff an immediate concern alongside the disruption to flights.
Questions remain over whether those inside the airport received an actionable public warning before Saturday’s strike, and what procedures were in place after the earlier attacks.
Saudi Arabia already operates a National Early Warning Platform. The Saudi Civil Defence says it uses cell-broadcast technology to send emergency messages, accompanied by a distinctive tone, to phones connected to mobile networks in the affected area. Its purpose is to warn the public and explain what action people should take to protect themselves.
That public-alert function is distinct from intercepting an incoming missile -- the questions concern both whether a threat was detected and whether information reached people in time to act.
During Iranian attacks in March, at the onset of the war launched by the US and Israel, residents of Riyadh received Arabic- and English-language messages warning of a "hostile aerial threat" and instructing them to remain indoors or in a safe place away from windows and doors. Reporting on a 18 March incident, however, placed the alerts shortly after explosions were heard.
The Civil Defence also issued mobile warnings for Riyadh and nearby Al-Kharj on 19 September amid escalating Houthi attacks, followed by all-clear messages – showing how the platform has been used during the current escalation.
The attacks come as Riyadh hosts major international energy meetings. The WPC Energy Congress, running from Sunday to Thursday, is proceeding as scheduled, while organisers previously said the Future Investment Initiative would go ahead from October 26 to 29. The latter announcement preceded the latest deadly strike.

articles.title: Zaporizhzhia airstrikes kill 17 as Russia intensifies attacks across Ukraine
articles.body:
Guided aerial bombs struck residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia on Saturday, 10 October, killing at least 17 people, including three children, and injuring at least 18 others, according to Ukrainian officials.
Emergency crews searched damaged apartments, cleared rubble and helped survivors escape as smoke rose over the southern city. Cars were left mangled in the streets and homes were badly damaged, while ambulances ferried the wounded to hospital.
The bombardment came amid escalating Russian strikes across Ukraine, which have killed more than 60 people in four days. Missiles also hit Kyiv on Saturday, injuring four people, according to the capital's mayor.
The attacks followed US President Donald Trump's announcement of a deal to buy Russian diesel, which Kyiv warned could help finance Moscow's war. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of exploiting any easing of economic pressure to continue its attacks. More than four years after the full-scale invasion, both countries remain locked in a prolonged conflict, with little movement along the front line.

articles.title: Kiev pushes back on Trump’s call for a new leader
articles.body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky attends a joint news conference with U.S. President Donald Trump’s Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner outside the Mariinskyi Palace following negotiations in Kyiv, Ukraine, on September 6, 2026. (Getty Images)
Only Russia is responsible for the war in Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 11 as he vowed to press ahead with strikes on Russian oil refineries, despite criticism from U.S. President Donald Trump, who blamed him for high diesel prices and said he should be replaced.
The exchange came as Kiev pressed its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia, with a drone attack on Oct. 11 shutting down a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days.
“Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure,” Zelensky wrote on X.
“It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not want to do so,” he said, adding that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha pushed back on Trump’s comments, writing on X late on Oct. 10 that Zelensky was leading the country through a war for its independence. “He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well,” Sybiha wrote.
Trump said on Oct. 10 it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelensky has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said.
The U.S. president, who on Oct. 9 struck a deal with Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelensky for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war effort.
The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, caused outages across the company’s services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.
“As a result of the drone attack, the infrastructure of Yandex’s data center in Vladimir was damaged. Operations at the data center have been completely halted,” said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel.
A Moscow resident, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had “direct impact” and weren’t just about “convenience.”
“It’s also about work,” he said, adding that they also affected “healthcare and everything else.”
Yandex, often described as Russia’s Google, runs the country’s most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia’s artificial intelligence development.

articles.title: Trump says ‘it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president’ who can ‘make a deal’ with Russia
articles.body:
Berk Kutay Gokmen, Burc Eruygur, and Esra Tekin
10 October 2026•Update: 11 October 2026
- Kyiv's foreign minister says Zelenskyy has Ukrainian people's support, 'they have the right to decide,' adds 'statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well'
US President Donald Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to “get a new president,” accusing President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of repeatedly failing to reach a deal to end the war with Russia.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals that, for some reason, he never does,” Trump said, criticizing the Ukrainian leader.
“I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president,” he added.
Trump also argued that the Russia-Ukraine war – which began in 2022, during Joe Biden’s presidency, before Trump’s second term began – could have been avoided.
“If I were president, you wouldn't have ever had that war. That war would have never started,” he said.
The US president also accused Zelenskyy of missing multiple opportunities to end the conflict.
“Zelenskyy could have settled this war many times, many, many times, and he chooses not to,” Trump said, describing the situation as “very difficult.”
Trump also criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, arguing that attacks on refineries could worsen global fuel shortages and affect American farmers and ranchers.
“We told them, do whatever you want, but don't hit the diesel fuel because there's a big problem. Big shortage,” he said.
‘Better deal’ was available 2 years ago, says Trump
At Joint Base Andrews, Trump continued his criticism of Zelenskyy, telling reporters that the Russia-Ukraine war “could have been solved many times, but for whatever reason Zelensky does not want to make a deal.”
Asserting Russian President Vladimir Putin's willingness to make a deal with Kyiv, Trump said that Zelenskyy “would have been a lot better off and he could have made a much better deal two years ago.”
"President Putin would like to see a settlement strongly and look, he's freeing up a lot of oil for the world," Trump added, referring to a new deal for Russia to sell diesel fuel, which Zelenskyy strongly criticized.
Moscow and Kyiv have stepped up strikes in recent months, targeting each other's logistics centers, ports, and energy infrastructure.
Both countries deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.
Soon after Trump's remarks, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on US social media platform X that Zelenskyy is leading Ukraine in a time of war “for independence, freedom, and dignity.”
"He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support," Sybiha added.

articles.title: Zelensky has gone too far – Musk
articles.body:
Zelensky has gone too far – Musk
Tech billionaire Elon Musk has lashed out at Vladimir Zelensky, siding with President Donald Trump, who has warned that Kiev’s continued attacks on Russian oil refineries are worsening a global fuel crisis and hurting American farmers.
Trump also called for a change of leadership in Kiev, accusing Zelensky of repeatedly rejecting opportunities to end the conflict and deliberately ignoring Washington’s requests.
“We told him, do whatever you want, but don’t hit the diesel fuel, because there’s a big problem, a big shortage. And what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday. “He wants to make problems for the world… for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel.”
“Zelensky has gone too far,” Musk wrote on X on Sunday, directly responding to a White House video of the remarks, which were part of Trump’s broader criticism of Zelensky, including his suggestion that “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
@RapidResponse47 @POTUS Zelensky has gone too far
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 10, 2026
The latest spat erupted after Washington agreed to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports following a phone call between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, a move intended to ease a global fuel shortage that has pushed up prices in the US and elsewhere.
Trump reached a diesel deal with Putin after Zelensky ignored at least half a dozen requests from Washington to stop striking Russian refineries, according to Axios. Zelensky denounced Trump’s move as a “weak decision,” while Ukrainian negotiators left the talks in Miami a day early.
Musk’s criticism carries particular weight given Ukraine’s heavy dependence on Starlink, the satellite internet network operated by his company, SpaceX. Since 2022, tens of thousands of Starlink terminals have been central to Kiev’s battlefield communications, drone operations, and coordination between military units. A complete loss of Starlink access could severely disrupt these capabilities and potentially trigger a major battlefield crisis.
Musk has repeatedly called for a negotiated settlement between Moscow and Kiev, and resisted Kiev’s attempts to expand its use of Starlink for attacks on Russian territory. In 2022, Musk refused to activate the network near Crimea to support a Ukrainian strike on Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, warning that doing so would make SpaceX complicit in a major escalation.
Recently, Zelensky appealed to Trump to persuade Musk to authorize Starlink-guided drone strikes deep inside Russia. He also sought a face-to-face meeting with the billionaire during a visit to Washington in July, but Musk refused, The Atlantic reported, citing a source familiar with the discussions.
“Elon keeps saying it’s time to make a deal,” an associate of former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov told the magazine.
In an apparent effort to court the billionaire’s favor, Zelensky awarded Musk the Order of Freedom, one of Ukraine’s highest state honors, in August, praising his contributions to protecting lives and strengthening Ukrainian-American relations.

articles.title: Russia quietly grows fleet that funds its war: one shell firm in Marshall Islands buys two gas tankers from Chinese and Greek owners
articles.body:
Ukraine has published data on 20 vessels that carry Russian oil and liquefied natural gas or refuel the sanctioned fleet, parts of the logistics network the Kremlin uses to fund its war, Ukraine's Defense Intelligence reports. All 20 are under British or Ukrainian sanctions, and only one faces US restrictions.
Russia’s shadow fleet runs on roughly 500 aging ships of uncertain ownership that dodge sanctions and keep oil money flowing. That seaborne oil trade is worth more than 80 billion euros a year.
The headline vessel is the Russian ship Portovyy, an LNG carrier and floating gas store owned by the sanctioned Gazprom since 2021, according to the agency. On 15 August 2026, it left the Gulf of Finland with Russian LNG for the first time since November 2021, sailing the Northern Sea Route to the Chinese port of Beihai to unload.
Portovyy is now at the Zhoushan Huafeng Shipyard in China, which has been set as the site for its maintenance, intelligence says, an example of the foreign yards Kyiv wants closed to the sanctioned fleet.
Russia buys up gas carriers through shells
Two more gas carriers show how Moscow expanded the fleet in spring 2026 through front companies, intelligence said. The Avacha, once owned by China’s Jovo Energy, was bought by the little-known Tudor Maritime of the Marshall Islands, took the Russian flag in June, and now ships gas from the Arctic LNG 2 project to Beihai.
The Chaivo, formerly owned by Greece’s Maran Gas Maritime, was also bought by Tudor Maritime and moved under the Russian flag in July. Now it carries cargo to Beihai from a floating gas storage facility off Kamchatka, intelligence says.
A call to close the loopholes
Intelligence urged partners to act together: tighten control over sales of commercially owned ships, block servicing of the sanctioned fleet at foreign yards, and cut off the energy revenue that Russia turns into weapons against civilians.
Russia is building ice-class ships at home and, at the same time, widening its shadow fleet through offshore networks. The UK Foreign Office made the same point on 1 October, saying Moscow is assembling a new shadow fleet to keep its gas revenues flowing.

articles.title: Ukrainian Specter EW Systems Pass US Counter-Drone Trials
articles.body:
Ukrainian defense technology company Phantom Defense has demonstrated its Specter family of electronic warfare systems and the Streamhunter video interception platform during the Gauntlet II trials in the US.
According to Militarnyi, during the operational evaluations, Phantom Defense deployed an integrated counter-unmanned aerial vehicle (C-UAV) architecture combining radio-frequency jamming, video signal interception, and an automated command-and-control (C2) interface designed to identify, classify, and neutralize airborne targets.
According to company representatives, all radio-controlled platforms evaluated during the relevant test phase were disrupted by the Ukrainian systems.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Not a single radio-controlled platform passed the tests without being affected by our systems,” Phantom Defense told Militarnyi.
“In various cases, the interference targeted the control channel, video channel, or other elements of the radio link.”
While specific drone models and competing manufacturers involved in the evaluations were not publicly disclosed, US evaluators invited Phantom Defense to participate in subsequent testing cycles and technical demonstrations under the program.
Streamhunter system
The company presented several electronic warfare configurations tailored for varied operational echelons during the US trials.
For fixed positions, the company demonstrated the Specter PRO, a directional and omnidirectional dome-type jamming complex engineered to protect platoon strongpoints, brigade command centers, and critical infrastructure installations from loitering munitions and tactical reconnaissance aircraft.
Interview: Georgian Conductor Nikoloz Rachveli on Music, Ukraine and Solidarity
For frontline tactical formations, Phantom Defense evaluated its compact mobile systems – including the Specter L, Specter X, and Specter XL.
These variants are designed for vehicle mounting and dismounted fire teams operating in electronically contested sectors near the forward edge of battle.
The trials also featured Streamhunter, a dedicated signal-interception system capable of capturing and decoding live video feeds transmitted by adversary drones. Data gathered by Streamhunter and the Specter jammers were fed into a unified C2 management system, which provided real-time situational awareness and automated jamming protocols.
Phantom Defense noted that testing inside the US took place under strict regulatory constraints on radio frequency emissions, which differed from the operational parameters encountered under electronic warfare conditions in Ukraine.
The manufacturer reported that its equipment has an established combat record in Ukraine, with company-tracked systems recording the detection of more than 11,000 reconnaissance and strike drones and confirming more than 7,000 video-verified neutralizations.
Pentagon’s Drone Dominance program
The evaluations form part of Gauntlet II, an assessment stage within the US Department of Defense’s $1 billion Drone Dominance program. The initiative aims to procure small unmanned aircraft and counter-drone systems over a two-year timeframe, with projected acquisitions exceeding 200,000 units through 2027.
The participation of Phantom Defense highlights expanding technical collaboration between the Ukrainian defense-industrial sector and the US armed forces.
In a related procurement under the Drone Dominance initiative, the US military ordered an additional 1,320 F10 combat strike drones from Ukrainian manufacturer F-Drones, extending the first commercial export of Ukrainian-produced strike drones to the Pentagon.
The contract followed an initial batch of 2,000 F10 drones shipped to US defense authorities in July under an official permit issued by Ukraine’s State Export Control Service.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis warn passengers not to use Saudi airports
articles.body:
Yemen's Houthis warn passengers not to use Saudi airports
October 11, 2026
Yemen's Houthi rebels on Sunday warned passengers not to use airports in Saudi Arabia, a day after a deadly missile attack on Riyadh airport.
The attack, which killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300, is the deadliest on any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war.
"The Yemeni armed forces renew their warning to all aviation and navigation companies, experts, staff, workers, and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on X.
"The airports and airspace are exposed to targeting and constitute a theater of operations for our forces," he said, adding that the airports of Mecca and Medina, the two holiest cities in Islam, would not be targeted.
The spokesman cautioned that the rebels' warning should be taken "seriously," and that Saudi Arabia "bore responsibility" for failing to intercept the missiles that struck the airport on Saturday.
Operations at Riyadh airport, which has no military facilities, were suspended after Saturday's attack.
Air traffic monitor Flightradar24 said the airport's closure has been extended until at least 9 p.m. Sunday.
What has Saudi Arabia said about the Riyadh airport attack?
Although the Houthis have not formally claimed responsibility, Saudi officials have blamed the Iran-backed rebel group for Saturday's attack on the airport in the Saudi capital.
The Saudi-led coalition, which supports the internationally recognized Yemeni government in its conflict against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, vowed a tough response to the attack, which it labeled a "full-fledged war crime."
Yemeni broadcaster Al Masirah TV, which is run by the Houthis, said Saudi Arabia had struck the international airport in Sanaa on Sunday afternoon.
The Houthi missile strike on Riyadh comes amid a surge in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia this week, which have targeted other airports, military sites and oil infrastructure.
The spike in attacks has followed a major military offensive by the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis.
The rebels, one of Tehran's regional proxies, have been fighting Yemen's government, which is recognized by the international community, since the outbreak of a civil war over a decade ago.
While a truce in 2022 froze the conflict, it failed to secure a lasting peace deal. The US-Israeli war with Iran has seen fighting flare up again in Yemen, worsening an already severe humantiarian crisis.
How has the international community reacted to the Riyadh strikes?
US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he would be speaking to Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in the wake of the attack, which he said was "not acceptable."
Trump also said that the US was "going to look" at potentially joining Saudi strikes against the rebels.
On Sunday, European leaders expressed their "shock" at the attack on Riyadh airport.
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia" as she condemned the "dangerous escalation."
"These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shockwaves sent through the world," von der Leyen said.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul "firmly" condemned what he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation".
"Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he said on X.
The UK's defense secretary Wes Streeting slammed the attacks as "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation," while the French Foreign Ministry condemned the "heinous attack" and stressed its "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia.
Russia, which is a strategic partner of Iran, also condemned the Houthis' attack and called for the hostilities to end "through political and diplomatic means."
Australia, meanwhile, has urged its citizens in the Saudi capital to "shelter in place" amid the escalating attacks.
