articles.title: Russia Plots Assassinations of European Arms Executives
articles.body:
European intelligence agencies have warned executives at defense manufacturing companies across Europe that Russia has intensified plots to assassinate industry leaders in an effort to disrupt military supplies to Ukraine.
Accoring to the Financial Times, citing officials from five European intelligence services, the Kremlin ordered an expansion of hybrid operations and kinetic sabotage across the continent to weaken Western backing for Kyiv.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Intelligence officials stated that targeting European civilians – previously considered an operational line avoided by Russian intelligence – has become an integral component of Moscow’s covert planning.
The warnings indicate that senior defense executives, as well as leaders of smaller enterprises specializing in unmanned aerial vehicles and drone components, have been designated as potential targets for Russian intelligence agents.
In Germany, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) has expanded security consultations with defense contractors, advising senior staff and executive leadership to contract private close-protection details, a BfV official confirmed.
“Russia is engaged in the targeted planning of acts of violence against individuals by state or state-controlled actors,” BfV Vice President Sinan Selen warned German lawmakers.
“We are observing a further evolution of these actions in terms of targets, methods, and the actors involved, notably the use of organized crime structures.”
Can Trump Sidestep Russia Sanctions as the Midterms Loom?
Several European defense executives confirmed to the Financial Times that they have upgraded personal security protocols over the past six months following specific guidance from national security agencies, while others noted they enact specialized protective measures primarily during international travel.
GRU operational methods
Western intelligence assessments attribute primary responsibility for the targeted assassination plots to Russia’s military intelligence directorate, the GRU.
Intelligence officials explained that Russian case officers have increasingly turned to transnational organized crime networks to execute operations.
Rather than relying solely on low-level individuals recruited through online platforms for financial bounties, Russian handlers are structuring specialized cross-border cells that divide surveillance, logistical staging, mission planning, and tactical execution among separate operational layers.
Security officials reported that several active plots have been identified and disrupted before execution. In other instances, security teams detected suspicious surveillance operations tracking the daily routines of targeted defense personnel at private residences and commercial facilities.
Intelligence coordinators stressed that the broader objective of the Russian campaign remains psychological coercion, noting that threats and surveillance alone serve to generate intimidation.
“The primary goal from the Russian perspective is still psychological,” an intelligence official stated. “The mere fact that people feel they might be targeted achieves the desired effect. They want people to think twice before doing business with Ukraine.”
European visa clampdown
The intelligence alerts arrive as European governments and security services move to restrict operational avenues utilized by Russian agents across the EU.
The European Commission is finalizing proposals to tighten Schengen visa regulations for Russian citizens visiting the EU as tourists, aiming to present a legislative package in January following sustained pressure from member states including Sweden, Poland, and Estonia.
Proponents of the measure argue that open travel channels provide hostile intelligence agencies with conduits to conduct surveillance, arson, and industrial sabotage.
Swedish Justice Minister Gunnar Strömmer warned that existing travel frameworks expose the continent to hostile infiltration, stating that the EU must address structural vulnerabilities exploited by foreign adversaries.
Frontline European governments plan to elevate the visa debate during a meeting of the EU Foreign Affairs Council on Monday, Oct. 12, where ministers will also consider travel curbs on accredited Russian diplomats moving between member states.
Estonia has concurrently advocated for an EU-wide entry ban targeting roughly 650,000 former Russian military combatants, warning that individuals with military training could be mobilized by Russian intelligence services to execute sabotage or penetrate European criminal networks.
The intensified security posture across Europe follows widespread investigations into state-sponsored hybrid operations over recent months, including arson attacks against logistics warehouses, GPS jamming affecting regional aviation, and reconnaissance operations directed against critical defense infrastructure.
